Qubit parametrization of the variational discrete action theory for the multiorbital Hubbard model

Zhengqian Cheng and Chris A. Marianetti Affiliation: Department of Applied Physics and Applied Mathematics, Columbia University, New York, NY 10027
August 24, 2026
Abstract

The variational discrete action theory (VDAT) at 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3 is a potent tool for accurately capturing Mott and Hund physics at zero temperature in d=∞d=\infty at a cost comparable to the Gutzwiller approximation, which is recovered by VDAT at 𝒩=2\mathcal{N}=2. Here we develop a qubit parametrization of the gauge constrained algorithm of VDAT at 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3 for the multiorbital Hubbard model with general density-density interactions. The qubit parametrization yields an explicit variational trial energy, and the variational parameters consist of the momentum density distribution, the shape of a reference fermi surface, and the pure state of a qubit system with dimension of the local Hilbert space. To illustrate the power of the qubit parametrization, we solve for the ground state properties of the multiorbital Hubbard model with Hund coupling for local orbital number No​r​b=2−7N_{orb}=2-7. A Taylor series expansion of the partially optimized trial energy is used to explain how the Hund’s coupling changes the order of the Mott transition. For the case of the S​U​(2​No​r​b)SU(2N_{orb}) Hubbard model, an explicit approach for computing the critical UcU_{c} for the Mott transition is provided, yielding an analytical expression for UcU_{c} in the large No​r​bN_{orb} limit. Additionally, we provide an analytical solution for the ground state properties of the single band Hubbard model with a special density of states. Finally, we demonstrate that the qubit parametrization can also be applied to 𝒩=2\mathcal{N}=2, for both G-type and B-type variants, where the G-type yields an identical expression to the slave spin mean-field theory. The qubit parametrization not only improves the efficiency and transparency of VDAT at 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3, but also provides the key advances for the construction of a one-body reduced density matrix functional capable of capturing Mott and Hund physics.

I Introduction

The multiorbital Hubbard model is a minimal model of interacting electrons which accounts for key elements of typical strongly correlated electron systems [34, 24], and the solution in infinite dimensions provides a natural starting point for understanding the solution in finite dimensions [26, 41]. The de facto standard for accurately solving the multiorbital Hubbard model in d=∞d=\infty is the dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) [26, 42, 41, 88], which requires self-consistently solving an effective Anderson impurity model. Therefore, the proficiency of DMFT is determined by the state-of-the-art for quantum impurity solvers [31], which are still extremely limited for the multiorbital case at zero temperature (see introduction of Ref. [12]). Alternatively, the standard for efficiently solving the multi-orbital Hubbard model is the Gutzwiller approximation (GA), which semi-quantitatively describes the Fermi liquid phase and the metal-insulator transition, but only produces a crude description of the insulating phase [60, 70, 7, 4, 6, 44]. A long standing goal has been to improve upon GA while not incurring the computational cost of DMFT. Fortunately, the variational discrete action theory (VDAT) provides an alternate route to the exact ground state properties in d=∞d=\infty [13, 14, 12, 15]. The variational ansatz of VDAT is the sequential product density matrix (SPD), which is characterized by an integer 𝒩\mathcal{N} and as either G-type or B-type, where G-type 𝒩=1\mathcal{N}=1 recovers the Hartree-Fock wave function, G-type 𝒩=2\mathcal{N}=2 recovers the Gutzwiller wave function, and 𝒩→∞\mathcal{N}\rightarrow\infty recovers the exact solution. A remarkable fact is that the G-type 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3 SPD accurately captures Mott and Hund physics in d=∞d=\infty [12, 15], while maintaining a computational cost comparable to the Gutzwiller wave function.

An SPD with arbitrary 𝒩\mathcal{N} can be exactly evaluated in d=∞d=\infty using the self-consistent canonical discrete action theory (SCDA) [13, 14]. There are currently three algorithms for executing VDAT within the SCDA, with the first two being completely general and the third one having some restrictions. The first approach is the most straightforward, requiring iterations over two steps [14]. In the first step, given the variational parameters, the SCDA equations can be self-consistently solved, yielding the energy for the corresponding SPD. In the second step, the variational parameters must be updated to minimize the energy. This straightforward approach was successfully executed on the single band Hubbard model in d=∞d=\infty. The second approach is the decoupled minimization algorithm [12], where one simultaneously minimizes the variational parameters and updates the SCDA equations towards self-consistency. This decoupled minimization algorithm was executed for the G-type 𝒩=2−4\mathcal{N}=2-4 SPD’s in the two orbital Hubbard model with the full rotationally invariant local interactions, demonstrating that 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3 accurately describes Mott and Hund physics over all parameter space. The third approach is the gauge constrained algorithm [15], which was originally applied to the case of a G-type 𝒩=2\mathcal{N}=2 and 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3 SPD with kinetic projectors that are diagonal in momentum space and interacting projectors that do not introduce off-diagonal terms at the single-particle level. The key feature of the gauge constrained algorithm is that the SCDA self-consistency can be automatically satisfied, greatly simplifying the task of minimizing over the variational parameters. Furthermore, the momentum density distribution is used to reparametrize the variational parameters in the kinetic projectors, and the trial energy can be straightforwardly optimized over the momentum density distribution. It is useful to note that the GA can only evaluate a G-type 𝒩=2\mathcal{N}=2 SPD under a Gutzwiller gauge [15]. The SCDA has no such restrictions, which is formally appealing, but imposing certain gauge constraints allows the SCDA self-consistency to be automatically satisfied, while not reducing the variational capacity.

One shortcoming of the original gauge constrained algorithm for the G-type 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3 SPD is that some of the variational parameters are unintuitive and there are two linear constraints on the momentum density distribution per spin-orbital [15]. In this paper, we introduce a new parametrization of the gauge constrained algorithm, referred to as the qubit parametrization, which is mathematically equivalent to the original gauge constrained algorithm and offers several important advantages. First, there is only one linear constraint per spin-orbital on the momentum density distribution, and therefore the number of variational parameters is reduced by one per spin-orbital. Second, the variational parameters are physically intuitive and facilitate a deeper understanding of how the SPD captures Mott and Hund physics. Therefore, the qubit parametrization achieves the long sought goal of resolving the shortcomings of the Gutzwiller approximation while maintaining the computational simplicity and physical appeal. The convenience of the qubit parametrization has allowed for the construction of a one-body reduced density matrix functional for the multi-orbital Hubbard model which exactly encapsulates the VDAT result at 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3, and this is presented in a companion manuscript [1].

It is useful to compare to existing approaches in the literature which seek to achieve our same goal of efficiently and accurately solving the ground state properties of multiorbital Hubbard models. One approach is the ghost Gutzwiller approximation (gGA) [45], which introduces the Gutzwiller wave function in an extended Hilbert space where the GA is then applied, though this comes with a substantial increase in computational cost over the usual GA given that ghost orbitals are introduced. In d=∞d=\infty, the gGA exactly evaluates the Gutzwiller wave function in the extended Hilbert space, and therefore provides an upper bound on the exact energy with increasing accuracy as the extended Hilbert space grows. The gGA has not been proven to converge to the exact solution of the multiorbital Hubbard model with increasing number of ghost orbitals, though numerical evidence suggests that this might be the case [48, 49]. Empirically, it has been demonstrated that at least two ghost orbitals per physical orbital are needed for a global improvement over the GA [45, 49, 48], which substantially increases the computational cost of the gGA relative to GA. Therefore, the important practical comparison between VDAT and gGA contrasts VDAT at 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3 to gGA with two ghost orbitals per physical orbital. VDAT at 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3 has been straightforwardly applied up to the eight orbital Hubbard model [15], while the gGA has been applied up to the three orbital model [63, 49, 29] using exact diagonalization and the five orbital model [50] using density matrix renormalization group (DMRG). The success of the gGA in the multiorbital Hubbard model critically depends on the ability of DMRG or related techniques to approximately obtain a ground state in an expanded local Hilbert space. In terms of accuracy, both approaches appear to be excellent over all parameter space, though it seems possible that VDAT is more adept at capturing subtle differences between competing phases (e.g. compare Fig. 4 in Ref. [12] with Fig. 2 in Ref. [63]).

Another attempt to resolve the limitations of the GA is the slave boson approach [40], which formally recasts the Hubbard model as a Hamiltonian of constrained fermions and auxiliary bosons. The simplest saddle point approximation is typically referred to as slave boson mean-field theory (SBMF), which exactly recovers the GA in the multi-orbital Hubbard model [6] and has extensive applications [47, 36, 5, 20, 73, 35, 9]. Given that the slave boson approach is an exact formalism, there have been various results including fluctuations beyond the mean-field solution [46, 37, 52, 78, 2, 53, 103], though none of these studies address corrections to the ground state properties in the thermodynamic limit. A related idea is the time dependent Gutzwiller approximation [83, 59, 80, 68, 69, 81, 8, 23], which has mainly focussed on computing response functions. One study did demonstrate that the ground state properties of the single orbital Hubbard model can be improved by updating the double occupancy based on the density-density response function [83], but this would be impractical in the multi-orbital Hubbard model, and we are not aware of any such applications. Therefore, neither slave bosons nor time dependent GA has provided a path beyond the GA for ground state properties, though the idea of ghost orbitals has recently been adopted into the slave boson methodology [43], where the saddle point solution recovers the gGA. Another approach related to SBMF is the slave spin approach [21], which recasts the Hubbard model with density-density interactions as a Hamiltonian of constrained fermions and auxiliary spins, and the saddle point approximation also recovers the GA. As in the case of slave bosons, the slave spin approach has produced many interesting results on the multi-orbital Hubbard model [33, 20, 27, 61, 62, 17, 30], but has not offered a path beyond the mean-field solution. In the present work, we demonstrate that the qubit parametrization for a G-type 𝒩=2\mathcal{N}=2 SPD is identical to the slave spin mean field theory (see Appendix B).

Finally, it is useful to discuss the off-shell effective energy theory (OET) [16], which can be reinterpreted through the G-type and B-type SPD for 𝒩=2\mathcal{N}=2. OET introduces an approximation to evaluate the energy under the SPD, known as the central point expansion (CPE), and this is applied to both the G-type and B-type SPD for 𝒩=2\mathcal{N}=2. Though the CPE is intrinsically different than the SCDA, it also exactly evaluates the 𝒩=2\mathcal{N}=2 SPD in d=∞d=\infty, which is proven in the present work (see Appendix C). OET introduces corrections to the CPE for the G-type and B-type SPD, guaranteeing the limiting behaviors for the weak and strong coupling limits, respectively. Subsequently, one evaluates the total energy in both cases and selects the solution with lower energy. OET has yielded accurate results for the single band Hubbard model in d=1d=1, d=2d=2, and d=∞d=\infty. The correction to the CPE becomes far more challenging in the multiorbital Hubbard model, which has not been pursued further. However, a similar idea of empirically correcting the Gutzwiller approximation has been developed in the context of the correlation matrix renormalization approximation [99, 56, 57, 55].

The paper is organized in the following manner. Section II provides an overview of the SPD ansatz, the gauge symmetry of the SPD, the SCDA, and the tensor product representation for evaluating expectation values. Additionally, several methodological generalizations are provided. Section III provides a high level overview of the qubit energy form for the G-type and B-type SPD at 𝒩=2\mathcal{N}=2 and the G-type SPD at 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3. Detailed derivations of the results from Section III are presented in Sections IV, V, and VI. Finally, the qubit energy form is used to examine the multi-orbital Hubbard model at half filling with J/U≥0J/U\geq 0 in Section VII.

II Review of the variational discrete action theory

Here we review several key ingredients of VDAT, including the sequential product density matrix (SPD), the self-consistent canonical discrete action theory (SCDA), and the tensor product representation for evaluating local expectation values within the SCDA. In addition to reviewing these concepts, we generalize the gauge symmetry of the SPD beyond the case of a diagonal transformation, and generalize the tensor product representation to arbitrary 𝒩\mathcal{N}. These developments will facilitate the subsequent analysis in this work.

II.1 The sequential product density matrix

The SPD is the variational ansatz used within VDAT [14, 13], and the SPD is a straightforward generalization of a variational wave function ansatz first articulated in Ref. [22]. In this work, we focus on the multiorbital Hubbard model, given as

H^=H^K+H^l​o​c=∑k​ℓϵk​ℓ​n^k​ℓ+∑i,ℓ<ℓ′Uℓ​ℓ′​n^i​ℓ​n^i​ℓ′,\hat{H}=\hat{H}_{K}+\hat{H}_{loc}=\sum_{k\ell}\epsilon_{k\ell}\hat{n}_{k\ell}+\sum_{i,\ell<\ell^{\prime}}U_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}\hat{n}_{i\ell}\hat{n}_{i\ell^{\prime}}, (1)

where kk and ii denote momentum and real-space site indices, respectively, ℓ=1,…,2​No​r​b\ell=1,\dots,2N_{orb} is the spin-orbital index within a local site, and Uℓ​ℓ′U_{\ell\ell^{\prime}} denotes the Coulomb interaction. In the context of the multiorbital Hubbard model, the SPD with an integer time step 𝒩≥1\mathcal{N\geq}1 is given as

ρ^=K^1​P^1​…​K^𝒩​P^𝒩,\hat{\rho}=\hat{K}_{1}\hat{P}_{1}\dots\hat{K}_{\mathcal{N}}\hat{P}_{\mathcal{N}}, (2)

where K^τ=exp⁡(∑k​ℓγk​ℓ​τ​n^k​ℓ)\hat{K}_{\tau}=\exp\left(\sum_{k\ell}\gamma_{k\ell\tau}\hat{n}_{k\ell}\right) is the kinetic projector, Pτ^=exp⁡(∑i​ΓυΓ​τ​X^i​Γ)\hat{P_{\tau}}=\exp(\sum_{i\Gamma}\upsilon_{\Gamma\tau}\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}) is the interacting projector, τ=1,…,𝒩\tau=1,\dots,\mathcal{N} is the integer time index, the diagonal Hubbard operator X^i​Γ\hat{X}_{i\Gamma} is defined as

X^i​Γ=∏ℓ=12​No​r​bX^i​Γ;ℓ,\displaystyle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}=\prod_{\ell=1}^{2N_{orb}}\hat{X}_{i\Gamma;\ell}, (3)
X^i​Γ;ℓ=(1−n^i​ℓ)​δ0,Γ⁡(ℓ)+n^i​ℓ​δ1,Γ⁡(ℓ),\displaystyle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma;\ell}=\left(1-\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right)\delta_{0,\Gamma\left(\ell\right)}+\hat{n}_{i\ell}\delta_{1,\Gamma\left(\ell\right)}, (4)

and Γ⁡(ℓ)\Gamma\left(\ell\right) is ℓ\ell-th bit in the binary representation of Γ−1\Gamma-1, given as (Γ⁡(1)​…​Γ​(2​No​r​b))2=Γ−1\left(\Gamma\left(1\right)\dots\Gamma\left(2N_{orb}\right)\right)_{2}=\Gamma-1, and Γ=1,…,22​No​r​b\Gamma=1,\dots,2^{2N_{orb}}. It should be noted that in general, P^τ\hat{P}_{\tau} is a direct product of local projectors from all sites while K^τ\hat{K}_{\tau} is a general non-interacting projector. There are two schemes to ensure that the SPD is Hermitian and positive semi-definite, denoted as G-type or B-type [13]. In the following, we will examine both types for 𝒩≤3\mathcal{N}\leq 3. For simplicity, we restrict γk​ℓ​τ\gamma_{k\ell\tau} and υΓ​τ\upsilon_{\Gamma\tau} to be real numbers. It is also useful to reparametrize, up to a constant, the K^τ\hat{K}_{\tau} and Pτ^\hat{P_{\tau}} as

K^τ=∏k​ℓ((1−λk​ℓ​τ)​(1−n^k​ℓ)+λk​ℓ​τ​n^k​ℓ),\displaystyle\hat{K}_{\tau}=\prod_{k\ell}\big((1-\lambda_{k\ell\tau})(1-\hat{n}_{k\ell})+\lambda_{k\ell\tau}\hat{n}_{k\ell}\big), (5)
P^τ=∏i(∑ΓuΓ​τ​X^i​Γ),\displaystyle\hat{P}_{\tau}=\prod_{i}\left(\sum_{\Gamma}u_{\Gamma\tau}\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\right), (6)

where the λk​ℓ​τ\lambda_{k\ell\tau} and uΓ​τu_{\Gamma\tau} are a reparametrization of γk​ℓ​τ\gamma_{k\ell\tau} and υΓ​τ\upsilon_{\Gamma\tau}, and this form is used to derive the qubit parametrization (see Section III).

We first examine the 𝒩=1\mathcal{N}=1 SPD. The G-type SPD for 𝒩=1\mathcal{N}=1 is defined by ρ^G​1=K^1\hat{\rho}_{G1}=\hat{K}_{1}, which is a non-interacting many-body density matrix. If K^1=|Ψ0⟩​⟨Ψ0|\hat{K}_{1}=|\Psi_{0}\rangle\langle\Psi_{0}| where |Ψ0⟩|\Psi_{0}\rangle is a single Slater determinant, then ρ^G​1\hat{\rho}_{G1} corresponds with the Hartree-Fock wave function. Conversely, the B-type SPD for 𝒩=1\mathcal{N}=1 is defined as ρ^B​1=P^1\hat{\rho}_{B1}=\hat{P}_{1}. Normally ρ^B​1\hat{\rho}_{B1} corresponds to a mixed state, but if P^1=|Ψa​t⟩​⟨Ψa​t|\hat{P}_{1}=|\Psi_{at}\rangle\langle\Psi_{at}| with |Ψa​t⟩|\Psi_{at}\rangle defined as a direct product of atomic states from all sites, then ρ^B​1\hat{\rho}_{B1} corresponds to a pure state.

The G-type SPD with 𝒩=2\mathcal{N}=2 is defined as

ρ^G​2=P^1​K^2​P^1†.\hat{\rho}_{G2}=\hat{P}_{1}\hat{K}_{2}\hat{P}_{1}^{\dagger}. (7)

If the center projector is taken as K^2=|Ψ0⟩​⟨Ψ0|\hat{K}_{2}=|\Psi_{0}\rangle\langle\Psi_{0}| with |Ψ0⟩|\Psi_{0}\rangle being a single Slater determinant, then ρ^G​2=|ΨG⟩​⟨ΨG|\hat{\rho}_{G2}=|\Psi_{G}\rangle\langle\Psi_{G}|, where |ΨG⟩=P^1​|Ψ0⟩|\Psi_{G}\rangle=\hat{P}_{1}|\Psi_{0}\rangle is the Gutzwiller wave function (GWF). The B-type SPD for 𝒩=2\mathcal{N}=2 is defined as

ρ^B​2=K^1​P^1​K^1†.\hat{\rho}_{B2}=\hat{K}_{1}\hat{P}_{1}\hat{K}_{1}^{\dagger}. (8)

If the center projector is taken as P^1=|Ψa​t⟩​⟨Ψa​t|\hat{P}_{1}=|\Psi_{at}\rangle\langle\Psi_{at}| with |Ψa​t⟩|\Psi_{at}\rangle defined as a direct product of atomic states from all sites, then ρ^B​2=|ΨB⟩​⟨ΨB|\hat{\rho}_{B2}=|\Psi_{B}\rangle\langle\Psi_{B}| , where |ΨB⟩=exp⁡(∑k​ℓγk​ℓ​n^k​ℓ)​|Ψa​t⟩|\Psi_{B}\rangle=\exp\left(\sum_{k\ell}\gamma_{k\ell}\hat{n}_{k\ell}\right)|\Psi_{at}\rangle and we have previously referred to |ΨB⟩|\Psi_{B}\rangle as the Bearyswil wave-function [14, 13]. However, it should be noted that |ΨB⟩|\Psi_{B}\rangle is distinct from the original Bearyswil wave-function |ΨB′⟩|\Psi^{\prime}_{B}\rangle [3], which is defined as |ΨB′⟩=exp⁡(α​∑k​ℓϵk​ℓ​n^k​ℓ)​|Ψ∞⟩|\Psi^{\prime}_{B}\rangle=\exp\left(\alpha\sum_{k\ell}\epsilon_{k\ell}\hat{n}_{k\ell}\right)|\Psi_{\infty}\rangle, where α\alpha is a variational parameter and |Ψ∞⟩|\Psi_{\infty}\rangle is the fully projected GWF. Though |ΨB′⟩|\Psi^{\prime}_{B}\rangle is technically a special case of a G-type 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3 SPD, which can also be evaluated using the SCDA, it yields the same energy as |ΨB⟩|\Psi_{B}\rangle for the insulating phase in d=∞d=\infty for the multi-orbital Hubbard model (see Section VI.4.3 and Figure 3).

The G-type SPD for 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3 combines the variational power of ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} and ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}, and is defined as

ρ^G​3=K^1​P^1​K^2​P^1†​K^1†.\hat{\rho}_{G3}=\hat{K}_{1}\hat{P}_{1}\hat{K}_{2}\hat{P}_{1}^{\dagger}\hat{K}_{1}^{\dagger}. (9)

If K^2\hat{K}_{2} corresponds to a single Slater determinant |Ψ0⟩|\Psi_{0}\rangle, then ρ^G​3=|ΨG​B⟩​⟨ΨG​B|\hat{\rho}_{G3}=|\Psi_{GB}\rangle\langle\Psi_{GB}|, where |ΨG​B⟩=exp⁡(∑k​ℓγk​ℓ​n^k​ℓ)​P^1​|Ψ0⟩|\Psi_{GB}\rangle=\exp\left(\sum_{k\ell}\gamma_{k\ell}\hat{n}_{k\ell}\right)\hat{P}_{1}|\Psi_{0}\rangle is a mild generalization of the original Gutzwiller-Baeriswyl wave function |ΨG​B′⟩|\Psi^{\prime}_{GB}\rangle introduced by Otsuka (see Eq. (2.3) in Ref. [72]), defined as |ΨG​B′⟩=exp⁡(α​∑k​ℓϵk​ℓ​n^k​ℓ)​P1^​|Ψ0⟩|\Psi^{\prime}_{GB}\rangle=\exp\left(\alpha\sum_{k\ell}\epsilon_{k\ell}\hat{n}_{k\ell}\right)\hat{P_{1}}|\Psi_{0}\rangle, where α\alpha is a variational parameter. Finally, the 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3 B-type SPD is defined as ρ^B​3=P^1​K^2​P^2​K^2†​P^1†\hat{\rho}_{B3}=\hat{P}_{1}\hat{K}_{2}\hat{P}_{2}\hat{K}_{2}^{\dagger}\hat{P}_{1}^{\dagger}. If P^2=|Ψa​t⟩​⟨Ψa​t|\hat{P}_{2}=|\Psi_{at}\rangle\langle\Psi_{at}|, then ρ^B​3=|ΨB​G⟩​⟨ΨB​G|\hat{\rho}_{B3}=|\Psi_{BG}\rangle\langle\Psi_{BG}| where |ΨB​G⟩=P^1​exp⁡(∑k​ℓγk​ℓ​n^k​ℓ)​|Ψa​t⟩|\Psi_{BG}\rangle=\hat{P}_{1}\exp\left(\sum_{k\ell}\gamma_{k\ell}\hat{n}_{k\ell}\right)|\Psi_{at}\rangle and we have previously referred to |ΨB​G⟩|\Psi_{BG}\rangle as the Baeriswyl-Gutzwiller wave-function. However, it should be noted that |ΨB​G⟩|\Psi_{BG}\rangle is distinct from the original Baeriswyl-Gutzwiller wave-function |ΨB​G′⟩|\Psi_{BG}^{\prime}\rangle [22], which is defined as |ΨB​G′⟩=P^1​exp⁡(α​∑k​ℓϵk​ℓ​n^k​ℓ)​|Ψ∞⟩|\Psi^{\prime}_{BG}\rangle=\hat{P}_{1}\exp\left(\alpha\sum_{k\ell}\epsilon_{k\ell}\hat{n}_{k\ell}\right)|\Psi_{\infty}\rangle, where α\alpha is a variational parameter and |Ψ∞⟩|\Psi_{\infty}\rangle is the fully projected GWF. The |ΨB​G′⟩|\Psi^{\prime}_{BG}\rangle is technically a special case of a G-type 𝒩=4\mathcal{N}=4 SPD, which can also be evaluated using the SCDA.

It is useful to understand how the SPD recovers the exact solution with increasing 𝒩\mathcal{N} [13]. The Trotter-Suzuki decomposition [86], given as

e−β​H≈(e−β𝒩​(∑k​ℓϵk​ℓ​n^k​ℓ)​e−β𝒩​(∑i,ℓ<ℓ′Uℓ​ℓ′​n^i​ℓ​n^i​ℓ′))𝒩,e^{-\beta H}\approx\left(e^{-\frac{\beta}{\mathcal{N}}\left(\sum_{k\ell}\epsilon_{k\ell}\hat{n}_{k\ell}\right)}e^{-\frac{\beta}{\mathcal{N}}\left(\sum_{i,\ell<\ell^{\prime}}U_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}\hat{n}_{i\ell}\hat{n}_{i\ell^{\prime}}\right)}\right)^{\mathcal{N}}, (10)

can be considered as a special case of the SPD where the variational parameters are set by the parameters of the Hamiltonian and the temperature. Given that the large 𝒩\mathcal{N} Trotter-Suzuki decomposition recovers the exact finite temperature density matrix, the SPD in the large 𝒩\mathcal{N} limit possesses sufficient variational power to solve the Hamiltonian exactly. However, for a finite 𝒩\mathcal{N}, the SPD leverages the full variational freedom while maintaining the integer time structure, leading to an observed exponential decrease of the energy error with increasing 𝒩\mathcal{N} [14, 12]. In contrast, the energy error for the Trotter-Suzuki decomposition diminishes polynomially with increasing 𝒩\mathcal{N} [86]. This key difference is the basis for the accuracy of the SPD for small 𝒩\mathcal{N}.

Our initial efforts using VDAT have been exactly evaluating the SPD in d=∞d=\infty via the SCDA, and this same approach can be used as a local approximation in finite dimensions. However, there is an existing body of literature which used variational quantum Monte-Carlo (VMC) to evaluate a simplified SPD in the Hubbard model. In the case of ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2}, it is most convenient to execute VMC in real space, which has been used to evaluate the Gutzwiller wave function in the Hubbard model [100, 101, 102]. For 𝒩>2\mathcal{N}>2 in the one and two dimensional Hubbard model, a restricted form of the SPD has been evaluated using quantum Monte-Carlo to solve the single-orbital Hubbard model in two dimensions [72, 89, 93, 94, 39, 90, 91, 96, 98, 92, 85, 51], the pp-dd model [97, 95], and selected molecules [11].

II.2 Gauge Symmetry of the SPD

A important aspect of the SPD is the corresponding gauge symmetry [12, 15], which will prove to be an important tool for reducing the redundancy of the parametrization of the SPD. Consider the general SPD ρ^=K^1​P^1​…​K^𝒩​P^𝒩\hat{\rho}=\hat{K}_{1}\hat{P}_{1}\dots\hat{K}_{\mathcal{N}}\hat{P}_{\mathcal{N}}, where K^τ=exp⁡(𝜸τ⋅𝒏^)\hat{K}_{\tau}=\exp\left(\bm{\gamma}_{\tau}\cdot\hat{\bm{n}}\right) is a kinetic projector and 𝜸⋅𝒏^≡∑ℓ​ℓ′[𝜸]ℓ​ℓ′​[𝒏^]ℓ​ℓ′\boldsymbol{\gamma}\cdot\hat{\boldsymbol{n}}\equiv\sum_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}[\boldsymbol{\gamma}]_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}[\hat{\boldsymbol{n}}]_{\ell\ell^{\prime}} and [𝒏^]ℓ​ℓ′=a^ℓ†​a^ℓ′[\hat{\boldsymbol{n}}]_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}=\hat{a}_{\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{\ell^{\prime}}, and P^τ\hat{P}_{\tau} is a general interacting projector. The essence of the gauge symmetry lies in the fact that only the total product ρ^\hat{\rho} determines physical observables, while there is considerable flexibility in the decomposition of ρ^\hat{\rho} into different time steps and the separation between kinetic and interacting projectors. In order to analyze the gauge symmetry, we utilize the discrete action theory [13], which is a formalism for studying integer time correlation functions of the SPD. The discrete action theory can be seen as a generalization of the many-body Green’s function formalism to the case of integer time, including an integer time Dyson equation given as

𝒈−1−𝟏=(𝒈0−1−𝟏)​𝑺\boldsymbol{g}^{-1}-\boldsymbol{1}=\left(\bm{g}_{0}^{-1}-\boldsymbol{1}\right)\boldsymbol{S} (11)

where 𝒈0\text{$\bm{g}$}_{0} is the non-interacting integer time Green’s functions, 𝒈\bm{g} is the interacting integer time Green’s functions, and 𝑺=exp⁡(−𝚺T)\boldsymbol{S}=\exp(-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{T}) is the exponential form of the integer time self-energy, where 𝚺\boldsymbol{\Sigma} is the integer time self-energy. The integer time Dyson equation recovers the usual Dyson when the SPD is chosen as the Trotter-Suzuki decomposition in the large 𝒩\mathcal{N} limit [13]. The 𝒈0\text{$\bm{g}$}_{0} and 𝒈\bm{g} are naturally defined in the compound space [13] as 𝒈0=⟨$̱\hat{\bm{n}}$⟩$̱\hat{\varrho}$0\text{$\bm{g}$}_{0}=\left\langle\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\bm{n}}$}}\right\rangle_{\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\spdsymb}$}}_{0}} and 𝒈=⟨$̱\hat{\bm{n}}$⟩$̱\hat{\varrho}$\text{$\bm{g}$}=\left\langle\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\bm{n}}$}}\right\rangle_{\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\spdsymb}$}}}, where [$̱\hat{\bm{n}}$]ℓ​τ,ℓ′​τ′=$̱\hat{a}$ℓ†(τ)​$̱\hat{a}$ℓ′(τ′)[\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\bm{n}}$}}]_{\ell\tau,\ell^{\prime}\tau^{\prime}}=\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{a}$}}_{\ell}^{\dagger(\tau)}\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{a}$}}_{\ell^{\prime}}^{(\tau^{\prime})}, the underbar indicates an operator in the compound space, ℓ=1,…,L\ell=1,\dots,L enumerates the spin-orbitals for the entire system, and τ=1,…,𝒩\tau=1,\dots,\mathcal{N} labels the integer time step. The discrete Dyson equation is a matrix equation of dimension of L​𝒩×L​𝒩L\mathcal{N}\times L\mathcal{N}, and it exactly relates the interacting and noninteracting integer time Green’s function via 𝑺\boldsymbol{S}. Given that 𝑺\boldsymbol{S} is more convenient to work with, we refer to 𝑺\boldsymbol{S} as the integer time self-energy for brevity. For the convenience of discussing the gauge transformation of the SPD, it is useful to define several additional quantities

𝑺0=𝑺Q​𝑺K,\displaystyle\bm{S}_{0}=\bm{S}_{Q}\bm{S}_{K}, (12)
𝑺F=𝑺Q​𝑺K​𝑺,\displaystyle\bm{S}_{F}=\bm{S}_{Q}\bm{S}_{K}\bm{S}, (13)

where [𝑺Q]τ​τ′=(−δτ+1,τ′+δτ−𝒩+1,τ′)​𝟏[\boldsymbol{S}_{Q}]_{\tau\tau^{\prime}}=(-\delta_{\tau+1,\tau^{\prime}}+\delta_{\tau-\mathcal{N}+1,\tau^{\prime}})\boldsymbol{1} and [𝑺K]τ​τ′=δτ​τ′​exp⁡(−𝜸τT)\left[\bm{S}_{K}\right]_{\tau\tau^{\prime}}=\delta_{\tau\tau^{\prime}}\exp\left(-\bm{\gamma}_{\tau}^{T}\right) are L×LL\times L matrices. Using these definitions, 𝒈0\bm{g}_{0} and 𝒈\bm{g} can be defined succinctly as

𝒈0=(𝟏+𝑺0)−1,\displaystyle\bm{g}_{0}=\left(\boldsymbol{1}+\bm{S}_{0}\right)^{-1}, (14)
𝒈=(𝟏+𝑺F)−1.\displaystyle\bm{g}=\left(\boldsymbol{1}+\bm{S}_{F}\right)^{-1}. (15)

Generally, there are two types of gauge transformations of the SPD: intra-time-step and inter-time-step. The intra-time-step transformation occurs at the boundary of the kinetic and interacting projector for time step τ\tau in the following way: K^τ→K^τ​exp⁡(𝝁τ⋅𝒏^)\hat{K}_{\tau}\rightarrow\hat{K}_{\tau}\exp\left(\bm{\mu}_{\tau}\cdot\hat{\bm{n}}\right) and P^τ→exp(−𝝁τ⋅𝒏^)P^τ\hat{P}_{\tau}\rightarrow\exp\left(-\bm{\mu}_{\tau}\cdot\hat{\bm{n}}\right)\hat{P}_{\tau}. Since the intra-time-step transformation does not alter the measurement at integer times, 𝒈\bm{g} is invariant to this transformation. However, given that K^τ\hat{K}_{\tau} changes after the intra-time-step transformation, we have 𝑺K′=𝑺K​𝑵a\bm{S}^{\prime}_{K}=\bm{S}_{K}\bm{N}_{a}, where [𝑵a]τ​τ′=δτ​τ′​exp⁡(−𝝁τT)\left[\bm{N}_{a}\right]_{\tau\tau^{\prime}}=\delta_{\tau\tau^{\prime}}\exp\left(-\bm{\mu}_{\tau}^{T}\right), while 𝑺F′=𝑺F\bm{S}^{\prime}_{F}=\bm{S}_{F}. Conversely, the inter-time-step transformation is defined at the boundary of the interacting projector at τ\tau and the kinectic projector at τ+1\tau+1 in the following way: P^τ→P^τexp(−𝝁τ⋅𝒏^)\hat{P}_{\tau}\rightarrow\hat{P}_{\tau}\exp\left(-\bm{\mu}_{\tau}\cdot\hat{\bm{n}}\right) and K^τ+1→exp⁡(𝝁τ⋅𝒏^)​K^τ+1\hat{K}_{\tau+1}\rightarrow\exp\left(\bm{\mu}_{\tau}\cdot\hat{\bm{n}}\right)\hat{K}_{\tau+1}, where 𝝁𝒩≡0\bm{\mu}_{\mathcal{N}}\equiv 0. We first discuss how 𝒈\bm{g} changes under this inter-time-step transformation, and it is useful to note the following identities (for details, see Eqns. (A22) and (A23) in Ref. [13] and Eqns. (A1)-(A4) in Ref. [12])

e−𝝁τ⋅𝒏^a^ℓ†e𝝁τ⋅𝒏^=∑ℓ′[e−𝝁τT]ℓ​ℓ′a^ℓ′†,\displaystyle e^{-\bm{\mu}_{\tau}\cdot\hat{\bm{n}}}\hat{a}_{\ell}^{\dagger}e^{\bm{\mu}_{\tau}\cdot\hat{\bm{n}}}=\sum_{\ell^{\prime}}\left[e^{-\bm{\mu}_{\tau}^{T}}\right]_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}\hat{a}_{\ell^{\prime}}^{\dagger}, (16)
e−𝝁τ⋅𝒏^a^ℓe𝝁τ⋅𝒏^=∑ℓ′a^ℓ′[e𝝁τT]ℓ′​ℓ.\displaystyle e^{-\bm{\mu}_{\tau}\cdot\hat{\bm{n}}}\hat{a}_{\ell}e^{\bm{\mu}_{\tau}\cdot\hat{\bm{n}}}=\sum_{\ell^{\prime}}\hat{a}_{\ell^{\prime}}\left[e^{\bm{\mu}_{\tau}^{T}}\right]_{\ell^{\prime}\ell}. (17)

Using the above two equations, we can determine the transformation 𝒈′=𝑵b​𝒈​𝑵b−1\bm{g}^{\prime}=\bm{N}_{b}\bm{g}\bm{N}_{b}^{-1}, where [𝑵b]τ​τ′=δτ​τ′​exp⁡(−𝝁τT)\left[\bm{N}_{b}\right]_{\tau\tau^{\prime}}=\delta_{\tau\tau^{\prime}}\exp\left(-\bm{\mu}_{\tau}^{T}\right), and correspondingly 𝑺F′=𝑵b​𝑺F​𝑵b−1\bm{S}^{\prime}_{F}=\bm{N}_{b}\bm{S}_{F}\bm{N}_{b}^{-1}. Using the transformation for the kinetic projector, we have 𝑺K′=𝑵~b​𝑺K\bm{S}^{\prime}_{K}=\tilde{\bm{N}}_{b}\bm{S}_{K}, where [𝑵~b]τ​τ′=δτ​τ′​exp⁡(−𝝁τ−1T)\left[\tilde{\bm{N}}_{b}\right]_{\tau\tau^{\prime}}=\delta_{\tau\tau^{\prime}}\exp\left(-\bm{\mu}_{\tau-1}^{T}\right) and 𝝁0≡0\bm{\bm{\mu}}_{0}\equiv 0, and 𝑵~b\tilde{\bm{N}}_{b} can be rewritten as 𝑵~b=𝑺Q−1​𝑵b​𝑺Q\tilde{\bm{N}}_{b}=\bm{S}_{Q}^{-1}\bm{N}_{b}\bm{S}_{Q}. It should be noted that a general gauge transformation includes both intra-time-step and inter-time-step transformations, which can be parametrized by 𝑵a\bm{N}_{a} and 𝑵b\bm{N}_{b}, and the above results can be synthesized as

𝒈′=𝑵b​𝒈​𝑵b−1,\displaystyle\bm{g}^{\prime}=\bm{N}_{b}\bm{g}\bm{N}_{b}^{-1}, (18)
𝑺F′=(𝒈′)−1−1=𝑵b​𝑺F​𝑵b−1,\displaystyle\bm{S}^{\prime}_{F}=\left(\bm{g}^{\prime}\right)^{-1}-1=\bm{N}_{b}\bm{S}_{F}\bm{N}_{b}^{-1}, (19)
𝑺K′=𝑵~b​𝑺K​𝑵a=𝑺Q−1​𝑵b​𝑺Q​𝑺K​𝑵a.\displaystyle\bm{S}^{\prime}_{K}=\tilde{\bm{N}}_{b}\bm{S}_{K}\bm{N}_{a}=\bm{S}_{Q}^{-1}\bm{N}_{b}\bm{S}_{Q}\bm{S}_{K}\bm{N}_{a}. (20)

Moreover, the form of the integer time Dyson equation is invariant after the transformation, which requires

𝑺0​𝑺=𝑺Q​𝑺K​𝑺=𝑺F,\displaystyle\bm{S}_{0}\bm{S}=\bm{S}_{Q}\bm{S}_{K}\bm{S}=\bm{S}_{F}, (21)
𝑺′0​𝑺′=𝑺Q​𝑺K′​𝑺′=𝑺F′.\displaystyle\bm{S^{\prime}}_{0}\bm{S}^{\prime}=\bm{S}_{Q}\bm{S}^{\prime}_{K}\bm{S}^{\prime}=\bm{S}^{\prime}_{F}. (22)

Using Eq. (20), we have

𝑺′0=𝑺Q​𝑺K′=𝑵b​𝑺Q​𝑺K​𝑵a=𝑵b​𝑺0​𝑵a,\displaystyle\bm{S^{\prime}}_{0}=\bm{S}_{Q}\bm{S}^{\prime}_{K}=\bm{N}_{b}\bm{S}_{Q}\bm{S}_{K}\bm{N}_{a}=\bm{N}_{b}\bm{S}_{0}\bm{N}_{a}, (23)

while using Eqns. (23), (19), (21), and (22), we have

𝑺′\displaystyle\bm{S}^{\prime} =(𝑺′0)−1​𝑺F′=(𝑵b​𝑺0​𝑵a)−1​𝑵b​𝑺F​𝑵b−1\displaystyle=\left(\bm{S^{\prime}}_{0}\right)^{-1}\bm{S}^{\prime}_{F}=\left(\bm{N}_{b}\bm{S}_{0}\bm{N}_{a}\right)^{-1}\bm{N}_{b}\bm{S}_{F}\bm{N}_{b}^{-1}
=𝑵a−1​𝑺​𝑵b−1,\displaystyle=\bm{N}_{a}^{-1}\bm{S}\bm{N}_{b}^{-1}, (24)

which can also be directly verified by assuming P^τ\hat{P}_{\tau} is non-interacting. Correspondingly, the non-interacting integer time Green’s function changes as

𝒈0′=(𝟏+𝑺0′)−1=(𝟏+𝑵b​(𝒈0−1−𝟏)​𝑵a)−1.\bm{g}^{\prime}_{0}=\left(\boldsymbol{1}+\bm{S}^{\prime}_{0}\right)^{-1}=\left(\boldsymbol{1}+\bm{N}_{b}\left(\bm{g}_{0}^{-1}-\boldsymbol{1}\right)\bm{N}_{a}\right)^{-1}. (25)

Notice that Eqns. (18)-(25) are exact relations. Within the SCDA [13], 𝓖\bm{\mathcal{G}} will transform similarly to 𝒈0\bm{g}_{0}, where 𝑵a\bm{N}_{a} and 𝑵b\bm{N}_{b} are local. These gauge transformations provide a rigorous theoretical foundation for simplifying the task of achieving self-consistency within the SCDA. Moreover, choosing the appropriate gauge condition will also help to improve the numerical stability when minimizing over the variational parameters.

II.3 Review of the SCDA

The discrete action theory is a formalism designed to study integer time correlation functions of the SPD, and the self-consistent canonical discrete action theory (SCDA) is the integer time analogue of the dynamical mean-field theory [14, 13]. The SCDA exactly evaluates the SPD in infinite dimensions, and can be used as a local approximation for the SPD in finite dimensions. To appreciate the idea of the SCDA, we define the discrete action which encodes the integer time correlation of the SPD as

$̱\hat{\varrho}$=$̱\hat{\varrho}$0​$̱\hat{P}$,\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\spdsymb}$}}=\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\spdsymb}$}}_{0}\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{P}$}}, (26)

where $̱\hat{\varrho}$0=$̱\hat{Q}$​∏τ=1𝒩$̱\hat{K}$τ(τ)\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\spdsymb}$}}_{0}=\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{Q}$}}\prod_{\tau=1}^{\mathcal{N}}\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{K}$}}_{\tau}^{\left(\tau\right)} and $̱\hat{P}$=∏τ=1𝒩$̱\hat{P}$τ(τ)\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{P}$}}=\prod_{\tau=1}^{\mathcal{N}}\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{P}$}}_{\tau}^{\left(\tau\right)} are the non-interacting and interacting parts of the discrete action $̱\hat{\varrho}$, and the underbar denotes operators in the compound space.

The SCDA can be formulated as a scheme to evaluate the kinetic energy and local interacting energy through two self-consistent approximations of $̱\hat{\varrho}$ [12], denoted as $̱\hat{\rho}$K\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{K} and $̱\hat{\rho}$l​o​c\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{loc}, respectively. Within the SCDA, the total energy is given as

⟨$̱\hat{H}$(𝒩)⟩$̱\hat{\varrho}$=⟨$̱\hat{H}$K(𝒩)⟩$̱\hat{\rho}$K+⟨$̱\hat{H}$l​o​c(𝒩)⟩$̱\hat{\rho}$l​o​c,\langle\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{H}$}}^{(\mathcal{N})}\rangle_{\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\spdsymb}$}}}=\langle\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{H}$}}_{K}^{\left(\mathcal{N}\right)}\rangle_{\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{K}}+\langle\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{H}$}}_{loc}^{\left(\mathcal{N}\right)}\rangle_{\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{loc}}, (27)

where $̱\hat{\rho}$K\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{K} and $̱\hat{\rho}$l​o​c\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{loc} are defined as

$̱\hat{\rho}$K\displaystyle\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{K} =$̱\hat{\varrho}$0exp(−ln𝑺T⋅$̱\hat{\bm{n}}$),\displaystyle=\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\spdsymb}$}}_{0}\exp(-\ln\boldsymbol{S}^{T}\cdot\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\bm{n}}$}}), (28)
$̱\hat{\rho}$l​o​c\displaystyle\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{loc} =exp(−ln(𝓖−1−1)T⋅$̱\hat{\bm{n}}$)$̱\hat{P}$,\displaystyle=\exp\left(-\ln\left(\bm{\mathcal{G}}^{-1}-1\right)^{T}\cdot\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\bm{n}}$}}\right)\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{P}$}}, (29)

where 𝓖\bm{\mathcal{G}} is the non-interacting integer time Green’s function for the local canonical discrete action $̱\hat{\rho}$l​o​c\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{loc}. Both 𝑺\bm{S} and 𝓖\bm{\mathcal{G}} are L​𝒩×L​𝒩L\mathcal{N}\times L\mathcal{N} matrices, where LL is the number of spin-orbitals of the entire system. In the SCDA, the key assumption is that 𝑺\bm{S} and 𝓖\bm{\mathcal{G}} are block diagonal in real space clusters, given by [𝑺]i​j=𝑺i​δi​j\left[\bm{S}\right]_{ij}=\bm{S}_{i}\delta_{ij} and [𝓖]i​j=𝓖i​δi​j\left[\bm{\mathcal{G}}\right]_{ij}=\bm{\mathcal{G}}_{i}\delta_{ij} where ii and jj are real space cluster indices. To determine 𝑺i\bm{S}_{i} and 𝓖i\bm{\mathcal{G}}_{i}, we have the following two sets of conditions for each cluster index ii,

  1. 1.

    The integer time Dyson equation, given as

    (𝒈i−1−𝟏)=(𝓖i−1−𝟏)​𝑺i,\left(\boldsymbol{g}_{i}^{-1}-\boldsymbol{1}\right)=\left(\bm{\mathcal{G}}_{i}^{-1}-\boldsymbol{1}\right)\boldsymbol{S}_{i}, (30)

    provides a way to compute 𝑺i\bm{S}_{i} by evaluating $̱\hat{\rho}$l​o​c;i=Tr/i​$̱\hat{\rho}$l​o​c\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{loc;i}=\text{Tr}_{/i}\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{loc}, which can be expressed as

    $̱\hat{\rho}$l​o​c;i=exp(−ln(𝓖i−1−1)T⋅$̱\hat{\bm{n}}$i)$̱\hat{P}$i.\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{loc;i}=\exp\left(-\ln\left(\bm{\mathcal{G}}_{i}^{-1}-1\right)^{T}\cdot\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\bm{n}}$}}_{i}\right)\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{P}$}}_{i}. (31)
  2. 2.

    The self-consistency condition for the local integer time Green’s function, given as

    𝒈i=𝒈i′,\bm{g}_{i}=\bm{g}^{\prime}_{i}, (32)

    where 𝒈i=⟨$̱\hat{\boldsymbol{n}}$i⟩$̱\hat{\rho}$l​o​c\boldsymbol{g}_{i}=\left\langle\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\boldsymbol{n}}$}}_{i}\right\rangle_{\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{loc}} and 𝒈i′=⟨$̱\hat{\boldsymbol{n}}$i⟩$̱\hat{\rho}$K\boldsymbol{g}^{\prime}_{i}=\left\langle\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\boldsymbol{n}}$}}_{i}\right\rangle_{\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{K}}.

It is interesting to examine the sufficiency of Eq. (30) and (32) to determine both 𝓖\bm{\mathcal{G}} and 𝑺\bm{S} by counting the number of unknown entries and equations. We denote the number of sites in the lattice as Ns​i​t​eN_{site} and the number of spin orbitals on site ii as NiN_{i}. The number of unknowns in 𝓖\bm{\mathcal{G}} and 𝑺\bm{S} is 2​∑i=1Ns​i​t​e(Ni​𝒩)22\sum_{i=1}^{N_{site}}\left(N_{i}\mathcal{N}\right)^{2}. For a given ii, the two matrix equations given by Eq. (30) and (32) provide 2​(Ni​𝒩)22\left(N_{i}\mathcal{N}\right)^{2} entries. Therefore, we have a sufficient number of equations to determine 𝓖\bm{\mathcal{G}} and 𝑺\bm{S}.

II.4 The tensor product representation for expectation values under $̱\hat{\rho}$l​o​c;i\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{loc;i}

The key computational cost of implementing the SCDA is to compute local observables under $̱\hat{\rho}$l​o​c;i\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{loc;i}, and a convenient approach was devised for 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3 using a tensor product representation [15]. Here we generalize the tensor product representation to arbitrary 𝒩\mathcal{N}. We assume that the interacting projector has the form P^τ;i=∑Γuτ​i​Γ​X^i​Γ\hat{P}_{\tau;i}=\sum_{\Gamma}u_{\tau i\Gamma}\hat{X}_{i\Gamma} and 𝓖i\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}}_{i} is diagonal in the spin orbital index ℓ\ell, given as [𝓖i]ℓ​ℓ=δℓ​ℓ′​𝒢i,ℓ\left[\bm{\mathcal{G}}_{i}\right]_{\ell\ell}=\delta_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}\mathcal{G}_{i,\ell}, where 𝒢i,ℓ\mathcal{G}_{i,\ell} is an 𝒩×𝒩\mathcal{N\times\mathcal{N}} matrix. For a local operator $̱\hat{O}$ at site ii, the expectation value can be written as

⟨$̱\hat{O}$⟩$̱\hat{\rho}$l​o​c;i=⟨$̱\hat{P}$i​$̱\hat{O}$⟩$̱\hat{\rho}$l​o​c;i,0⟨$̱\hat{P}$i⟩$̱\hat{\rho}$l​o​c;i,0=($̱\hat{O}$)u⋅(⊗τuτ)($̱\hat{1}$)u⋅(⊗τuτ),\langle\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{O}$}}\rangle_{\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{loc;i}}=\frac{\langle\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{P}$}}_{i}\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{O}$}}\rangle_{\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{loc;i,0}}}{\langle\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{P}$}}_{i}\rangle_{\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{loc;i,0}}}=\frac{\left(\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{O}$}}\right)_{u}\cdot\left(\otimes_{\tau}u_{\tau}\right)}{\left(\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{1}$}}\right)_{u}\cdot\left(\otimes_{\tau}u_{\tau}\right)}, (33)

where the non-interacting discrete action for $̱\hat{\rho}$l​o​c;i,0\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{loc;i,0} is given by

$̱\hat{\rho}$l​o​c;i,0=exp(−ln(𝓖i−1−𝟏)T⋅$̱\hat{\bm{n}}$i),\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{loc;i,0}=\exp(-\ln\left(\bm{\mathcal{G}}_{i}^{-1}-\boldsymbol{1}\right)^{T}\cdot\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\bm{n}}$}}_{i}), (34)

where the vector uτ=(uτ​i​1,…,uτ​i​NΓ)u_{\tau}=\left(u_{\tau i1},\dots,u_{\tau iN_{\Gamma}}\right) enumerates over the index Γ\Gamma with NΓN_{\Gamma} as the number of local diagonal Hubbard operators at site ii, the 𝒩\mathcal{N} dimensional tensor ($̱\hat{O}$)u\left(\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{O}$}}\right)_{u} is defined as

[($̱\hat{O}$)u]Γ1,…,Γ𝒩=⟨(∏τ=1𝒩$̱\hat{X}$i​Γτ(τ))​$̱\hat{O}$⟩$̱\hat{\rho}$l​o​c;i,0,\left[\left(\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{O}$}}\right)_{u}\right]_{\Gamma_{1},\dots,\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}}}=\left\langle\left(\prod_{\tau=1}^{\mathcal{N}}\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{X}$}}_{i\Gamma_{\tau}}^{\left(\tau\right)}\right)\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{O}$}}\right\rangle_{\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{loc;i,0}}, (35)

the direct product is defined as [⊗τ=1𝒩uτ]Γ1,…,Γ𝒩=∏τ=1𝒩uτ​i​Γτ\left[\otimes_{\tau=1}^{\mathcal{N}}u_{\tau}\right]_{\Gamma_{1},\dots,\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}}}=\prod_{\tau=1}^{\mathcal{N}}u_{\tau i\Gamma_{\tau}}, and 𝑨⋅𝑩\bm{A}\cdot\bm{B} is the contraction between two 𝒩\mathcal{N}-dimensional tensors as

𝑨⋅𝑩=∑Γ1,…,Γ𝒩[𝑨]Γ1,…,Γ𝒩​[𝑩]Γ1,…,Γ𝒩.\bm{A}\cdot\bm{B}=\sum_{\Gamma_{1},\dots,\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}}}\left[\bm{A}\right]_{\Gamma_{1},\dots,\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}}}\left[\bm{B}\right]_{\Gamma_{1},\dots,\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}}}. (36)

We now consider operators that can be written as a product over the spin orbitals, given as $̱\hat{O}$=∏ℓ$̱\hat{O}$ℓ\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{O}$}}=\prod_{\ell}\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{O}$}}_{\ell}. Assuming that 𝓖i\mathcal{\bm{\mathcal{G}}}_{i} is diagonal in the spin orbital index ℓ\ell, we have

[($̱\hat{O}$)u]Γ1,…,Γ𝒩=∏ℓ=12​No​r​b⟨(∏τ=1𝒩$̱\hat{X}$i​Γτ;ℓ(τ))​$̱\hat{O}$ℓ⟩$̱\hat{\rho}$l​o​c;i,\left[\left(\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{O}$}}\right)_{u}\right]_{\Gamma_{1},\dots,\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}}}=\prod_{\ell=1}^{2N_{orb}}\left\langle\left(\prod_{\tau=1}^{\mathcal{N}}\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{X}$}}_{i\Gamma_{\tau};\ell}^{\left(\tau\right)}\right)\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{O}$}}_{\ell}\right\rangle_{\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{loc;i}}, (37)

where X^i​Γ;ℓ\hat{X}{}_{i\Gamma;\ell} is defined in Eq. (4). Therefore, we can write ($̱\hat{O}$)u\left(\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{O}$}}\right)_{u} as a direct product

($̱\hat{O}$)u=⊗ℓ=12​No​r​b($̱\hat{O}$ℓ)u;ℓ,\left(\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{O}$}}\right)_{u}=\otimes_{\ell=1}^{2N_{orb}}\left(\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{O}$}}_{\ell}\right)_{u;\ell}, (38)

where the direct product is defined as

[⊗ℓ=12​No​r​b𝑴ℓ]Γ1,…,Γ𝒩=∏ℓ=12​No​r​b[𝑴ℓ]Γ1​(ℓ),…,Γ𝒩​(ℓ),\left[\otimes_{\ell=1}^{2N_{orb}}\boldsymbol{M}_{\ell}\right]_{\Gamma_{1},\dots,\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}}}=\prod_{\ell=1}^{2N_{orb}}\left[\boldsymbol{M}_{\ell}\right]_{\Gamma_{1}(\ell),\dots,\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}}(\ell)}, (39)

with ($̱\hat{O}$ℓ)u;ℓ\left(\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{O}$}}_{\ell}\right)_{u;\ell} defined as

[($̱\hat{O}$ℓ)u;ℓ]Γ1​(ℓ),…,Γ𝒩​(ℓ)≡⟨(∏τ=1𝒩$̱\hat{X}$i​Γτ;ℓ(τ))​$̱\hat{O}$ℓ⟩$̱\hat{\rho}$l​o​c;i,0,\left[\left(\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{O}$}}_{\ell}\right)_{u;\ell}\right]_{\Gamma_{1}(\ell),\dots,\Gamma_{\mathcal{N}}(\ell)}\equiv\left\langle\left(\prod_{\tau=1}^{\mathcal{N}}\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{X}$}}_{i\Gamma_{\tau};\ell}^{\left(\tau\right)}\right)\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{O}$}}_{\ell}\right\rangle_{\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{loc;i,0}}, (40)

which only depends [𝓖i]ℓ​ℓ\left[\bm{\mathcal{G}}_{i}\right]_{\ell\ell}. For some cases, there is no interacting projector on a given time step, and the corresponding dimension of ($̱\hat{O}$ℓ)u;ℓ\left(\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{O}$}}_{\ell}\right)_{u;\ell} can be traced out. Moreover, Eq. (33) can be conveniently rewritten into a matrix product for all cases we study, which will be further discussed in Sections IV, V, and VI.

III Overview of the qubit energy form

The SCDA can exactly evaluate an SPD in d=∞d=\infty with arbitrary 𝒩\mathcal{N} via a self-consistent solution, as outlined in Section II, and therefore the total energy can only be numerically evaluated for a given set of variational parameters in general. However, the recently developed gauge constrained SCDA algorithm [15] allows for an explicit evaluation of a G-type SPD with 𝒩≤3\mathcal{N}\leq 3, circumventing the need for self-consistent solution (see Section VI.2 for a review). In the present work, we offer a further refinement of the gauge constrained SCDA by transforming all variational parameters into physically intuitive variables, referred to as the qubit parametrization. Moreover, the qubit parametrization analytically resolves one constraint, reducing the number of variational parameters by one per spin orbital. Given the complexity of deriving the qubit parametrization, we collect all key results in this section, providing a self-contained presentation of all details needed to implement a practical calculation. A G-type and B-type SPD at 𝒩\mathcal{N} will be denoted as ρ^G​𝒩\hat{\rho}_{G\mathcal{N}} and ρ^B​𝒩\hat{\rho}_{B\mathcal{N}}, respectively. For pedagogical purposes, we first present results for ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} and ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2} before finally considering ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3}, illustrating that ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3} can be seen as a unification of ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} and ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}. Detailed derivations of all results for ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2}, ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}, and ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3} are provided in Sections IV, V, and VI, respectively, while explicit applications are presented in Section VII. It should be emphasized that all qubit parametrization results are mathematically identical to corresponding VDAT results.

For the sake of generality, we consider the multiorbital Hubbard Hamiltonian given as

H^=∑k​ℓϵk​ℓ​n^k​ℓ+∑iHl​o​c​({n^i​ℓ}),\hat{H}=\sum_{k\ell}\epsilon_{k\ell}\hat{n}_{k\ell}+\sum_{i}H_{loc}\left(\left\{\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\}\right), (41)

where Hl​o​cH_{loc} is a polynomial function of the local density operators, given as

Hl​o​c​({n^i​ℓ})=\displaystyle H_{loc}\left(\left\{\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\}\right)= ∑ℓcℓ​n^i​ℓ+∑ℓ1​ℓ2cℓ1​ℓ2​n^i​ℓ1​n^i​ℓ2\displaystyle\sum_{\ell}c_{\ell}\hat{n}_{i\ell}+\sum_{\ell_{1}\ell_{2}}c_{\ell_{1}\ell_{2}}\hat{n}_{i\ell_{1}}\hat{n}_{i\ell_{2}}
+∑ℓ1​ℓ2​ℓ3cℓ1​ℓ2​ℓ3n^i​ℓ1n^i​ℓ2n^i​ℓ3+…,\displaystyle+\sum_{\ell_{1}\ell_{2}\ell_{3}}c_{\ell_{1}\ell_{2}\ell_{3}}\hat{n}_{i\ell_{1}}\hat{n}_{i\ell_{2}}\hat{n}_{i\ell_{3}}+\dots, (42)

where cℓ1​…​ℓnc_{\ell_{1}\dots\ell_{n}} are parameters that define the n-body interactions. For a typical Hubbard model, only two-body interactions will be needed.

We begin by defining the local Hilbert space and the corresponding fermionic operators, and the corresponding map to qubit operators via the Jordan-Wigner transformation. For a given site ii, the atomic configurations {|Γ⟩}\{|\Gamma\rangle\} form a complete basis for the local Hilbert space with dimension 22​No​r​b2^{2N_{orb}}, and we use a^ℓ†\hat{a}_{\ell}^{\dagger} and a^ℓ\hat{a}_{\ell} to represent the creation and annihilation operators for spin-orbital ℓ\ell. Then we express the fermionic operators in terms of spin operators via the Jordan-Wigner transformation defined as

a^ℓ†=(∏ℓ′<ℓσ^ℓ′z)​σ^ℓ−,\displaystyle\hat{a}_{\ell}^{\dagger}=\left(\prod_{\ell^{\prime}<\ell}\hat{\sigma}_{\ell^{\prime}}^{z}\right)\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{-}, (43)
a^ℓ=(∏ℓ′<ℓσ^ℓ′z)​σ^ℓ+,\displaystyle\hat{a}_{\ell}=\left(\prod_{\ell^{\prime}<\ell}\hat{\sigma}_{\ell^{\prime}}^{z}\right)\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{+}, (44)
a^ℓ†​a^ℓ=n^ℓ=12​(1−σ^ℓz),\displaystyle\hat{a}_{\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{\ell}=\hat{n}_{\ell}=\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{z}\right), (45)

where σ^ℓ±=(σ^ℓx±i​σ^ℓy)/2\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{\pm}=\left(\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{x}\pm i\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{y}\right)/2 and σ^ℓμ\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{\mu} is defined as

σ^ℓμ=I^2ℓ−1⊗σ^μ⊗I^22​No​r​b−ℓ,\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{\mu}=\hat{I}_{2^{\ell-1}}\otimes\hat{\sigma}^{\mu}\otimes\hat{I}_{2^{2N_{orb}-\ell}}, (46)

where μ∈{x,y,z}\mu\in\{x,y,z\} and σ^μ\hat{\sigma}^{\mu} is a standard 2×22\times 2 Pauli matrix. It should be noted that we choose a convention for the Jordan-Wigner transformation such that |0⟩|0\rangle is associated with |↑⟩|\uparrow\rangle and |1⟩|1\rangle is associated with |↓⟩|\downarrow\rangle. This local Jordan-Wigner transformation can be used to transform the usual Gutzwiller energy form into the qubit energy form, though spin operators will naturally emerge when using the tensor representation of local observables within the SCDA.

We proceed by evaluating the ground state energy under ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2}, where ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} is parametrized as

ρ^G​2=P^​({uΓ})​K^​({nk​ℓ,0})​P^​({uΓ}),\displaystyle\hat{\rho}_{G2}=\hat{P}\left(\{u_{\Gamma}\}\right)\hat{K}\left(\{n_{k\ell,0}\}\right)\hat{P}\left(\{u_{\Gamma}\}\right), (47)
P^​({uΓ})=∏i(∑ΓuΓ​X^i​Γ),\displaystyle\hat{P}\left(\{u_{\Gamma}\}\right)=\prod_{i}\left(\sum_{\Gamma}u_{\Gamma}\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\right), (48)
K^​({nk​ℓ,0})=∏k​ℓ((1−nk​ℓ,0)​(1−n^k​ℓ)+nk​ℓ,0​n^k​ℓ),\displaystyle\hat{K}\left(\{n_{k\ell,0}\}\right)=\prod_{k\ell}\big((1-n_{k\ell,0})(1-\hat{n}_{k\ell})+n_{k\ell,0}\hat{n}_{k\ell}\big), (49)

where the variational parameters {uΓ}\{u_{\Gamma}\} and {nk​ℓ,0}\{n_{k\ell,0}\} are real and nk​ℓ,0∈[0,1]n_{k\ell,0}\in[0,1]. The variational parameters {uΓ}\{u_{\Gamma}\} can be reparametrized as a pure state of an effective 2​No​r​b2N_{orb} qubit system (i.e. a 2​No​r​b2N_{orb} spin 1/21/2 system) characterized by a many-body density matrix 𝝆\bm{\rho}. The total trial energy E⁡(𝝆,{nk​ℓ,0})E(\bm{\rho},\{n_{k\ell,0}\}) for ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} can then be written as

E⁡(𝝆,{nk​ℓ,0})=∑ℓ∫d​k​ϵk​ℓ​nk​ℓ+⟨Hl​o​c​({n^ℓ})⟩𝝆,\displaystyle E(\bm{\rho},\{n_{k\ell,0}\})=\sum_{\ell}\int dk\epsilon_{k\ell}n_{k\ell}+\left\langle H_{loc}\left(\left\{\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\}\right)\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}, (50)
nk​ℓ=⟨n^ℓ⟩𝝆+ξℓ2ξℓ,02​(nk​ℓ,0−⟨n^ℓ⟩𝝆),\displaystyle n_{k\ell}=\left\langle\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}+\frac{\xi_{\ell}^{2}}{\xi_{\ell,0}^{2}}\left(n_{k\ell,0}-\left\langle\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}\right), (51)
ξℓ=12​⟨σ^ℓx⟩𝝆,\displaystyle\xi_{\ell}=\frac{1}{2}\langle\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{x}\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}, (52)
ξℓ,0=⟨n^ℓ⟩𝝆​⟨1−n^ℓ⟩𝝆,\displaystyle\xi_{\ell,0}=\sqrt{\left\langle\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}\left\langle 1-\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}}, (53)

with a constraint for each ℓ\ell

∫d​k​nk​ℓ;0=⟨n^ℓ⟩𝝆.\int dkn_{k\ell;0}=\left\langle\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}. (54)

Here we have taken the continuum limit of the discretized nk​ℓn_{k\ell} and choose the convention ∫𝑑k=1\int dk=1. Equations (50)-(54) give an explicit functional form for the trial energy as a function of the variational parameters. The qubit energy form in Eqns. (50)-(54) is equivalent to a previous result obtained using the slave spin mean-field method [21] (see Appendix B for a detailed comparison). It should be emphasized that Eqns. (50)-(54) are simply a transformation of the SCDA algorithm, and therefore are completely equivalent to the usual Gutzwiller approximation.

We now proceed to study ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}, which is the dual of ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2}, given as

ρ^B​2=K^​({λk​ℓ})​P^​({uΓ})​K^​({λk​ℓ}),\hat{\rho}_{B2}=\hat{K}\left(\{\lambda_{k\ell}\}\right)\hat{P}\left(\{u_{\Gamma}\}\right)\hat{K}\left(\{\lambda_{k\ell}\}\right), (55)

where the variational parameters {uΓ}\{u_{\Gamma}\} and {λk​ℓ}\{\lambda_{k\ell}\} are real and uΓ≥0u_{\Gamma}\geq 0. The qubit parametrization reparametrizes the {uΓ}\{u_{\Gamma}\} and {λk​ℓ}\{\lambda_{k\ell}\} into 𝝆\bm{\rho} and nk​ℓ∈[0,1]n_{k\ell}\in[0,1], where 𝝆\bm{\rho} is a diagonal, positive semi-definite 22​No​r​b×22​No​r​b2^{2N_{orb}}\times 2^{2N_{orb}} matrix and nk​ℓn_{k\ell} is the physical single particle density matrix, yielding the following total energy:

E⁡(𝝆,{nk​ℓ})=∑ℓ∫d​k​ϵk​ℓ​nk​ℓ+⟨Hl​o​c​({n^e​f​f,ℓ})⟩𝝆,\displaystyle E(\bm{\rho},\{n_{k\ell}\})=\sum_{\ell}\int dk\epsilon_{k\ell}n_{k\ell}+\left\langle H_{loc}\left(\left\{\hat{n}_{eff,\ell}\right\}\right)\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}, (56)
n^e​f​f,ℓ=⟨n^ℓ⟩𝝆+Aℓ2ξℓ,02​(n^ℓ−⟨n^ℓ⟩𝝆),\displaystyle\hat{n}_{eff,\ell}=\left\langle\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}+\frac{A_{\ell}^{2}}{\xi_{\ell,0}^{2}}\left(\hat{n}_{\ell}-\left\langle\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}\right), (57)
Aℓ=∫d​k​nk​ℓ​(1−nk​ℓ),\displaystyle A_{\ell}=\int dk\sqrt{n_{k\ell}\left(1-n_{k\ell}\right)}, (58)
ξℓ,0=⟨n^ℓ⟩𝝆​⟨1−n^ℓ⟩𝝆,\displaystyle\xi_{\ell,0}=\sqrt{\left\langle\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}\left\langle 1-\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}}, (59)

with a constraint for each ℓ\ell

∫d​k​nk​ℓ=⟨n^ℓ⟩𝝆.\int dkn_{k\ell}=\left\langle\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}. (60)

It should be noted that the operators n^e​f​f,ℓ\hat{n}_{eff,\ell} and n^ℓ\hat{n}_{\ell} have the same expectation values under 𝝆\bm{\rho}, which is evident from Eq. (57). This energy form provides a minimal description for the Mott insulating state in the multiorbital Hubbard model in d=∞d=\infty, much like the result of the Gutzwiller approximation for the metallic phase.

We now proceed to study ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3}, which combines the variational capacity of both ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} and ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}. The key result of this paper is to recast the previously obtained explicit evaluation of the energy under ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3} into a physically intuitive form which can be viewed as a combination of the variational parameters of the qubit energy form for ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} and ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}. The ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3} is given as

ρ^G​3=\displaystyle\hat{\rho}_{G3}= K^​({λk​ℓ})​P^​({uΓ})​K^​({nk​ℓ,0})\displaystyle\hat{K}\left(\{\lambda_{k\ell}\}\right)\hat{P}\left(\{u_{\Gamma}\}\right)\hat{K}\left(\{n_{k\ell,0}\}\right)
×P^​({uΓ})​K^​({λk​ℓ}),\displaystyle\times\hat{P}\left(\{u_{\Gamma}\}\right)\hat{K}\left(\{\lambda_{k\ell}\}\right), (61)

where the variational parameters {λk​ℓ}\{\lambda_{k\ell}\}, {uΓ}\{u_{\Gamma}\}, and {nk​ℓ,0}\{n_{k\ell,0}\} are real and nk​ℓ;0∈[0,1]n_{k\ell;0}\in[0,1]. As demonstrated in Ref. [15], when K^​({nk​ℓ,0})\hat{K}\left(\{n_{k\ell,0}\}\right) corresponds to a Slater determinant (i.e. nk​ℓ;0=0n_{k\ell;0}=0 or nk​ℓ;0=1n_{k\ell;0}=1), the total energy can be explicitly evaluated, and therefore we follow this condition. Under this restricted form of {nk​ℓ,0}\{n_{k\ell,0}\}, it is useful to introduce the concept of a reference Fermi surface, which delineates the boundary between nk​ℓ;0=0n_{k\ell;0}=0 and nk​ℓ;0=1n_{k\ell;0}=1 throughout the Brillouin zone. We can reparametrize {λk​ℓ}\{\lambda_{k\ell}\} and {uΓ}\{u_{\Gamma}\} in terms of {nk​ℓ}\{n_{k\ell}\} and 𝝆\bm{\rho}, where 𝝆\bm{\rho} is 22​No​r​b×22​No​r​b2^{2N_{orb}}\times 2^{2N_{orb}} matrix corresponding to a pure state of a 2​No​r​b2N_{orb} qubit system and nk​ℓ∈[0,1]n_{k\ell}\in[0,1] is the physical momentum density distribution. The total trial energy is given as

E⁡(𝝆,{nk​ℓ},{nk​ℓ,0})=∑ℓ∫d​k​ϵk​ℓ​nk​ℓ\displaystyle E(\bm{\rho},\{n_{k\ell}\},\{n_{k\ell,0}\})=\sum_{\ell}\int dk\epsilon_{k\ell}n_{k\ell}
+⟨Hl​o​c​({n^e​f​f,ℓ})⟩𝝆,\displaystyle+\left\langle H_{loc}\left(\left\{\hat{n}_{eff,\ell}\right\}\right)\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}, (62)
n^e​f​f,ℓ=fℓ,0+fℓ,x​σ^ℓx+fℓ,z​σ^ℓz,\displaystyle\hat{n}_{eff,\ell}=f_{\ell,0}+f_{\ell,x}\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{x}+f_{\ell,z}\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{z}, (63)

and there are two constraints for each ℓ\ell given as

∫<𝑑k=∫d​k​nk​ℓ=⟨n^ℓ⟩ρ,\int_{<}dk=\int dkn_{k\ell}=\left\langle\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\rangle_{\rho}, (64)

where the symbol << indicates that the integration is over the region where nk​ℓ,0=1n_{k\ell,0}=1 for a given ℓ\ell, and the symbol >> indicates the region where nk​ℓ,0=0n_{k\ell,0}=0. For a given ℓ\ell, the quantities fℓ,0f_{\ell,0}, fℓ,xf_{\ell,x} and fℓ,zf_{\ell,z} are nontrivial analytical functions of the following five variables

nℓ=⟨n^ℓ⟩𝝆,\displaystyle n_{\ell}=\left\langle\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}, (65)
ξℓ=12​⟨σ^ℓx⟩𝝆,\displaystyle\xi_{\ell}=\frac{1}{2}\langle\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{x}\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}, (66)
Δℓ=∫>d​k​nk​ℓ=∫<d​k​(1−nk​ℓ),\displaystyle\Delta_{\ell}=\int_{>}dkn_{k\ell}=\int_{<}dk\left(1-n_{k\ell}\right), (67)
𝒜<ℓ=∫<d​k​nk​ℓ​(1−nk​ℓ),\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{<\ell}=\int_{<}dk\sqrt{n_{k\ell}\left(1-n_{k\ell}\right)}, (68)
𝒜>ℓ=∫>d​k​nk​ℓ​(1−nk​ℓ),\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{>\ell}=\int_{>}dk\sqrt{n_{k\ell}\left(1-n_{k\ell}\right)}, (69)

where 𝝆\bm{\rho} and nk​ℓn_{k\ell} are constrained such that

|ξℓ|≤(1−nℓ)​nℓ−(1−Δℓ)​Δℓ,\left|\xi_{\ell}\right|\leq\sqrt{(1-n_{\ell})n_{\ell}-(1-\Delta_{\ell})\Delta_{\ell}}, (70)

which ensures that fℓ,0f_{\ell,0}, fℓ,xf_{\ell,x} and fℓ,zf_{\ell,z} are real numbers (see Eq. (73)). The explicit functional dependence is given by the following list of equations

ξℓ,0=(1−nℓ)​nℓ,\displaystyle\xi_{\ell,0}=\sqrt{\left(1-n_{\ell}\right)n_{\ell}}, (71)
δ​nℓ=nℓ−12,\displaystyle\delta n_{\ell}=n_{\ell}-\frac{1}{2}, (72)
θℓ=cos−1⁡(ξℓξℓ,02+(Δℓ−1)​Δℓ),\displaystyle\theta_{\ell}=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{\xi_{\ell}}{\sqrt{\xi_{\ell,0}^{2}+\left(\Delta_{\ell}-1\right)\Delta_{\ell}}}\right), (73)
gℓ,12=Δℓ​cot⁡(θℓ),\displaystyle g_{\ell,12}=\Delta_{\ell}\cot\left(\theta_{\ell}\right), (74)
cℓ=1−2​δnℓgℓ,122+nℓ2,\displaystyle c_{\ell}=\sqrt{1-\frac{2\text{$\delta$n}_{\ell}}{g_{\ell,12}^{2}+n_{\ell}^{2}}}, (75)
ϕℓ=tan−1⁡(gℓ,12gℓ,122−ξℓ,02),\displaystyle\phi_{\ell}=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{g_{\ell,12}}{g_{\ell,12}^{2}-\xi_{\ell,0}^{2}}\right), (76)
ϕℓ,0=ϕℓ−θℓ,\displaystyle\phi_{\ell,0}=\phi_{\ell}-\theta_{\ell}, (77)
𝒢ℓ,12=−12​tan⁡(ϕℓ,02),\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{\ell,12}=-\frac{1}{2}\tan\left(\frac{\phi_{\ell,0}}{2}\right), (78)
ℐℓ=gℓ,12​𝒢ℓ,12+nℓ2,\displaystyle\mathcal{I}_{\ell}=g_{\ell,12}\mathcal{G}_{\ell,12}+\frac{n_{\ell}}{2}, (79)
𝒥ℓ=gℓ,122−nℓ​𝒢ℓ,12,\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\ell}=\frac{g_{\ell,12}}{2}-n_{\ell}\mathcal{G}_{\ell,12}, (80)
𝒜<,ℓ′=𝒜<,ℓ+sin⁡(θℓ)​𝒜>,ℓ,\displaystyle\mathcal{A}^{\prime}_{<,\ell}=\mathcal{A}_{<,\ell}+\sin\left(\theta_{\ell}\right)\mathcal{A}_{>,\ell}, (81)
𝒜>,ℓ′=cos⁡(θℓ)​𝒜>,ℓ,\displaystyle\mathcal{A}^{\prime}_{>,\ell}=\cos\left(\theta_{\ell}\right)\mathcal{A}_{>,\ell}, (82)
𝒢ℓ,13=−𝒢ℓ,32=ℐℓ​𝒜>,ℓ′−𝒥ℓ​𝒜<,ℓ′(gℓ,122+nℓ2)​cℓ​sin⁡(θℓ),\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{\ell,13}=-\mathcal{G}_{\ell,32}=\frac{\mathcal{I}_{\ell}\mathcal{A}^{\prime}_{>,\ell}-\mathcal{J}_{\ell}\mathcal{A}^{\prime}_{<,\ell}}{\left(g_{\ell,12}^{2}+n_{\ell}^{2}\right)\sqrt{c_{\ell}\sin\left(\theta_{\ell}\right)}}, (83)
𝒢ℓ,23=−𝒢ℓ,31=ℐℓ​𝒜<,ℓ′+𝒥ℓ​𝒜>,ℓ′(gℓ,122+nℓ2)​cℓ​sin⁡(θℓ),\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{\ell,23}=-\mathcal{G}_{\ell,31}=\frac{\mathcal{I}_{\ell}\mathcal{A}^{\prime}_{<,\ell}+\mathcal{J}_{\ell}\mathcal{A}^{\prime}_{>,\ell}}{\left(g_{\ell,12}^{2}+n_{\ell}^{2}\right)\sqrt{c_{\ell}\sin\left(\theta_{\ell}\right)}}, (84)
iℓ=8​𝒢ℓ,13​𝒢ℓ,234​𝒢ℓ,122+1,\displaystyle i_{\ell}=\frac{8\mathcal{G}_{\ell,13}\mathcal{G}_{\ell,23}}{4\mathcal{G}_{\ell,12}^{2}+1}, (85)
jℓ=4​(𝒢ℓ,132−𝒢ℓ,232)4​𝒢ℓ,122+1,\displaystyle j_{\ell}=\frac{4\left(\mathcal{G}_{\ell,13}^{2}-\mathcal{G}_{\ell,23}^{2}\right)}{4\mathcal{G}_{\ell,12}^{2}+1}, (86)
𝒢ℓ,33=nℓ+jℓ​(gℓ,12−𝒢ℓ,12)−iℓ​δnℓ,\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{\ell,33}=n_{\ell}+j_{\ell}\left(g_{\ell,12}-\mathcal{G}_{\ell,12}\right)-i_{\ell}\text{$\delta$n}_{\ell}, (87)
pℓ=ξℓ​(cot⁡(ϕℓ,0)−2​gℓ,12)−2​δnℓ22​(ξℓ2+δnℓ2),\displaystyle p_{\ell}=\frac{\xi_{\ell}\left(\cot\left(\phi_{\ell,0}\right)-2g_{\ell,12}\right)-2\text{$\delta$n}_{\ell}^{2}}{2\left(\xi_{\ell}^{2}+\text{$\delta$n}_{\ell}^{2}\right)}, (88)
