fℓ,0=𝒢ℓ,33−12​jℓ​csc⁡(ϕℓ,0),\displaystyle f_{\ell,0}=\mathcal{G}_{\ell,33}-\frac{1}{2}j_{\ell}\csc\left(\phi_{\ell,0}\right), (90)
fℓ,z=12​(iℓ​pℓ−jℓ​qℓ),\displaystyle f_{\ell,z}=\frac{1}{2}\left(i_{\ell}p_{\ell}-j_{\ell}q_{\ell}\right), (91)
fℓ,x=12​(iℓ​qℓ+jℓ​pℓ).\displaystyle f_{\ell,x}=\frac{1}{2}\left(i_{\ell}q_{\ell}+j_{\ell}p_{\ell}\right). (92)

Several important points should be noted. First, the {nk​ℓ}\{n_{k\ell}\} only enter the local interaction energy through Δℓ\Delta_{\ell}, 𝒜<ℓ\mathcal{A}_{<\ell}, 𝒜>ℓ\mathcal{A}_{>\ell}, and the constraint ∫d​k​nk​ℓ=nℓ\int dkn_{k\ell}=n_{\ell}. Second, the {nk​ℓ,0}\{n_{k\ell,0}\} only enter the local interaction energy through the regions of integration (i.e. >> and <<) and the constraint ∫d​k​nk​ℓ,0=nℓ\int dkn_{k\ell,0}=n_{\ell}. Third, the operators n^e​f​f,ℓ\hat{n}_{eff,\ell} and n^ℓ\hat{n}_{\ell} have the same expectation values under 𝝆\bm{\rho}, as in the case of the ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}. Finally, it should be clear that evaluating the ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3} has a similar computational cost as compared to ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} and ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}, where the largest computational cost is associated with evaluating the local interaction energy.

In the following, we briefly discuss how to numerically minimize the qubit energy form for ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3}. For a multiorbital Hubbard model with 2​No​r​b2N_{orb} spin-orbitals, the formal variational parameters are {nk​ℓ}\left\{n_{k\ell}\right\}, {nk​ℓ;0}\left\{n_{k\ell;0}\right\}, and 𝝆\bm{\rho} with ℓ=1,…,2​No​r​b\ell=1,\dots,2N_{orb}, and there are two local density constraints per spin orbital (see Eqn. (64)). We choose {nk​ℓ;0}\left\{n_{k\ell;0}\right\} corresponding to the momentum density distribution for the non-interacting Hamiltonian with local density {nℓ}\left\{n_{\ell}\right\}, and therefore {nk​ℓ;0}\left\{n_{k\ell;0}\right\} is determined from {nℓ}\left\{n_{\ell}\right\}. It is important to realize that the local interaction energy ⟨Hl​o​c​({n^e​f​f,ℓ})⟩𝝆\left\langle H_{loc}\left(\left\{\hat{n}_{eff,\ell}\right\}\right)\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}} does not depend on the full details of {nk​ℓ}\{n_{k\ell}\}, but instead only on {nℓ}\left\{n_{\ell}\right\}, {Δℓ},\left\{\Delta_{\ell}\right\}, {𝒜<ℓ}\left\{\mathcal{A}_{<\ell}\right\}, and {𝒜>ℓ}\left\{\mathcal{A}_{>\ell}\right\}. Therefore, for a given spin orbital ℓ\ell, four Lagrange multipliers, a<ℓa_{<\ell}, b<ℓb_{<\ell}, a>ℓa_{>\ell}, and b>ℓb_{>\ell}, can be used to obtain the partially optimized nk​ℓn_{k\ell} as [15]

nk​ℓ|k∈X=12​(aXℓ−ϵk​ℓ(aXℓ−ϵk​ℓ)2+bXℓ2+1),n_{k\ell}\big|_{k\in X}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{a_{\text{X$\ell$}}-\epsilon_{k\ell}}{\sqrt{\left(a_{\text{X$\ell$}}-\epsilon_{k\ell}\right){}^{2}+b_{\text{X$\ell$}}^{2}}}+1\right), (93)

where XX is either << or >>. Interestingly, the optimized nk​ℓn_{k\ell} yields a non-trivial dependence on ϵk​ℓ\epsilon_{k\ell}, in contrast to the Gutzwiller approximation (see Figure 1). There is a local density constraint between {nk​ℓ}\{n_{k\ell}\} and 𝝆\bm{\rho} given by Eqn. (64), and there are two strategies to enforce this. The first strategy is to start from {nk​ℓ}\{n_{k\ell}\}, which are parametrized by 5×2​No​r​b5\times 2N_{orb} variational parameters {nℓ}\{n_{\ell}\}, {a<ℓ}\{a_{<\ell}\}, {a>ℓ}\{a_{>\ell}\}, {b<ℓ}\{b_{<\ell}\} and {b>ℓ}\{b_{>\ell}\}, though only 4×2​No​r​b4\times 2N_{orb} are independent given Eqn. (64). Subsequently, the 𝝆\bm{\rho} can be parametrized by 22​No​r​b−2​No​r​b−12^{2N_{orb}}-2N_{orb}-1 independent variational parameters [15]. Therefore, there are a total of 22​No​r​b+3×2​No​r​b−12^{2N_{orb}}+3\times 2N_{orb}-1 independent variational parameters. This strategy motivates the construction of a one-body reduced density matrix functional, as presented in our companion paper [1]. The second strategy is to start from 𝝆\bm{\rho}, which can be parametrized by 22​No​r​b−12^{2N_{orb}}-1 independent variational parameters, which determines {nℓ}\{n_{\ell}\}. Subsequently, the {Δℓ}\{\Delta_{\ell}\} , {b<ℓ}\{b_{<\ell}\}, and {b>ℓ}\{b_{>\ell}\} are chosen as independent variational parameters, which determines {aX​ℓ}\{a_{X\ell}\}, yielding 22​No​r​b+3×2​No​r​b−12^{2N_{orb}}+3\times 2N_{orb}-1 independent variational parameters. The second strategy allows for a trivial implementation of the inequality constraint among Δℓ\Delta_{\ell}, nℓn_{\ell}, and ξℓ\xi_{\ell} (see Eq. (342)), for a given ℓ\ell, which is very important in practice. In either case, one is left with minimizing over 22​No​r​b+3×2​No​r​b−12^{2N_{orb}}+3\times 2N_{orb}-1 variational parameters, which may be achieved using a variety of standard approaches.

Finally, we summarize the applications that are studied in Section VII.2. Consider the multiorbital Hubbard model with density-density interactions given as

H^l​o​c=U​O^1+(U−2​J)​O^2+(U−3​J)​O^3,\hat{H}_{loc}=U\hat{O}_{1}+\left(U-2J\right)\hat{O}_{2}+\left(U-3J\right)\hat{O}_{3}, (94)

where O^1=∑αδ​n^α↑​δ​n^α↓\hat{O}_{1}=\sum_{\alpha}\delta\hat{n}_{\alpha\uparrow}\delta\hat{n}_{\alpha\downarrow}, O^2=∑α<β,σδ​n^α​σ​δ​n^β​σ¯\hat{O}_{2}=\sum_{\alpha<\beta,\sigma}\delta\hat{n}_{\alpha\sigma}\delta\hat{n}_{\beta\bar{\sigma}}, O^3=∑α<β,σδ​n^α​σ​δ​n^β​σ\hat{O}_{3}=\sum_{\alpha<\beta,\sigma}\delta\hat{n}_{\alpha\sigma}\delta\hat{n}_{\beta\sigma}, and δ​n^α​σ=n^α​σ−12\delta\hat{n}_{\alpha\sigma}=\hat{n}_{\alpha\sigma}-\frac{1}{2}, with the orbital indices α,β\alpha,\beta taking values of 1,…,No​r​b1,\dots,N_{orb} and σ∈{↑,↓}\sigma\in\{\uparrow,\downarrow\}. We consider the special case where ϵk​ℓ\epsilon_{k\ell} is independent of ℓ\ell and has particle-hole symmetry. In this case, we show that Eq. (62) can be optimized over 𝝆\bm{\rho} and {nk​ℓ;0}\{n_{k\ell;0}\}, with the assumption that the optimized nk​ℓ;0n_{k\ell;0} is given as θ⁡(nk​ℓ−nℓ⋆)\theta(n_{k\ell}-n_{\ell}^{\star}) where θ\theta is the Heaviside function and nℓ⋆n_{\ell}^{\star} is chosen such that ∫d​k​nk​ℓ;0=nℓ\int dkn_{k\ell;0}=n_{\ell}, yielding a trial energy purely as a functional of {nk​ℓ}\{n_{k\ell}\} as

E⁡({nk​ℓ})=∑ℓ∫d​k​ϵk​ℓ​nk​ℓ+U​A4​O~​(Δ),E(\{n_{k\ell}\})=\sum_{\ell}\int dk\epsilon_{k\ell}n_{k\ell}+UA^{4}\widetilde{O}\left(\Delta\right), (95)

where O~​(Δ)\widetilde{O}\left(\Delta\right) depends on No​r​bN_{orb} and J/UJ/U, and nk​ℓn_{k\ell} is independent of ℓ\ell and has particle-hole symmetry. Here we have dropped the spin-orbital index ℓ\ell (e. g. Δℓ→Δ\Delta_{\ell}\rightarrow\Delta) and define A=𝒜<+𝒜>A=\mathcal{A}_{<}+\mathcal{A}_{>}. An important result is that O~​(Δ)\widetilde{O}\left(\Delta\right) is non-analytic at Δ=Δc\Delta=\Delta_{c}, which can be used to infer the nature of the Mott transition. For No​r​b>1N_{orb}>1, the O~​(Δ)\tilde{O}\left(\Delta\right) can be numerically represented by a one dimensional spline function [1], while No​r​b=1N_{orb}=1 has an explicit expression which can be derived as

O~​(Δ)={−1−4​d1​(Δ)4​(2−4​Δ)2​Δ2,Δ<Δc−4,Δ≥Δc,\displaystyle\tilde{O}\left(\Delta\right)=\begin{cases}-\frac{1-4d_{1}\left(\Delta\right)}{4(2-4\Delta)^{2}\Delta^{2}},&\Delta<\Delta_{c}\\ -4,&\Delta\geq\Delta_{c}\end{cases}, (96)
d1​(Δ)=14−223Δ2(−4Δ+h2+2)23(4(Δ−1)Δ+(2Δ−1)h1+3)3/2,\displaystyle d_{1}(\Delta)=\frac{1}{4}-\frac{2\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\Delta^{2}\left(-4\Delta+h_{2}+2\right){}^{2}}{3\left(4(\Delta-1)\Delta+(2\Delta-1)h_{1}+3\right){}^{3/2}}, (97)
h1=4​(Δ−1)​Δ+9,\displaystyle h_{1}=\sqrt{4(\Delta-1)\Delta+9}, (98)
h2=4​Δ​(10​Δ+3​h1−10)−6​h1+18,\displaystyle h_{2}=\sqrt{4\Delta\left(10\Delta+3h_{1}-10\right)-6h_{1}+18}, (99)
Δc=16​(3−3).\displaystyle\Delta_{c}=\frac{1}{6}\left(3-\sqrt{3}\right). (100)

The above equations finally deliver a closed form expression for a trial energy which qualitatively and quantitatively captures the Mott transition in the single band Hubbard model at half-filling in d=∞d=\infty, exactly reproducing the VDAT results for a G-type SPD at 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3.

IV Derivation of the qubit energy form for ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2}

In this section, we derive Eq. (50) using several different approaches. In Section IV.1, we review the GA using both a heuristic derivation and the central point expansion (CPE), and convert the standard energy form of the GA to the qubit energy form using the Jordan-Wigner transformation. In Section IV.2, we use the SCDA within the Gutzwiller gauge to evaluate ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2}, and the tensor product representation is used to obtain the qubit energy form.

IV.1 The derivation of the qubit energy form from the GA

In this section, we provide an elementary derivation of the qubit energy form, which consists of two steps. In the first step, we derive the standard form of the GA, using both a heuristic argument and the CPE [16], where the energy is parametrized by {nk​ℓ;0}\left\{n_{k\ell;0}\right\} and ρl​o​c\rho_{loc}, where ρl​o​c\rho_{loc} is the local reduced density matrix of the ansatz, which is a diagonal matrix in the basis of |Γ⟩|\Gamma\rangle. The quasi-particle weight is constructed from ρl​o​c\rho_{loc} and the fermionic creation and annihilation operators. In the second step, we convert the standard form of the GA to the qubit energy form which is parametrized by {nk​ℓ;0}\left\{n_{k\ell;0}\right\} and 𝝆\bm{\rho}, where 𝝆\bm{\rho} is a pure state in a 2​No​r​b2N_{orb}-qubit space, and the quasi-particle weight is constructed from 𝝆\bm{\rho} and the Pauli spin operators.

IV.1.1 Derivation of the GA: a heuristic argument and the CPE

While the Gutzwiller approximation is well known, it is normally applied to the special case where ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} is a pure state. Here we provide a heuristic derivation for a general ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2}. Additionally, we use the CPE to derive the same result from a different perspective. We begin by presenting the heuristic derivation of the GA. First consider the expectation values for the diagonal Hubbard operator X^i​Γ\hat{X}_{i\Gamma} measured under K^2=K^​({nk​ℓ;0})\hat{K}_{2}=\hat{K}\left(\left\{n_{k\ell;0}\right\}\right), given as

⟨X^i​Γ⟩K^2=∏ℓ=1N(δΓℓ,0​(1−nℓ)+δΓℓ,1​nℓ),\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\rangle_{\hat{K}_{2}}=\prod_{\ell=1}^{N}\left(\delta_{\Gamma_{\ell},0}\left(1-n_{\ell}\right)+\delta_{\Gamma_{\ell},1}n_{\ell}\right), (101)

where nℓ=⟨n^i​ℓ⟩K^2n_{\ell}=\left\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{K}_{2}} denotes the local density at a given site ii for the spin orbital ℓ\ell under K^2\hat{K}_{2}. The first assumption of the GA is that the atomic configuration distribution under ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} can be approximated as

⟨X^i​Γ⟩ρ^G​2=uΓ2​⟨X^i​Γ⟩K^2/∑ΓuΓ2​⟨X^i​Γ⟩K^2,\left\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}}=u_{\Gamma}^{2}\left\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\right\rangle_{\hat{K}_{2}}\bigg/\sum_{\Gamma}u_{\Gamma}^{2}\left\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\right\rangle_{\hat{K}_{2}}, (102)

which ignores off-site contributions in K^2\hat{K}_{2}. Additionally, a constraint is applied to P^1\hat{P}_{1} such that the local density is invariant, given as

⟨n^i​ℓ⟩ρ^G​2=⟨n^i​ℓ⟩K^2,\left\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}}=\left\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{K}_{2}}, (103)

which we refer to as the Gutzwiller constraint. The denominator in Eq. (102) ensures that the sum of all expectation values for the diagonal Hubbard operators are normalized. Given that the off-diagonal Hubbard operators have zero expectation value due to the restriction of the SPD used in this study, the expectation values for all diagonal Hubbard operators allow the evaluation of any local observable. The second assumption of the GA lies within the evaluation for the hopping term between two distinct sites. The idea is to break a hopping term like a^i​ℓ†​a^j​ℓ\hat{a}_{i\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{j\ell} into two processes: first annihilating an electron at site jj and then creating an electron at site ii, and the GA assumes the probabilities for the two steps are independent and only depend on the atomic distributions on site ii and jj. The probability of creating or destroying an electron is renormalized by the interacting projector, and the GA assumes this is obtained by counting all relevant one-particle excitation processes as

ℛℓ=∑Γ​Γ′⟨X^i​Γ⟩ρ^G​2​⟨X^i​Γ′⟩ρ^G​2​|⟨Γ′|a^i​ℓ†|Γ⟩|2∑Γ​Γ′⟨X^i​Γ⟩K^2​⟨X^i​Γ′⟩K^2​|⟨Γ′|a^i​ℓ†|Γ⟩|2.\mathcal{R}_{\ell}=\frac{\sum_{\Gamma\Gamma^{\prime}}\sqrt{\left\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}}\left\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma^{\prime}}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}}}\left|\left\langle\Gamma^{\prime}|\hat{a}_{i\ell}^{\dagger}|\Gamma\right\rangle\right|^{2}}{\sum_{\Gamma\Gamma^{\prime}}\sqrt{\left\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\right\rangle_{\hat{K}_{2}}\left\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma^{\prime}}\right\rangle_{\hat{K}_{2}}}\left|\left\langle\Gamma^{\prime}|\hat{a}_{i\ell}^{\dagger}|\Gamma\right\rangle\right|^{2}}. (104)

To simply this expression, we introduce ρl​o​c\rho_{loc} and ρl​o​c;0\rho_{loc;0}, which are defined within the local Hilbert space as

[ρl​o​c]Γ​Γ′=δΓ​Γ′​⟨X^i​Γ⟩ρ^G​2,\displaystyle\left[\rho_{loc}\right]_{\Gamma\Gamma^{\prime}}=\delta_{\Gamma\Gamma^{\prime}}\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}}, (105)
[ρl​o​c;0]Γ​Γ′=δΓ​Γ′​⟨X^i​Γ⟩K^2,\displaystyle\left[\rho_{loc;0}\right]_{\Gamma\Gamma^{\prime}}=\delta_{\Gamma\Gamma^{\prime}}\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\rangle_{\hat{K}_{2}}, (106)

which are matrices of dimension 22​No​r​b×22​No​r​b2^{2N_{orb}}\times 2^{2N_{orb}}, yielding

ℛℓ=Tr​(ρl​o​c​a^ℓ†​ρl​o​c​a^ℓ)Tr​(ρl​o​c;0​a^ℓ†​ρl​o​c;0​a^ℓ).\mathcal{R}_{\ell}=\frac{\text{Tr}\left(\sqrt{\rho_{loc}}\hat{a}_{\ell}^{\dagger}\sqrt{\rho_{loc}}\hat{a}_{\ell}\right)}{\text{Tr}\left(\sqrt{\rho_{loc;0}}\hat{a}_{\ell}^{\dagger}\sqrt{\rho_{loc;0}}\hat{a}_{\ell}\right)}. (107)

The Gutzwiller constraint, Eq. (103), can be rewritten as ⟨n^ℓ⟩ρl​o​c=⟨n^ℓ⟩ρl​o​c;0\langle\hat{n}_{\ell}\rangle_{\rho_{loc}}=\langle\hat{n}_{\ell}\rangle_{\rho_{loc;0}}. Given the second assumption of the GA, the single particle density matrix between two different sites jj and j′j^{\prime} is renormalized as

𝒵ℓ≡⟨a^j​ℓ†​a^j′​ℓ⟩ρ^G​2⟨a^j​ℓ†​a^j′​ℓ⟩K^2=ℛℓ2.\mathcal{Z}_{\ell}\equiv\frac{\langle\hat{a}_{j\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{j^{\prime}\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}}}{\langle\hat{a}_{j\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{j^{\prime}\ell}\rangle_{\hat{K}_{2}}}=\mathcal{R}_{\ell}^{2}. (108)

Combining Eq. (108) with the Gutzwiller constraint, the single particle density matrix for arbitrary jj and j′j^{\prime} is given as

⟨a^j​ℓ†​a^j′​ℓ⟩ρ^G​2=𝒵ℓ​⟨a^j​ℓ†​a^j′​ℓ⟩K^2+δj​j′​(1−𝒵ℓ)​nℓ.\left\langle\hat{a}_{j\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{j^{\prime}\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}}=\mathcal{Z}_{\ell}\left\langle\hat{a}_{j\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{j^{\prime}\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{K}_{2}}+\delta_{jj^{\prime}}\left(1-\mathcal{Z}_{\ell}\right)n_{\ell}. (109)

The momentum density distribution nk​ℓ=⟨a^k​ℓ†​a^k​ℓ⟩ρ^G​2n_{k\ell}=\langle\hat{a}_{k\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{k\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}} can then be computed as

nk​ℓ\displaystyle n_{k\ell} =1Ns​i​t​e​∑j​j′ei​k​(j−j′)​⟨a^j​ℓ†​a^j′​ℓ⟩ρ^G​2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N_{site}}\sum_{jj^{\prime}}e^{ik\left(j-j^{\prime}\right)}\left\langle\hat{a}_{j\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{j^{\prime}\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}} (110)
=𝒵ℓ​nk​ℓ;0+(1−𝒵ℓ)​nℓ,\displaystyle=\mathcal{Z}_{\ell}n_{k\ell;0}+\left(1-\mathcal{Z}_{\ell}\right)n_{\ell}, (111)

where Ns​i​t​eN_{site} is the number of kk-points, a^k†=(1/Ns​i​t​e)​∑jei​k⋅j​a^j†\hat{a}_{k}^{\dagger}=\left(1/\sqrt{N_{site}}\right)\sum_{j}e^{ik\cdot j}\hat{a}_{j}^{\dagger}, and nk​ℓ;0=⟨ak​ℓ†​ak​ℓ⟩K^2n_{k\ell;0}=\langle a_{k\ell}^{\dagger}a_{k\ell}\rangle_{\hat{K}_{2}}. Therefore, the standard form for the total energy per site of the GA is given by

E⁡({nk​ℓ,0},ρl​o​c)=∑ℓ∫d​k​ϵk​ℓ​nk​ℓ+⟨Hl​o​c​({n^ℓ})⟩ρl​o​c,\displaystyle E(\{n_{k\ell,0}\},\rho_{loc})=\sum_{\ell}\int dk\epsilon_{k\ell}n_{k\ell}+\left\langle H_{loc}\left(\left\{\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\}\right)\right\rangle_{\rho_{loc}}, (112)
nk​ℓ=⟨n^ℓ⟩ρl​o​c+ℛℓ2​(nk​ℓ,0−⟨n^ℓ⟩ρl​o​c),\displaystyle n_{k\ell}=\left\langle\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\rangle_{\rho_{loc}}+\mathcal{R}_{\ell}^{2}\left(n_{k\ell,0}-\left\langle\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\rangle_{\rho_{loc}}\right), (113)
ℛℓ=Tr​(ρl​o​c​a^ℓ†​ρl​o​c​a^ℓ)⟨n^ℓ⟩ρl​o​c​⟨1−n^ℓ⟩ρl​o​c,\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\ell}=\frac{\text{Tr}\left(\sqrt{\rho_{loc}}\hat{a}_{\ell}^{\dagger}\sqrt{\rho_{loc}}\hat{a}_{\ell}\right)}{\sqrt{\left\langle\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\rangle_{\rho_{loc}}\left\langle 1-\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\rangle_{\rho_{loc}}}}, (114)

with the density constraint

∫d​k​nk​ℓ;0=⟨n^ℓ⟩ρl​o​c.\int dkn_{k\ell;0}=\left\langle\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\rangle_{\rho_{loc}}. (115)

The variational parameters satisfy nk​l;0∈[0,1]n_{kl;0}\in\left[0,1\right] and ρl​o​c\rho_{loc} is a diagonal positive semi-definite matrix.

We now provide an overview of how to derive Eq. (112) using the CPE (see Appendix C.1). We begin by making several observations about the GA. First, when nk​ℓ;0=nℓn_{k\ell;0}=n_{\ell}, the ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} describes a collection of atoms, and in this case Eq. (112) yields an exact evaluation in any dimension. Second, there is a linear relation between nk​ℓn_{k\ell} and nk​ℓ;0n_{k\ell;0} given by

nk​ℓ−nℓ=𝒵ℓ​(nk​ℓ;0−nℓ).n_{k\ell}-n_{\ell}=\mathcal{Z}_{\ell}\left(n_{k\ell;0}-n_{\ell}\right). (116)

Third, ρl​o​c\rho_{loc} is directly determined by nℓn_{\ell} and {uΓ}\{u_{\Gamma}\}, and is independent of nk​ℓ;0n_{k\ell;0}. Recall that the ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} is defined as ρ^G​2=P^1​K^2​P^1\hat{\rho}_{G2}=\hat{P}_{1}\hat{K}_{2}\hat{P}_{1}, where K^2=K^​({nk​ℓ;0})\hat{K}_{2}=\hat{K}\left(\left\{n_{k\ell;0}\right\}\right) and P^1=P^​({uΓ})\hat{P}_{1}=\hat{P}\left(\left\{u_{\Gamma}\right\}\right). We now introduce K^2⋆=K^({nk​ℓ;0=nℓ})\hat{K}_{2}^{\star}=\hat{K}\left(\left\{n_{k\ell;0}=n_{\ell}\right\}\right), which has the same local density matrix as K^2\hat{K}_{2}, and ρG​2⋆=P^1​K^2⋆​P^1\rho_{G2}^{\star}=\hat{P}_{1}\hat{K}_{2}^{\star}\hat{P}_{1}, which describes a collection of atoms. The {uΓ}\{u_{\Gamma}\} can be reparametrized by the local reduced density matrix ρl​o​c⋆\rho_{loc}^{\star} of ρG​2⋆\rho_{G2}^{\star}, where [ρl​o​c⋆]Γ​Γ′=δΓ​Γ′​⟨X^i​Γ⟩ρG​2⋆\left[\rho_{loc}^{\star}\right]_{\Gamma\Gamma^{\prime}}=\delta_{\Gamma\Gamma^{\prime}}\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\rangle_{\rho_{G2}^{\star}} and is constrained by nℓ=⟨a^ℓ†​a^ℓ⟩ρl​o​c⋆.n_{\ell}=\langle\hat{a}_{\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{\ell}\rangle_{\rho_{loc}^{\star}}. Therefore, nk​ℓn_{k\ell} and ρl​o​c\rho_{loc} are functionals of {nk​ℓ;0}\left\{n_{k\ell;0}\right\} and ρl​o​c⋆\rho_{loc}^{\star}. The CPE amounts to the expansion of observables in terms of {nk​ℓ;0}\{n_{k\ell;0}\} about {nk​ℓ;0=nℓ}\left\{n_{k\ell;0}=n_{\ell}\right\}, and up to the first order, one recovers Eq. (116) and ρl​o​c=ρl​o​c⋆\rho_{loc}=\rho_{loc}^{\star}, proving that the first-order CPE recovers the GA.

IV.1.2 Converting the GA energy into the qubit form using the Jordan-Wigner transformation

Here we discuss how to convert the standard form of the GA energy into the qubit form, which is mathematically equivalent. The qubit form provides a unified view of the energy evaluated using ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2}, ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}, and ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3}. The qubit parametrization consists of two steps. First, we introduce a purified many-body density matrix 𝝆\bm{\rho} from ρl​o​c\rho_{loc}. Second, we perform the Jordan-Wigner transformation, which converts ℛℓ\mathcal{R}_{\ell} (Eq. (114)) from an expression involving fermionic operators a^ℓ†\hat{a}_{\ell}^{\dagger} and a^ℓ\hat{a}_{\ell} into an expression involving spin operators σ^ℓx\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{x}. We begin by defining 𝝆=|Ψ⟩​⟨Ψ|\bm{\rho}=|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|, where |Ψ⟩=∑Γ[ρl​o​c]Γ​Γ​|Γ⟩|\Psi\rangle=\sum_{\Gamma}\sqrt{\left[\rho_{loc}\right]_{\Gamma\Gamma}}|\Gamma\rangle, which yields

[𝝆]Γ​Γ′=[ρl​o​c]Γ​Γ​[ρl​o​c]Γ′​Γ′.\left[\bm{\rho}\right]_{\Gamma\Gamma^{\prime}}=\sqrt{\left[\rho_{loc}\right]_{\Gamma\Gamma}\left[\rho_{loc}\right]_{\Gamma^{\prime}\Gamma^{\prime}}}. (117)

Using the Jordan-Wigner transformation (see Eqns. (43) and (44)), we obtain

|⟨Γ′|a^ℓ†|Γ⟩|2=⟨Γ′|a^ℓ†|Γ⟩​⟨Γ​|a^ℓ|​Γ′⟩\displaystyle\left|\left\langle\Gamma^{\prime}|\hat{a}_{\ell}^{\dagger}|\Gamma\right\rangle\right|^{2}=\langle\Gamma^{\prime}|\hat{a}_{\ell}^{\dagger}|\Gamma\rangle\langle\Gamma|\hat{a}_{\ell}|\Gamma^{\prime}\rangle (118)
=⟨Γ′|(∏ℓ′<ℓσ^ℓ′z)​σ^ℓ+|Γ⟩​⟨Γ|(∏ℓ′<ℓσ^ℓ′z)​σ^ℓ−|Γ′⟩\displaystyle=\langle\Gamma^{\prime}|\left(\prod_{\ell^{\prime}<\ell}\hat{\sigma}_{\ell^{\prime}}^{z}\right)\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{+}|\Gamma\rangle\langle\Gamma|\left(\prod_{\ell^{\prime}<\ell}\hat{\sigma}_{\ell^{\prime}}^{z}\right)\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{-}|\Gamma^{\prime}\rangle (119)
=⟨Γ′|σ^ℓ+​|Γ⟩​⟨Γ|​σ^ℓ−|Γ′⟩=|⟨Γ′|σ^ℓ+|Γ⟩|2.\displaystyle=\langle\Gamma^{\prime}|\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{+}|\Gamma\rangle\langle\Gamma|\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{-}|\Gamma^{\prime}\rangle=\left|\langle\Gamma^{\prime}|\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{+}|\Gamma\rangle\right|^{2}. (120)

Therefore, we can rewrite the numerator of ℛℓ\mathcal{R}_{\ell} (see Eq. (107)) as

∑Γ​Γ′[ρl​o​c]Γ​Γ​[ρl​o​c]Γ′​Γ′​|⟨Γ′|a^ℓ†|Γ⟩|2\displaystyle\sum_{\Gamma\Gamma^{\prime}}\sqrt{\left[\rho_{loc}\right]_{\Gamma\Gamma}\left[\rho_{loc}\right]_{\Gamma^{\prime}\Gamma^{\prime}}}\left|\left\langle\Gamma^{\prime}|\hat{a}_{\ell}^{\dagger}|\Gamma\right\rangle\right|^{2} (121)
=∑Γ​Γ′[𝝆]Γ​Γ′​|⟨Γ′|σℓ+|Γ⟩|2\displaystyle=\sum_{\Gamma\Gamma^{\prime}}\left[\bm{\rho}\right]_{\Gamma\Gamma^{\prime}}\left|\langle\Gamma^{\prime}|\sigma_{\ell}^{+}|\Gamma\rangle\right|^{2} (122)
=12​∑Γ​Γ′[𝝆]Γ​Γ′​⟨Γ′|σ^ℓx|Γ⟩=12​⟨σ^ℓx⟩𝝆=ξℓ,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\Gamma\Gamma^{\prime}}\left[\bm{\rho}\right]_{\Gamma\Gamma^{\prime}}\langle\Gamma^{\prime}|\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{x}|\Gamma\rangle=\frac{1}{2}\left\langle\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{x}\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}=\xi_{\ell}, (123)

where we used the fact that 𝝆\bm{\rho} is a real symmetric matrix and the following relation

⟨Γ′|σ^ℓx|Γ⟩=|⟨Γ′|σ^ℓ+|Γ⟩|2+|⟨Γ|σ^ℓ+|Γ′⟩|2.\langle\Gamma^{\prime}|\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{x}|\Gamma\rangle=\left|\langle\Gamma^{\prime}|\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{+}|\Gamma\rangle\right|^{2}+\left|\langle\Gamma|\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{+}|\Gamma^{\prime}\rangle\right|^{2}. (124)

Moreover, the denominator of ℛℓ\mathcal{R}_{\ell} (see Eq. (107)) is given as

Therefore, we have demonstrated that ℛℓ=ξℓ/ξℓ;0\mathcal{R}_{\ell}=\xi_{\ell}/\xi_{\ell;0}, and the local interaction can be written as

⟨Hl​o​c​({n^ℓ})⟩ρl​o​c=⟨Hl​o​c​({n^ℓ})⟩𝝆\left\langle H_{loc}\left(\left\{\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\}\right)\right\rangle_{\rho_{loc}}=\left\langle H_{loc}\left(\left\{\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\}\right)\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}} (126)

Using the expression for ℛℓ\mathcal{R}_{\ell} and the local energy, we arrive at the energy expressions given in Eqns. (50)-(53). This proof demonstrates that the usual Gutzwiller approximation can be straightforwardly transformed into the qubit energy form, which is equivalent to the result of the slave spin mean-field theory [21] (see Appendix B for additional details).

IV.2 The derivation of the qubit energy form using the SCDA

In this section, we use the gauge constrained SCDA to derive the qubit energy form. The derivation consists of two steps. First, in Section IV.2.1, the Gutzwiller gauge is used to rederive the standard form of the GA energy. Second, in Section IV.2.2, we derive the qubit energy form using the tensor representation, which does not rely on the Jordan-Wigner transformation. Additionally, in Section IV.2.3, we discuss how the quantities 𝓖\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}} , 𝑺\boldsymbol{S}, and 𝒈\boldsymbol{g} change under a general gauge transformation.

IV.2.1 The SCDA within the Gutzwiller gauge

In this section, we demonstrate how the gauge of the SPD can be used to automatically satisfy the SCDA self-consistency condition [13], and we utilize some notation from the CPE. Interestingly, the Gutzwiller constraint of the GA can be used to define an appropriate gauge for the SPD, which we refer to as the Gutzwiller gauge. Starting from ρ^G​2=P^1​K^2​P^1\hat{\rho}_{G2}=\hat{P}_{1}\hat{K}_{2}\hat{P}_{1} with an arbitrary gauge, a gauge transformation P^1→P^1​N^−1\hat{P}_{1}\rightarrow\hat{P}_{1}\hat{N}^{-1} and K^2→N^​K^2​N^\hat{K}_{2}\rightarrow\hat{N}\hat{K}_{2}\hat{N} can always be performed to ensure that ⟨n^i​ℓ⟩ρ^G​2=⟨n^i​ℓ⟩K^2=nℓ\left\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}}=\left\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{K}_{2}}=n_{\ell}, where N^=exp⁡(∑i​ℓμℓ​n^i​ℓ)\hat{N}=\exp\left(\sum_{i\ell}\mu_{\ell}\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right) is chosen to satisfy the Gutzwiller constraint. Within this Gutzwiller gauge, we can choose [𝓖i]ℓ​ℓ′=δℓ​ℓ′​𝒢ℓ\left[\bm{\mathcal{G}}_{i}\right]_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}=\delta_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}\mathcal{G}_{\ell}, where the component for the spin-orbital ℓ\ell is given by

𝒢ℓ=(nℓ1−nℓ−nℓnℓ).\mathcal{G}_{\ell}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}n_{\ell}&1-n_{\ell}\\ -n_{\ell}&n_{\ell}\end{array}\right). (127)

We now prove that this 𝒢ℓ\mathcal{G}_{\ell} ensures that the SCDA self-consistency condition is automatically satisfied. The first step of the proof relies on the fact that under the Gutzwiller gauge $̱\hat{\rho}$l​o​c\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{loc} within the SCDA is the discrete action of the central point of the SPD ρG​2⋆=P^1​K^2⋆​P^1\rho_{G2}^{\star}=\hat{P}_{1}\hat{K}_{2}^{\star}\hat{P}_{1}, which can be shown as follows. The local reduced density matrix of ρG​2⋆\rho_{G2}^{\star} at site ii is ρ^G​2;i⋆=P^1;i​K^2;i⋆​P^1;i\hat{\rho}_{G2;i}^{\star}=\hat{P}_{1;i}\hat{K}_{2;i}^{\star}\hat{P}_{1;i}, which yields a discrete action $̱\hat{\rho}$G​2;i⋆=$̱\hat{\rho}$G​2;i;0⋆​$̱\hat{P}$1;i(1)​$̱\hat{P}$1;i(2)\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{G2;i}^{\star}=\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{G2;i;0}^{\star}\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{P}$}}_{1;i}^{\left(1\right)}\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{P}$}}_{1;i}^{\left(2\right)}, where $̱\hat{\rho}$G​2;i;0⋆=$̱\hat{Q}$$̱\hat{K}$2;i⋆\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{G2;i;0}^{\star}=\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{Q}$}}\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{K}$}}_{2;i}^{\star}. Given that ⟨n^i​ℓ⟩K^2;i⋆=nℓ\left\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{K}_{2;i}^{\star}}=n_{\ell}, the integer time Green’s function for $̱\hat{\rho}$G​2;i;0⋆\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{G2;i;0}^{\star} is given by Eq. (127), and correspondingly $̱\hat{\rho}$G​2;i⋆\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{G2;i}^{\star} is equivalent to the local discrete action $̱\hat{\rho}$l​o​c;i\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{loc;i} for the SCDA, proving $̱\hat{\rho}$G​2⋆=$̱\hat{\rho}$l​o​c\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{G2}^{\star}=\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{loc}. Local observables within the SCDA can then be evaluated under the central point of the SPD as

⟨X^i​Γ⟩ρ^G​2;i=⟨$̱\hat{X}$i​Γ(2)⟩$̱\hat{\rho}$l​o​c;i=⟨X^i​Γ⟩ρ^G​2;i⋆,\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2;i}}=\langle\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{X}$}}_{i\Gamma}^{\left(2\right)}\rangle_{\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{loc;i}}=\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2;i}^{\star}}, (128)

consistent with the relation derived from the CPE (see Eq. (546)). Similarly, the local interacting integer time Green’s function [𝒈i]ℓ​ℓ′=δℓ​ℓ′​gℓ\left[\bm{g}_{i}\right]_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}=\delta_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}g_{\ell} can be evaluated as

gℓ=(nℓ(1−nℓ)​ℛℓ,12−nℓ​ℛℓ,21nℓ),g_{\ell}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}n_{\ell}&\left(1-n_{\ell}\right)\mathcal{R}_{\ell,12}\\ -n_{\ell}\mathcal{R}_{\ell,21}&n_{\ell}\end{array}\right), (129)

IV.2.3 SCDA under a general gauge transformation

Here we discuss the SCDA within an arbitrary gauge, where ρ^G​2=P^1​K^2​P^1†\hat{\rho}_{G2}=\hat{P}_{1}\hat{K}_{2}\hat{P}_{1}^{\dagger}, as this will be important to understanding the gauge constrained algorithm for 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3. A general gauge transformation which maintains a G-type form is defined as P^1→P^1​N^−1\hat{P}_{1}\rightarrow\hat{P}_{1}\hat{N}^{-1}, K^2→N^​K^2​N^†\hat{K}_{2}\rightarrow\hat{N}\hat{K}_{2}\hat{N}^{\dagger} , P^1†→(N^†)−1​P^1†\hat{P}_{1}^{\dagger}\rightarrow\left(\hat{N}^{\dagger}\right)^{-1}\hat{P}_{1}^{\dagger}, where N^=exp⁡(𝝁⋅𝒏^)\hat{N}=\exp\left(\bm{\mu}\cdot\hat{\bm{n}}\right). Using the results of Section II.2, this gauge transformation can be decomposed in terms of an intra-time-step transformation given by 𝑵a=diag​(𝟏,exp⁡(−𝝁∗))\bm{N}_{a}=\text{diag}\left(\boldsymbol{1},\exp\left(-\bm{\mu}^{*}\right)\right), and an inter-time-step transformation given by 𝑵b=diag​(exp⁡(−𝝁T),𝟏)\bm{N}_{b}=\text{diag}\left(\exp\left(-\bm{\mu}^{T}\right),\boldsymbol{1}\right). The corresponding transformations for the integer time Green’s functions can be found in Section II.2. In the following, we focus on the transformation with the form [𝝁]i​ℓ,i′​ℓ=δi​i′​δℓ​ℓ′​μℓ\left[\bm{\mu}\right]_{i\ell,i^{\prime}\ell}=\delta_{ii^{\prime}}\delta_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}\mu_{\ell} where μℓ\mu_{\ell} is a real number. Using Eq. (18), the transformation of [𝒈i]ℓ​ℓ′=δℓ​ℓ′​gℓ\left[\bm{g}_{i}\right]_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}=\delta_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}g_{\ell} with the component gℓg_{\ell} is given as

Using Eq. (24), the transformation for 𝑺i\bm{S}_{i} is given by

We proceed by exploring a particular choice of gauge for the SPD, referred to as the anti-symmetric gauge, which will motivate the gauge choice for the case of 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3. The essence of the anti-symmetric gauge is to choose μℓ\mu_{\ell} such that [gℓ′]12=−[gℓ′]21\left[g^{\prime}_{\ell}\right]_{12}=-\left[g^{\prime}_{\ell}\right]_{21}, which can be accomplished as

Under the anti-symmetric gauge, we have

The anti-symmetric gauge can also automatically satisfy the SCDA self-consistency condition, and be used to derive the qubit energy form.

V Derivation of the qubit energy form for ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}

In this section, we derive Eq. (56) using several different approaches. In Section V.1, we present two derivations: a heuristic approach and the central point expansion (CPE). In Section V.2, we use the SCDA to evaluate ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}, and the tensor product representation is used to obtain the qubit energy form.

V.1 Derivation of the qubit energy form: a heuristic approach and the CPE

To begin, it is useful to rewrite the local interaction Hamiltonian given in Eq. (42) as

Hl​o​c​({n^i​ℓ})=∑IEI​δ​D^i​I,H_{loc}\left(\left\{\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\}\right)=\sum_{I}E_{I}\delta\hat{D}_{iI}, (180)

where δ​D^i​I=∏ℓ∈Iδ​n^i​ℓ\delta\hat{D}_{iI}=\prod_{\ell\in I}\delta\hat{n}_{i\ell}, the density fluctuation is defined as δ​n^i​ℓ=n^i​ℓ−nℓ\delta\hat{n}_{i\ell}=\hat{n}_{i\ell}-n_{\ell}, the index II enumerates all possible subsets of the local spin orbitals, with δ​D^i​I=1\delta\hat{D}_{iI}=1 when I={}I=\left\{\right\}, and the parameters EIE_{I} reparametrize the coefficients in Eq. (42). Using the alternative form of the local interaction Hamiltonian given in Eq. (180), the corresponding qubit form of the trial energy is given as

E⁡({nk​ℓ},𝝆)=∑ℓ∫d​k​ϵk​ℓ​nk​ℓ+∑IEI​δ​DI,\displaystyle E\left(\left\{n_{k\ell}\right\},\bm{\rho}\right)=\sum_{\ell}\int dk\epsilon_{k\ell}n_{k\ell}+\sum_{I}E_{I}\delta D_{I}, (181)
δ​DI=(∏ℓ∈Iℱℓ)​⟨δ​D^I⟩𝝆,\displaystyle\delta D_{I}=\left(\prod_{\ell\in I}\mathcal{F}_{\ell}\right)\langle\delta\hat{D}_{I}\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}, (182)
ℱℓ=Aℓ2ξℓ,02=(∫d​k​nk​ℓ​(1−nk​ℓ)nℓ​(1−nℓ))2,\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{\ell}=\frac{A_{\ell}^{2}}{\xi_{\ell,0}^{2}}=\left(\frac{\int dk\sqrt{n_{k\ell}\left(1-n_{k\ell}\right)}}{\sqrt{n_{\ell}\left(1-n_{\ell}\right)}}\right)^{2}, (183)

where the variational parameters nk​ℓ∈[0,1]n_{k\ell}\in\left[0,1\right], the 𝝆\bm{\rho} is a many-body density matrix for a 2​No​r​b2N_{orb} qubit system which is diagonal in the Pauli-Z basis, δ​D^I=∏ℓ∈I(n^ℓ−nℓ)\delta\hat{D}_{I}=\prod_{\ell\in I}(\hat{n}_{\ell}-n_{\ell}), and nℓ=∫d​k​nk​ℓn_{\ell}=\int dkn_{k\ell}. For a given ℓ\ell, there is constraint given by

∫d​k​nk​ℓ=⟨n^ℓ⟩𝝆.\int dkn_{k\ell}=\left\langle\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}. (184)

Below, we present two approaches for deriving Eq. (181).

A heuristic approach for deriving Eq. (181) is via the formal duality between ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} and ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}. First, in ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2}, the center projector K^2\hat{K}_{2} is constrained to have the same local density as ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2}, i.e., ⟨n^i​ℓ⟩K^2=⟨n^i​ℓ⟩ρ^G​2\left\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{K}_{2}}=\left\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}}. Similarly, the center projector P^1\hat{P}_{1} in ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2} is constrained to have the same local density as ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}, i.e., ⟨n^i​ℓ⟩P^1=⟨n^i​ℓ⟩ρ^B​2\left\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{P}_{1}}=\left\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}}. Second, in ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} (see Eq. (50)), the momentum density fluctuation δ​nk​ℓ=nk​ℓ−nℓ\delta n_{k\ell}=n_{k\ell}-n_{\ell} is renormalized from the bare momentum density fluctuation δ​nk​ℓ;0=nk​ℓ;0−nℓ\delta n_{k\ell;0}=n_{k\ell;0}-n_{\ell} with a factor 𝒵=ξℓ2/ξℓ;02\mathcal{Z}=\xi_{\ell}^{2}/\xi_{\ell;0}^{2}, which depends on 𝝆\bm{\rho}. To the contrary, ⟨δ​D^i​I⟩ρ^B​2\langle\delta\hat{D}_{iI}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}} is renormalized from the reference value ⟨δ​D^i​I⟩P^1\langle\delta\hat{D}_{iI}\rangle_{\hat{P}_{1}} with a factor ∏ℓ∈Iℱℓ\prod_{\ell\in I}\mathcal{F_{\ell}}, where ℱℓ\mathcal{F}_{\ell} depends on nk​ℓn_{k\ell}. The expression for ℱℓ\mathcal{F}_{\ell} can be determined using a counting scheme similar to the one used within the GA. We begin by transforming δ​D^i​I\delta\hat{D}_{iI} into momentum space, which requires a summation over terms consisting of NIN_{I} creation and NIN_{I} annihilation operators, where NIN_{I} is the number of spin orbitals in set II. Each creation or annihilation process for k​ℓk\ell will be scaled by

∑Γ​Γ′⟨X^k​ℓ​Γ⟩ρ^B​2​⟨X^k​ℓ​Γ′⟩ρ^B​2​|⟨Γ′|a^k​ℓ†|Γ⟩|2∑Γ​Γ′⟨X^k​ℓ​Γ⟩P^1​⟨X^k​ℓ​Γ′⟩P^1​|⟨Γ′|a^k​ℓ†|Γ⟩|2\displaystyle\frac{\sum_{\Gamma\Gamma^{\prime}}\sqrt{\left\langle\hat{X}_{k\ell\Gamma}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}}\left\langle\hat{X}_{k\ell\Gamma^{\prime}}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}}}\left|\left\langle\Gamma^{\prime}|\hat{a}_{k\ell}^{\dagger}|\Gamma\right\rangle\right|^{2}}{\sum_{\Gamma\Gamma^{\prime}}\sqrt{\left\langle\hat{X}_{k\ell\Gamma}\right\rangle_{\hat{P}_{1}}\left\langle\hat{X}_{k\ell\Gamma^{\prime}}\right\rangle_{\hat{P}_{1}}}\left|\left\langle\Gamma^{\prime}|\hat{a}_{k\ell}^{\dagger}|\Gamma\right\rangle\right|^{2}}
=nk​ℓ​(1−nk​ℓ)nℓ​(1−nℓ),\displaystyle=\frac{\sqrt{n_{k\ell}\left(1-n_{k\ell}\right)}}{\sqrt{n_{\ell}\left(1-n_{\ell}\right)}}, (185)

where Γ∈{1,2}\Gamma\in\{1,2\} enumerates the empty and occupied states for a given k​ℓk\ell and

X^k​ℓ​Γ=δΓ−1,0​(1−n^k​ℓ)+δΓ−1,1​n^k​ℓ.\displaystyle\hat{X}_{k\ell\Gamma}=\delta_{\Gamma-1,0}(1-\hat{n}_{k\ell})+\delta_{\Gamma-1,1}\hat{n}_{k\ell}. (186)

Using the infinite dimensional approximation where momentum conservation can be neglected, we obtain ⟨δ​D^i​I⟩ρ^B​2=(∏ℓ∈Iℱℓ)​⟨δ​D^i​I⟩P^1\langle\delta\hat{D}_{iI}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}}=\left(\prod_{\ell\in I}\mathcal{F}_{\ell}\right)\langle\delta\hat{D}_{iI}\rangle_{\hat{P}_{1}}. By identifying 𝝆\bm{\rho} as the local reduced density matrix of P^1\hat{P}_{1}, we obtain the form given in Eq. (182).

A more rigorous way to derive the factor in Eq. (182) is to use the CPE. We outline the derivation here, and the details can be found in Appendix C.2. The CPE for ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2} is a dual version to the CPE of ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2}, where the latter is described in Section IV.1.1. We start by defining the central point as ρ^B​2⋆=K^1​P^1⋆​K^1\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}=\hat{K}_{1}\hat{P}_{1}^{\star}\hat{K}_{1}, where P^1⋆\hat{P}_{1}^{\star} is a non-interacting projector chosen such that nℓ≡⟨n^i​ℓ⟩P^1=⟨n^i​ℓ⟩P^1⋆n_{\ell}\equiv\left\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{P}_{1}}=\left\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{P}_{1}^{\star}}. The kinetic projector K^1\hat{K}_{1} can be parametrized using nk​ℓ⋆=⟨n^k​ℓ⟩ρ^B​2⋆n_{k\ell}^{\star}=\langle\hat{n}_{k\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}} with the constraint∫d​k​nk​ℓ⋆=nℓ,\int dkn_{k\ell}^{\star}=n_{\ell}, while P^1\hat{P}_{1} can be parametrized using δ​Di​I;0=⟨δ​D^i​I⟩P^1\delta D_{iI;0}=\langle\delta\hat{D}_{iI}\rangle_{\hat{P}_{1}} and {nℓ}\{n_{\ell}\}. Therefore, the observables under ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2} are functionals of nk​ℓ⋆n_{k\ell}^{\star} and {δ​Di​I;0}\left\{\delta D_{iI;0}\right\}. Performing a first order expansion in terms of {δ​Di​I;0}\left\{\delta D_{iI;0}\right\} about {δDi​I;0=0}\left\{\delta D_{iI;0}=0\right\}, we obtain nk​ℓ=nk​ℓ⋆n_{k\ell}=n_{k\ell}^{\star} and

δ​Di​I=(∏ℓ∈Iℱℓ)​δ​Di​I;0.\delta D_{iI}=\left(\prod_{\ell\in I}\mathcal{F}_{\ell}\right)\delta D_{iI;0}. (187)

Finally, we explain how to obtain Eqns. (56)-(58) from Eq. (187). We begin by defining the effective density operator n^e​f​f,ℓ=nℓ+ℱℓ​δ​n^ℓ\hat{n}_{eff,\ell}=n_{\ell}+\mathcal{F}_{\ell}\delta\hat{n}_{\ell} where δ​n^ℓ=n^ℓ−nℓ\delta\hat{n}_{\ell}=\hat{n}_{\ell}-n_{\ell}, the corresponding fluctuation form δ​n^e​f​f,ℓ≡n^e​f​f,ℓ−n^ℓ=ℱℓ​δ​n^ℓ\delta\hat{n}_{eff,\ell}\equiv\hat{n}_{eff,\ell}-\hat{n}_{\ell}=\mathcal{F}_{\ell}\delta\hat{n}_{\ell}, and a diagonal many-body density matrix 𝝆\bm{\rho} for a 2​No​r​b2N_{orb} qubit system [𝝆]Γ​Γ′=δΓ​Γ′​⟨X^i​Γ⟩P^1\left[\bm{\rho}\right]_{\Gamma\Gamma^{\prime}}=\delta_{\Gamma\Gamma^{\prime}}\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\rangle_{\hat{P}_{1}}. Using δ​Di​I,0=⟨∏i∈Iδ​n^ℓ⟩𝝆\delta D_{iI,0}=\left\langle\prod_{i\in I}\delta\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}} and Eq. (187), we have δ​Di​I=⟨∏i∈Iδ​n^e​f​f,ℓ⟩𝝆\delta D_{iI}=\left\langle\prod_{i\in I}\delta\hat{n}_{eff,\ell}\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}. Furthermore, nℓ=⟨n^ℓ⟩𝝆n_{\ell}=\left\langle\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}} implies that ⟨δ​n^ℓ⟩𝝆=⟨δ​n^e​f​f,ℓ⟩𝝆=0\left\langle\delta\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}=\left\langle\delta\hat{n}_{eff,\ell}\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}=0. Therefore, the expectation value of Hl​o​c​({n^i​ℓ})H_{loc}\left(\left\{\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\}\right) is given by ⟨Hl​o​c​({n^e​f​f,ℓ})⟩𝝆\left\langle H_{loc}\left(\left\{\hat{n}_{eff,\ell}\right\}\right)\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}, providing the connection to Eqns. (56)-(58).

V.2 The derivation of the qubit energy form via the SCDA

In this section, we use the gauge constrained SCDA to derive the qubit energy form. The derivation consists of two steps. First, in Section V.2.1, we use the Gutzwiller gauge to automatically satisfy the SCDA self-consistency condition. Second, in Section V.2.2, we derive the qubit energy form using the tensor representation. Additionally, in Section V.2.3, we discuss how the quantities 𝓖\boldsymbol{\mathcal{G}} , 𝑺\boldsymbol{S}, and 𝒈\boldsymbol{g} change under a general gauge transformation.

V.2.1 SCDA within the Gutzwiller gauge

In this section, we use the gauge constrained SCDA to evaluate ρ^B​2=K^1​P^1​K^1\hat{\rho}_{B2}=\hat{K}_{1}\hat{P}_{1}\hat{K}_{1}, where P^1=exp⁡(∑i​ΓυΓ​X^i​Γ)\hat{P}_{1}=\exp\left(\sum_{i\Gamma}\upsilon_{\Gamma}\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\right) and K^1=exp⁡(∑k​ℓγk​ℓ​n^k​ℓ)\hat{K}_{1}=\exp\left(\sum_{k\ell}\gamma_{k\ell}\hat{n}_{k\ell}\right), recovering the results from Section V.1. The key observation is that for ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}, the interacting projectors only act on the first integer time step. Consider a gauge transformation for ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2} given as K^1→K^1​N^\hat{K}_{1}\rightarrow\hat{K}_{1}\hat{N} and P1^→N^−1​P^1​N^−1\hat{P_{1}}\rightarrow\hat{N}^{-1}\hat{P}_{1}\hat{N}^{-1} where N^=exp⁡(∑i​ℓμℓ​n^i​ℓ)\hat{N}=\exp\left(\sum_{i\ell}\mu_{\ell}\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right). We choose the gauge transformation such that 𝓖i\bm{\mathcal{G}}_{i} is given as [𝓖i]ℓ​ℓ′=δℓ​ℓ′​𝒢ℓ\left[\bm{\mathcal{G}}_{i}\right]_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}=\delta_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}\mathcal{G}_{\ell}, where

𝒢ℓ=(nℓ𝒢ℓ,1,2𝒢ℓ,2,1𝒢ℓ,2,2),\mathcal{G}_{\ell}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}n_{\ell}&\mathcal{G}_{\ell,1,2}\\ \mathcal{G}_{\ell,2,1}&\mathcal{G}_{\ell,2,2}\end{array}\right), (188)

and nℓ=⟨n^i​ℓ⟩ρ^B​2;0n_{\ell}=\left\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2;0}} is the local density for the non-interacting SPD ρ^B​2;0=K^1​K1^\hat{\rho}_{B2;0}=\hat{K}_{1}\hat{K_{1}}. Under this gauge choice, P^1\hat{P}_{1} will ensure that [𝒈i]ℓ​ℓ′=δℓ​ℓ′​gℓ\left[\bm{g}_{i}\right]_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}=\delta_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}g_{\ell} with [gℓ]11=[𝒢ℓ]11=nℓ\left[g_{\ell}\right]_{11}=\left[\mathcal{G}_{\ell}\right]_{11}=n_{\ell}. The integer time self-energy [𝑺i]\left[\bm{S}_{i}\right]ℓ​ℓ′=δℓ​ℓ′Sℓ{}_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}=\delta_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}S_{\ell} can then be determined as

Sℓ=(1001).S_{\ell}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}1&0\\ 0&1\end{array}\right). (189)

The remaining entries of Eq. (188) should be determined from the self-consistency condition in Eq. (32). Given that SℓS_{\ell} is the identity matrix, the non-interacting and interacting integer time Green’s functions are given by [𝒈k;0]ℓ​ℓ′=δℓ​ℓ′​gk​ℓ;0\left[\bm{g}_{k;0}\right]_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}=\delta_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}g_{k\ell;0} and [𝒈k]ℓ​ℓ′=δℓ​ℓ′​gk​ℓ\left[\bm{g}_{k}\right]_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}=\delta_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}g_{k\ell} where

gk​ℓ;0=gk​ℓ=(nk​ℓ(1−nk​ℓ)​nk​ℓ−(1−nk​ℓ)​nk​ℓnk​ℓ),g_{k\ell;0}=g_{k\ell}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}n_{k\ell}&\sqrt{\left(1-n_{k\ell}\right)n_{k\ell}}\\ -\sqrt{\left(1-n_{k\ell}\right)n_{k\ell}}&n_{k\ell}\end{array}\right), (190)

and nk​ℓn_{k\ell} is the momentum density distribution. We can then verify that the self-consistency condition 𝒈i=(1/Nsite)​∑k𝒈k\bm{g}_{i}=\left(1/N_{\textrm{site}}\right)\sum_{k}\bm{g}_{k} is fulfilled, given that

gℓ=𝒢ℓ=(nℓAℓ−Aℓnℓ),g_{\ell}=\mathcal{G}_{\ell}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}n_{\ell}&A_{\ell}\\ -A_{\ell}&n_{\ell}\end{array}\right), (191)

where nℓ=(1/Ns​i​t​e)​∑knk​ℓn_{\ell}=\left(1/N_{site}\right)\sum_{k}n_{k\ell} and the AℓA_{\ell} is defined as

Aℓ=1Ns​i​t​e​∑k(1−nk​ℓ)​nk​ℓ.A_{\ell}=\frac{1}{N_{site}}\sum_{k}\sqrt{\left(1-n_{k\ell}\right)n_{k\ell}}. (192)

We analogously refer to this gauge as the Gutzwiller gauge given that gℓ=𝒢ℓg_{\ell}=\mathcal{G}_{\ell}, and therefore the diagonal elements of the two matrices are the same.

V.2.2 Derivation of the qubit energy form

In this section, we use the tensor product representation to derive the qubit energy form, paralleling the procedure in Section IV.2.2. V.2.3 SCDA under a general gauge transformation

Here we discuss the SCDA within an arbitrary gauge, analogous to Section IV.2.3. Given ρ^B​2=K^1​P^1​K^1†\hat{\rho}_{B2}=\hat{K}_{1}\hat{P}_{1}\hat{K}_{1}^{\dagger}, a general gauge transformation is given as: K^1→K^1​N^\hat{K}_{1}\rightarrow\hat{K}_{1}\hat{N}, P^1→N^−1​P^1​(N^†)−1\hat{P}_{1}\rightarrow\hat{N}^{-1}\hat{P}_{1}\left(\hat{N}^{\dagger}\right)^{-1}, K^1†→N^†​K^1†\hat{K}_{1}^{\dagger}\rightarrow\hat{N}^{\dagger}\hat{K}_{1}^{\dagger}, where N^=exp⁡(𝝁⋅𝒏^)\hat{N}=\exp\left(\bm{\mu}\cdot\hat{\bm{n}}\right). VI Derivation of the qubit energy form for ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3}

In this section, we derive Eq. (62) using the gauge constrained SCDA. In section VI.1, we provide a high level comparison of the original gauge constrained algorithm and the qubit parametrization. In section VI.2, we provide a review of the original gauge constrained algorithm, which is necessary to understand the qubit parametrization in this work. In section VI.3, we propose the qubit parametrization which yields the qubit energy form. In section VI.4, we examine the case of half-filling, and explore how the qubit energy form for ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3} can recover the cases of ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} and ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}.

VI.1 Comparing the original gauge constrained trial energy to the qubit energy form

In this section, we outline how the qubit parametrization improves the original gauge constrained algorithm [15]. In the original gauge constrained algorithm, the trial energy under ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3} is given as

∑ℓ∫d​k​ϵk​ℓ​nk​ℓ+El​o​c​({𝒢12,ℓ},{uΓ},{𝒜<ℓ},{𝒜>ℓ}),\sum_{\ell}\int dk\epsilon_{k\ell}n_{k\ell}+E_{loc}\left(\left\{\mathcal{G}_{12,\ell}\right\},\{u_{\Gamma}\},\left\{\mathcal{A}_{<\ell}\right\},\left\{\mathcal{A}_{>\ell}\right\}\right), (225)

which is a function of {nk​ℓ}\{n_{k\ell}\}, {𝒢12,ℓ}\left\{\mathcal{G}_{12,\ell}\right\}, {uΓ}\{u_{\Gamma}\}, and {nk​ℓ;0}\{n_{k\ell;0}\}, given that {𝒜<ℓ}\left\{\mathcal{A}_{<\ell}\right\} and {𝒜>ℓ}\left\{\mathcal{A}_{>\ell}\right\} are functions of {nk​ℓ}\{n_{k\ell}\} and {nk​ℓ;0}\{n_{k\ell;0}\}. It should be noted that nk​ℓ;0∈{0,1}n_{k\ell;0}\in\{0,1\} and nk​ℓ∈[0,1]n_{k\ell}\in[0,1], and there are three constraints for a given ℓ\ell

∫<𝑑k=nℓ​({𝒢12;ℓ},{uΓ}),\displaystyle\int_{<}dk=n_{\ell}\left(\left\{\mathcal{G}_{12;\ell}\right\},\{u_{\Gamma}\}\right), (226)
∫nk​ℓ​𝑑k=nℓ​({𝒢12;ℓ},{uΓ}),\displaystyle\int n_{k\ell}dk=n_{\ell}\left(\left\{\mathcal{G}_{12;\ell}\right\},\{u_{\Gamma}\}\right), (227)
Δℓ≡∫>nk​ℓ​𝑑k=Δℓ​({𝒢12;ℓ},{uΓ}),\displaystyle\Delta_{\ell}\equiv\int_{>}n_{k\ell}dk=\Delta_{\ell}\left(\left\{\mathcal{G}_{12;\ell}\right\},\{u_{\Gamma}\}\right), (228)

where the functions nℓ​({𝒢12;ℓ},{uΓ})n_{\ell}\left(\left\{\mathcal{G}_{12;\ell}\right\},\{u_{\Gamma}\}\right) and Δℓ​({𝒢12;ℓ},{uΓ})\Delta_{\ell}\left(\left\{\mathcal{G}_{12;\ell}\right\},\{u_{\Gamma}\}\right) are explicitly defined in Ref. [15]. While this parametrization allows for an explicit evaluation of the total energy, there are several shortcomings of this parametrization. First, the function nℓ​({𝒢12;ℓ},{uΓ})n_{\ell}\left(\left\{\mathcal{G}_{12;\ell}\right\},\{u_{\Gamma}\}\right) is highly non-trivial and thus the minimization under a fixed density is cumbersome. Previously, this problem was addressed by introducing a linear transformation over {uΓ}\{u_{\Gamma}\}, known as the ww representation. Second, the function Δℓ​({𝒢12;ℓ},{uΓ})\Delta_{\ell}\left(\left\{\mathcal{G}_{12;\ell}\right\},\{u_{\Gamma}\}\right) may yield a value outside the allowed bounds for Δℓ\Delta_{\ell}. This problem can be addressed by imposing appropriate restrictions on {𝒢12;ℓ}\left\{\mathcal{G}_{12;\ell}\right\}. Finally, {𝒢12;ℓ}\left\{\mathcal{G}_{12;\ell}\right\} makes the physical interpretation of the total energy expression somewhat obscure.

In this paper, the aforementioned shortcomings are resolved using the qubit parametrization (see Section III). The qubit parametrization has two important differences. First, the qubit parametrization employs an effective many-body density matrix 𝝆,\bm{\rho}, having dimension 22​No​r​b×22​No​r​b2^{2N_{orb}}\times 2^{2N_{orb}}, corresponding to a pure state of a 2​No​r​b2N_{orb} qubit system. The 𝝆\bm{\rho} is constructed such that the density of 𝝆\bm{\rho} is the same as the physical local density, and it can be viewed as a function of {uΓ}\{u_{\Gamma}\} and {𝒢12,ℓ}\left\{\mathcal{G}_{12,\ell}\right\}. Second, the qubit parametrization uses Δℓ​({𝒢12;ℓ},{uΓ})\Delta_{\ell}\left(\left\{\mathcal{G}_{12;\ell}\right\},\{u_{\Gamma}\}\right) to solve {𝒢12,ℓ}\left\{\mathcal{G}_{12,\ell}\right\} as a function of 𝝆\bm{\rho} and {Δℓ}\left\{\Delta_{\ell}\right\}, reducing the total number of constraints per spin orbital from three to two.

VI.2 Review of the gauge constrained SCDA algorithm

In this section, we use original gauge constrained SCDA to evaluate ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3}. It should be noted that there are several restrictions on the variational freedom of the SPD when using the gauge constrained SCDA. First, the kinetic projector must be diagonal in momentum space. Second, the interacting projector may not introduce off-diagonal terms at the single-particle level. These two restrictions guarantee that the local integer time self-energy and Green’s function are diagonal in the original basis. For Hamiltonians with density-density interactions and hopping parameters that are diagonal in the orbital index, such as the ones treated in this paper, the aforementioned variational restrictions do not limit the variational power of the SPD. There are two critical insights in the gauge constrained algorithm. First, the integer time self-energy only has non-trivial values within the time steps containing the interacting projector, and therefore 𝓖\bm{\mathcal{G}} only needs to be specified in the corresponding regions. Second, the gauge symmetry can be used to restrict the form of 𝓖\bm{\mathcal{G}}.

We start by examining the gauge symmetry of ρ^G​3=K^1​P^1​K^2​P^1†​K^1†\hat{\rho}_{G3}=\hat{K}_{1}\hat{P}_{1}\hat{K}_{2}\hat{P}_{1}^{\dagger}\hat{K}_{1}^{\dagger}, where the gauge transformation is given by K^1→K^1​N^1\hat{K}_{1}\rightarrow\hat{K}_{1}\hat{N}_{1}, P^1→N^1−1​P^1​N^2−1\hat{P}_{1}\rightarrow\hat{N}_{1}^{-1}\hat{P}_{1}\hat{N}_{2}^{-1}, and K^2→N^2​K^2​N^2†\hat{K}_{2}\rightarrow\hat{N}_{2}\hat{K}_{2}\hat{N}_{2}^{\dagger}, where N^1=exp⁡(𝝁1⋅𝒏^)\hat{N}_{1}=\exp\left(\bm{\mu}_{1}\cdot\hat{\bm{n}}\right) and N^2=exp⁡(𝝁2⋅𝒏^)\hat{N}_{2}=\exp\left(\bm{\mu}_{2}\cdot\hat{\bm{n}}\right). The gauge transformation can be parametrized by

𝑵a\displaystyle\bm{N}_{a} =diag​(exp⁡(−𝝁1T),exp⁡(−𝝁2∗),1),\displaystyle=\text{diag}\left(\exp\left(-\bm{\mu}_{1}^{T}\right),\exp\left(-\bm{\mu}_{2}^{*}\right),1\right), (229)
𝑵b\displaystyle\bm{N}_{b} =diag​(exp⁡(−𝝁2T),exp⁡(−𝝁1⋆),1),\displaystyle=\text{diag}\left(\exp\left(-\bm{\mu}_{2}^{T}\right),\exp\left(-\bm{\mu}_{1}^{\star}\right),1\right), (230)

as explained in Section II.2. In the following, we assume [𝝁i]ℓ​ℓ′=δℓ​ℓ′​μi,ℓ\left[\bm{\mu}_{i}\right]_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}=\delta_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}\mu_{i,\ell} where μi,ℓ\mu_{i,\ell} is a real number, yielding

gℓ′=diag​(e−μ2,ℓ,e−μ1,ℓ,1)​gℓ​diag​(eμ2,ℓ,eμ1,ℓ,1),\displaystyle g^{\prime}_{\ell}=\text{diag}\left(e^{-\mu_{2,\ell}},e^{-\mu_{1,\ell}},1\right)g_{\ell}\text{diag}\left(e^{\mu_{2,\ell}},e^{\mu_{1,\ell}},1\right), (231)
Sℓ′=diag​(eμ1,ℓ,eμ2,ℓ,1)​Sℓ​diag​(eμ2,ℓ,eμ1,ℓ,1),\displaystyle S^{\prime}_{\ell}=\text{diag}\left(e^{\mu_{1,\ell}},e^{\mu_{2,\ell}},1\right)S_{\ell}\text{diag}\left(e^{\mu_{2,\ell}},e^{\mu_{1,\ell}},1\right), (232)
(𝒢ℓ′)−1−1=diag​(e−μ2,ℓ,e−μ1,ℓ,1)\displaystyle\left(\mathcal{G}^{\prime}_{\ell}\right)^{-1}-1=\text{diag}\left(e^{-\mu_{2,\ell}},e^{-\mu_{1,\ell}},1\right)
×(𝒢−−1ℓ1)diag(e−μ1,ℓ,e−μ2,ℓ,1).\displaystyle\hskip 30.00005pt\times\left(\mathcal{G}{}_{\ell}^{-1}-1\right)\text{diag}\left(e^{-\mu_{1,\ell}},e^{-\mu_{2,\ell}},1\right). (233)

Notice that the interacting projectors only act on the first and second time step, and therefore it is useful to split 𝒢ℓ\mathcal{G}_{\ell} into the following block structure:

It is useful to appreciate what can be gleaned from the form of the preceding equations. The gℓ,A′g^{\prime}_{\ell,A} block is reminiscent of the ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} case where Δℓ\Delta_{\ell} captures the quasi-particle renormalization, while gℓ,B′g^{\prime}_{\ell,B} and gℓ,C′g^{\prime}_{\ell,C} are reminiscent of the ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2} case where 𝒜<ℓ\mathcal{A}_{<\ell} and 𝒜>ℓ\mathcal{A}_{>\ell} capture the super-exchange effects. This observation helps illustrate how the ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3} simultaneously captures the physics of both ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} and ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}.

In the following, we further elaborate on two points which were not fully elucidated in Ref. [15]. First, we provide explicit expressions for the tensor product representation in the case of 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3. Second, we explore various relations derived using the block structure of the integer time Dyson equation.

VI.2.2 Block structure of the integer time Dyson equation

Here we derive various useful equations using the block form of the integer time Dyson equation. To make our discussion general, we assume that the integer time Green’s functions are not diagonal in the orbital index, resulting in the following block matrix equation

VI.3 Derivation of the qubit energy form

In this section, we derive the qubit energy form, given in Eq. (62), in several steps. First, in Section VI.3.1, we introduce a polar representation for the AA block. Second, in Section VI.3.2, we introduce 𝝆\bm{\rho} as a unitary transformation of w​wTww^{T}, and we solve the self-consistency condition for the AA block using nℓn_{\ell}, ξℓ\xi_{\ell}, and Δℓ\Delta_{\ell}. Third, in Section VI.3.3, we resolve the self-consistency of the BB, CC, and DD blocks using the extra information provided by 𝒜<ℓ\mathcal{A}_{<\ell} and 𝒜>ℓ\mathcal{A}_{>\ell}.

VI.3.1 Polar Representation of the A block

We first review some mathematical properties of the matrix group with following form

𝒮⁡(c,ϕ)=c⁡(cos⁡(ϕ)sin⁡(ϕ)−sin⁡(ϕ)cos⁡(ϕ)),\mathcal{S}\left(c,\phi\right)=c\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\cos(\phi)&\sin(\phi)\\ -\sin(\phi)&\cos(\phi)\end{array}\right), (296)

where c>0c>0 and ϕ∈[0,2​π]\phi\in\left[0,2\pi\right] and the group multiplication is

𝒮⁡(c1,ϕ1)​𝒮​(c2,ϕ2)=𝒮⁡(c,ϕ).\mathcal{S}\left(c_{1},\phi_{1}\right)\mathcal{S}\left(c_{2},\phi_{2}\right)=\mathcal{S}\left(c,\phi\right). (297)

There is an isomorphism for this matrix group to ℝ+×S1\mathbb{R}^{+}\times S^{1} with 𝒮⁡(c,ϕ)→(c,ϕ)\mathcal{S}\left(c,\phi\right)\rightarrow\left(c,\phi\right), with the group product taken as

Interpreting 𝒮⁡(c,ϕ)\mathcal{S}\left(c,\phi\right) as the integer time self-energy, the corresponding integer time Green’s function is given as

g⁡(c,ϕ)=11+𝒮=(c​cos⁡(ϕ)+1c2+2​c​cos⁡(ϕ)+1−c​sin⁡(ϕ)c2+2​c​cos⁡(ϕ)+1c​sin⁡(ϕ)c2+2​c​cos⁡(ϕ)+1c​cos⁡(ϕ)+1c2+2​c​cos⁡(ϕ)+1),g\left(c,\phi\right)=\frac{1}{1+\mathcal{S}}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\frac{c\cos(\phi)+1}{c^{2}+2c\cos(\phi)+1}&-\frac{c\sin(\phi)}{c^{2}+2c\cos(\phi)+1}\\ \frac{c\sin(\phi)}{c^{2}+2c\cos(\phi)+1}&\frac{c\cos(\phi)+1}{c^{2}+2c\cos(\phi)+1}\end{array}\right), (299)

and it can be seen that

g11\displaystyle g_{11} ≡[g⁡(c,ϕ)]11=[g⁡(c,ϕ)]22,\displaystyle\equiv\left[g\left(c,\phi\right)\right]_{11}=\left[g\left(c,\phi\right)\right]_{22}, (300)
g12\displaystyle g_{12} ≡[g⁡(c,ϕ)]12=−[g⁡(c,ϕ)]21.\displaystyle\equiv\left[g\left(c,\phi\right)\right]_{12}=-\left[g\left(c,\phi\right)\right]_{21}. (301)

It is also useful to express cc and ϕ\phi in terms of g11g_{11} and g12g_{12} as

tan⁡(ϕ)\displaystyle\tan\left(\phi\right) =g12g122+(g11−1)​g11.\displaystyle=\frac{g_{12}}{g_{12}^{2}+\left(g_{11}-1\right)g_{11}}. (303)

We now use the preceding results to study the AA block of the integer time Green’s function. Given that gℓ,Ag_{\ell,A} and 𝒢ℓ,A\mathcal{G}_{\ell,A} have the form given by Eq. VI.3.2 Resolving the self-consistency in the AA-block

A key ingredient of the qubit parametrization is the introduction of the qubit representation, defined by

($̱\hat{O}$)q=𝒰†​($̱\hat{O}$)w​𝒰,\displaystyle\left(\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{O}$}}\right)_{q}=\mathcal{U}^{\dagger}\left(\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{O}$}}\right)_{w}\mathcal{U}, (320)

where 𝒰\mathcal{U} is a unitary matrix defined as 𝒰=𝒰1⊗⋯⊗𝒰2​No​r​b\mathcal{U}=\mathcal{U}_{1}\otimes\dots\otimes\mathcal{U}_{2N_{orb}} and

𝒰ℓ=(cos⁡(ψℓ)sin⁡(ψℓ)−sin⁡(ψℓ)cos⁡(ψℓ)),\mathcal{U}_{\ell}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\cos\left(\psi_{\ell}\right)&\sin\left(\psi_{\ell}\right)\\ -\sin\left(\psi_{\ell}\right)&\cos\left(\psi_{\ell}\right)\end{array}\right), (322)

where ψℓ\psi_{\ell} is a parameter that will be determined by demanding that 𝝆\bm{\rho} yields the physical density. This should be contrasted to the ww representation, where the local density of w​wTww^{T} is generally different from the physical density.

We begin by deriving Eq. (73), which determines θℓ\theta_{\ell} for a given nℓ,n_{\ell}, ξℓ\xi_{\ell}, and Δℓ\Delta_{\ell}. Using Eq. (320), Eqns. (315)-(VI.3.1) are transformed to

($̱\hat{a}$ℓ†(1)​$̱\hat{a}$ℓ(1))q;ℓ,S=(12​(pℓ+1)qℓ2qℓ212​(1−pℓ)),\displaystyle\left(\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{a}$}}_{\ell}^{\dagger\left(1\right)}\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{a}$}}_{\ell}^{\left(1\right)}\right)_{q;\ell,S}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\frac{1}{2}\left(p_{\ell}+1\right)&\frac{q_{\ell}}{2}\\ \frac{q_{\ell}}{2}&\frac{1}{2}\left(1-p_{\ell}\right)\end{array}\right),
[($̱\hat{a}$ℓ†(1)​$̱\hat{a}$ℓ(2))q;ℓ,S]11=12​(cot⁡(ϕℓ,0)+qℓ),\displaystyle\left[\left(\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{a}$}}_{\ell}^{\dagger\left(1\right)}\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{a}$}}_{\ell}^{\left(2\right)}\right)_{q;\ell,S}\right]_{11}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\cot\left(\phi_{\ell,0}\right)+q_{\ell}\right), (325)
[($̱\hat{a}$ℓ†(1)​$̱\hat{a}$ℓ(2))q;ℓ,S]22=12​(cot⁡(ϕℓ,0)−qℓ),\displaystyle\left[\left(\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{a}$}}_{\ell}^{\dagger\left(1\right)}\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{a}$}}_{\ell}^{\left(2\right)}\right)_{q;\ell,S}\right]_{22}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\cot\left(\phi_{\ell,0}\right)-q_{\ell}\right), (326)
[($̱\hat{a}$ℓ†(1)​$̱\hat{a}$ℓ(2))q;ℓ,S]12=[($̱\hat{a}$ℓ†(1)​$̱\hat{a}$ℓ(2))q;ℓ,S]21=−pℓ2,\displaystyle\left[\left(\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{a}$}}_{\ell}^{\dagger\left(1\right)}\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{a}$}}_{\ell}^{\left(2\right)}\right)_{q;\ell,S}\right]_{12}=\left[\left(\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{a}$}}_{\ell}^{\dagger\left(1\right)}\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{a}$}}_{\ell}^{\left(2\right)}\right)_{q;\ell,S}\right]_{21}=-\frac{p_{\ell}}{2}, (327)

where

pℓ=cos⁡(2​ψℓ)​csc⁡(ϕℓ,0),\displaystyle p_{\ell}=\cos\left(2\psi_{\ell}\right)\csc\left(\phi_{\ell,0}\right), (328)
qℓ=sin⁡(2​ψℓ)​csc⁡(ϕℓ,0).\displaystyle q_{\ell}=\sin\left(2\psi_{\ell}\right)\csc\left(\phi_{\ell,0}\right). (329)

Using the self-consistency condition for the 1,1 and 1,2 entries, we have

Tr​(($̱\hat{a}$ℓ†(1)​$̱\hat{a}$ℓ(1))q;ℓ,S​𝝆ℓ)=nℓ,\displaystyle\text{Tr}\left(\left(\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{a}$}}_{\ell}^{\dagger\left(1\right)}\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{a}$}}_{\ell}^{\left(1\right)}\right)_{q;\ell,S}\bm{\rho}_{\ell}\right)=n_{\ell}, (330)

(339)

VI.3.3 Resolving the BB, CC, and DD blocks

We begin by deriving a subtle symmetry between 𝒢B\mathcal{G}_{B} and 𝒢C\mathcal{G}_{C}, described by Eq. (83) and Eq. (84), which can be rewritten as

𝒢CT~=−𝒢B,\widetilde{\mathcal{G}_{C}^{T}}=-\mathcal{G}_{B}, (343)

where the tilde is defined by the following rules. For a 2×12\times 1 matrix mm, we have [m~]21=[m]11\left[\tilde{m}\right]_{21}=\left[m\right]_{11} and [m~]11=[m]21\left[\tilde{m}\right]_{11}=\left[m\right]_{21}. For a 1×21\times 2 matrix mm, we have [m~]12=[m]11\left[\tilde{m}\right]_{12}=\left[m\right]_{11} and [m~]11=[m]12\left[\tilde{m}\right]_{11}=\left[m\right]_{12}. For a 2×22\times 2 matrix mm, we have [m~]11=[m]22\left[\tilde{m}\right]_{11}=\left[m\right]_{22}, [m~]22=[m]11\left[\tilde{m}\right]_{22}=\left[m\right]_{11}, [m~]12=[m]21\left[\tilde{m}\right]_{12}=\left[m\right]_{21}, and [m~]21=[m]12\left[\tilde{m}\right]_{21}=\left[m\right]_{12}. VI.4 Examining the qubit energy form in special cases

In this section, we showcase the qubit energy form for the special case of half-filled orbitals. Additionally, we examine how the qubit energy form for ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3} recovers the qubit energy forms for ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} and ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}.

VI.4.2 Recovering the qubit energy form for ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2}

Given that ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} is a special case of ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3}, it is clear that the former can be obtained by constraining the latter.
