VI.4.3 Recovering the qubit energy form for ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}

Given that ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2} is a special case of ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3}, it is clear that the former can be obtained by constraining the latter. However, it should be noted that in the qubit parametrization, K^2\hat{K}_{2} in ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3} is assumed to correspond to a Slater determinant, but K^2\hat{K}_{2} must be the identity to recover ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}. Nonetheless, we demonstrate that the qubit energy form of ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3} can still be constrained to recover the qubit energy form of ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}. The solution is to restrict 𝝆\bm{\rho} to be a diagonal matrix, implying that ξℓ=0\xi_{\ell}=0, yielding θℓ=π2\theta_{\ell}=\frac{\pi}{2}, gℓ,12=0g_{\ell,12}=0, cℓ=1nℓ−1c_{\ell}=\frac{1}{n_{\ell}}-1, ϕℓ=0\phi_{\ell}=0, ϕℓ,0=−π2\phi_{\ell,0}=-\frac{\pi}{2}, 𝒢ℓ,12=12\mathcal{G}_{\ell,12}=\frac{1}{2}, ℐℓ=nℓ2\mathcal{I}_{\ell}=\frac{n_{\ell}}{2}, 𝒥ℓ=−nℓ2\mathcal{J}_{\ell}=-\frac{n_{\ell}}{2}, 𝒜<,ℓ′=𝒜<,ℓ+𝒜>,ℓ=Aℓ\mathcal{A}^{\prime}_{<,\ell}=\mathcal{A}_{<,\ell}+\mathcal{A}_{>,\ell}=A_{\ell}, 𝒜>,ℓ′=0\mathcal{A}^{\prime}_{>,\ell}=0, 𝒢ℓ,13=𝒢ℓ,23=Aℓ2​ξℓ,0\mathcal{G}_{\ell,13}=\mathcal{G}_{\ell,23}=\frac{A_{\ell}}{2\xi_{\ell,0}}, iℓ=Aℓ2ξℓ,02i_{\ell}=\frac{A_{\ell}^{2}}{\xi_{\ell,0}^{2}}, jℓ=0j_{\ell}=0, 𝒢ℓ,33=nℓ−Aℓ2​δ​nℓξℓ,02\mathcal{G}_{\ell,33}=n_{\ell}-\frac{A_{\ell}^{2}\delta n_{\ell}}{\xi_{\ell,0}^{2}}, pℓ=−1p_{\ell}=-1, qℓ=0q_{\ell}=0, fℓ,0=nℓ−Aℓ2​δnℓξℓ,02f_{\ell,0}=n_{\ell}-\frac{A_{\ell}^{2}\text{$\delta$n}_{\ell}}{\xi_{\ell,0}^{2}}, fℓ,z=−Aℓ22​ξℓ,02f_{\ell,z}=-\frac{A_{\ell}^{2}}{2\xi_{\ell,0}^{2}}, and fℓ,x=0f_{\ell,x}=0. Finally, we have

($̱\hat{n}$ℓ(3))q,ℓ=nℓ+Aℓ2ξℓ,02​(−nℓ001−nℓ),\displaystyle\left(\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{n}$}}_{\ell}^{\left(3\right)}\right)_{q,\ell}=n_{\ell}+\frac{A_{\ell}^{2}}{\xi_{\ell,0}^{2}}\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}-n_{\ell}&0\\ 0&1-n_{\ell}\end{array}\right),
n^e​f​f,ℓ=nℓ+Aℓ2ξℓ,02​(n^ℓ−nℓ),\displaystyle\hat{n}_{eff,\ell}=n_{\ell}+\frac{A_{\ell}^{2}}{\xi_{\ell,0}^{2}}\left(\hat{n}_{\ell}-n_{\ell}\right), (395)

recovering the qubit energy form of ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}. The preceding result demonstrates that when all orbitals have ξℓ=0\xi_{\ell}=0, implying that the system is a Mott insulator, the ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3} solution can be recovered by ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}, demonstrating the power of ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2} in the Mott phase.

VII Applications: multiorbital Hubbard model at half filling with particle-hole symmetry in d=∞d=\infty

Here we showcase how to use the qubit energy form for ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3} to study the multiorbital Hubbard model in d=∞d=\infty with density-density interactions. While the qubit energy form can be applied to arbitrary densities, here we study the case of half-filling where the local interaction energy takes a simple form. In Section VII.1, we explicitly evaluate the qubit energy form for half-filling and demonstrate how to analytically minimize over the momentum density distribution, yielding a final energy form which can straightforwardly be numerically minimized. In Section VII.2, we demonstrate that Δℓ\Delta_{\ell}, defined in Eq. (67), is a key variable for understanding the Mott transition. For a special density-of-states, the minimization can be analytically performed, yielding an analytical relation between the ground state energy and the Hubbard UU via Δℓ\Delta_{\ell}. In Section VII.3, we study the effect of the Hund coupling JJ on the nature of the Mott transition in the multiorbital Hubbard model.

VII.1 Numerical minimization of the qubit trial energy

VII.1.1 Evaluating the qubit trial energy

In order to elucidate the results of the multiorbital Hubbard model, we first begin by considering the single orbital case with density of states D⁡(ϵ)D\left(\epsilon\right) having particle-hole symmetry. Due to spin symmetry, we omit the spin-orbital index ℓ\ell in ξℓ,\xi_{\ell},Δℓ\Delta_{\ell}, and Aℓ=𝒜<ℓ+𝒜>ℓA_{\ell}=\mathcal{A}_{<\ell}+\mathcal{A}_{>\ell}. The qubit energy form for ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3} is given as (see Section VI.4.1 for derivation)

E⁡(n⁡(ϵ),𝝆)=2​∫−∞∞d​ϵ​D​(ϵ)​ϵ​n​(ϵ)+U​⟨n^e​f​f,↑​n^e​f​f,↓⟩𝝆,\displaystyle E(n(\epsilon),\bm{\rho})=2\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\epsilon D\left(\epsilon\right)\epsilon n\left(\epsilon\right)+U\langle\hat{n}_{eff,\uparrow}\hat{n}_{eff,\downarrow}\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}, (396)
n^e​f​f,ℓ=12+ℱ⁡(Δ,A,ξ)​(n^ℓ−12),\displaystyle\hat{n}_{eff,\ell}=\frac{1}{2}+\mathcal{F}(\Delta,A,\xi)\left(\hat{n}_{\ell}-\frac{1}{2}\right), (397)
ℱ⁡(Δ,A,ξ)=2​A21−4​ξ2​(1−4​ξ2(1−2Δ)2+1),\displaystyle\mathcal{F}(\Delta,A,\xi)=\frac{2A^{2}}{1-4\xi^{2}}\left(\sqrt{1-\frac{4\xi^{2}}{\left(1-2\Delta\right){}^{2}}}+1\right), (398)
A=∫−∞∞d​ϵ​D​(ϵ)​n​(ϵ)​(1−n​(ϵ)),\displaystyle A=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\epsilon D(\epsilon)\sqrt{n(\epsilon)\left(1-n(\epsilon)\right)}, (399)
Δ=∫0∞d​ϵ​D​(ϵ)​n​(ϵ),\displaystyle\Delta=\int_{0}^{\infty}d\epsilon D(\epsilon)n(\epsilon), (400)
ξ=12​⟨σ^ℓx⟩𝝆,\displaystyle\xi=\frac{1}{2}\langle\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{x}\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}, (401)

where particle-hole symmetry implies n⁡(ϵ)+n⁡(−ϵ)=1n\left(\epsilon\right)+n\left(-\epsilon\right)=1, and in order to ensure that ℱ⁡(Δ,A,ξ)\mathcal{F}(\Delta,A,\xi) is real, ξ\xi must satisfy the following constraint

|ξ|≤12−Δ.\displaystyle\left|\xi\right|\leq\frac{1}{2}-\Delta. (402)

The effective many-body density matrix 𝝆\bm{\rho} can be encoded as 𝝆=|Ψ⟩​⟨Ψ|\bm{\rho}=|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi| where |Ψ⟩|\Psi\rangle can be parametrized using a single parameter 𝒟∈[0,1/2]\mathcal{D}\in[0,1/2] as

|Ψ⟩=(𝒟12−𝒟12−𝒟𝒟)T.|\Psi\rangle=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccc}\sqrt{\mathcal{D}}&\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}-\mathcal{D}}&\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}-\mathcal{D}}&\sqrt{\mathcal{D}}\end{array}\right)^{T}. (403)

This parametrization ensures that nℓ=1/2n_{\ell}=1/2 and ξ\xi can be determined as

ξ=2​(12−𝒟)​𝒟.\xi=2\sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{2}-\mathcal{D}\right)\mathcal{D}}. (404)

The double occupancy is given as

d⁡(Δ,A,𝒟)=⟨n^e​f​f,↑​n^e​f​f,↓⟩𝝆=(𝒟−14)​ℱ2+14\displaystyle d(\Delta,A,\mathcal{D})=\left\langle\hat{n}_{eff,\uparrow}\hat{n}_{eff,\downarrow}\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}=\left(\mathcal{D}-\frac{1}{4}\right)\mathcal{F}^{2}+\frac{1}{4} (405)
=14​(4​A4​(1−2​Δ+h⁡(Δ,𝒟))2(1−2Δ)2(4𝒟−1)3+1),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{4A^{4}(1-2\Delta+h\left(\Delta,\mathcal{D}\right))^{2}}{(1-2\Delta)^{2}\left(4\mathcal{D}-1\right){}^{3}}+1\right), (406)
h⁡(Δ,𝒟)=8​𝒟​(2​𝒟−1)+(1−2​Δ)2\displaystyle h(\Delta,\mathcal{D})=\sqrt{8\mathcal{D}\left(2\mathcal{D}-1\right)+(1-2\Delta)^{2}} (407)

and to have a real d⁡(Δ,A,𝒟)d(\Delta,A,\mathcal{D}), the h⁡(Δ,𝒟)h(\Delta,\mathcal{D}) must be real which requires 𝒟\mathcal{D} to satisfy the following constraint

𝒟∈[0,𝒟−]∪[𝒟+,12],\displaystyle\mathcal{D}\in[0,\mathcal{D}_{-}]\cup[\mathcal{D}_{+},\frac{1}{2}], (408)
𝒟±=14±12​(1−Δ)​Δ.\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\pm}=\frac{1}{4}\pm\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{(1-\Delta)\Delta}. (409)

Finally, the trial energy for the single orbital case is a function only of n⁡(ϵ)n(\epsilon) and 𝒟\mathcal{D}, given as

E⁡(n⁡(ϵ),𝒟)=2​∫−∞∞d​ϵ​D​(ϵ)​ϵ​n​(ϵ)+U​d​(Δ,A,𝒟).E(n(\epsilon),\mathcal{D})=2\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\epsilon D\left(\epsilon\right)\epsilon n\left(\epsilon\right)+Ud(\Delta,A,\mathcal{D}). (410)

We now proceed to the multiorbital case, with a local interaction given as

H^l​o​c=∑ℓ<ℓ′Uℓ​ℓ′​δ​n^ℓ​δ​n^ℓ′,\hat{H}_{loc}=\sum_{\ell<\ell^{\prime}}U_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}\delta\hat{n}_{\ell}\delta\hat{n}_{\ell^{\prime}}, (411)

where δ​n^ℓ=n^ℓ−12\delta\hat{n}_{\ell}=\hat{n}_{\ell}-\frac{1}{2}. The qubit trial energy is given as

E⁡({nℓ​(ϵ)},𝝆)=∑ℓ∫−∞∞d​ϵ​Dℓ​(ϵ)​ϵ​nℓ​(ϵ)\displaystyle E(\{n_{\ell}(\epsilon)\},\bm{\rho})=\sum_{\ell}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\epsilon D_{\ell}\left(\epsilon\right)\epsilon n_{\ell}\left(\epsilon\right)
+∑ℓ<ℓ′ℱ(Δℓ,Aℓ,ξℓ)ℱ(Δℓ′,Aℓ′,ξℓ′)Uℓ​ℓ′⟨δn^ℓδn^ℓ′⟩𝝆,\displaystyle+\sum_{\ell<\ell^{\prime}}\mathcal{F}(\Delta_{\ell},A_{\ell},\xi_{\ell})\mathcal{F}(\Delta_{\ell^{\prime}},A_{\ell^{\prime}},\xi_{\ell^{\prime}})U_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}\langle\delta\hat{n}_{\ell}\delta\hat{n}_{\ell^{\prime}}\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}, (412)

where 𝝆\bm{\rho} is a pure state that is restricted to ⟨n^ℓ⟩𝝆=12\langle\hat{n}_{\ell}\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}=\frac{1}{2}, particle-hole symmetry implies nℓ​(ϵ)+nℓ​(−ϵ)=1n_{\ell}\left(\epsilon\right)+n_{\ell}\left(-\epsilon\right)=1, and ξℓ\xi_{\ell} must satisfy the following constraint

|ξℓ|≤12−Δℓ.\displaystyle\left|\xi_{\ell}\right|\leq\frac{1}{2}-\Delta_{\ell}. (413)

The expression for ℱ⁡(Δℓ,Aℓ,ξℓ)\mathcal{F}(\Delta_{\ell},A_{\ell},\xi_{\ell}) is given in Eq. (398). The most straightforward approach to satisfying Eq. (413) is to first choose 𝝆\bm{\rho}, and then Eq. (413) becomes a linear constraint on nℓ​(ϵ)n_{\ell}(\epsilon) (see Section III for further discussion).

VII.1.2 Numerical minimization of the qubit trial energy

We now proceed to minimizing the qubit trial energy. As before, we first focus on the single orbital model for clarity, and then consider the multiorbital case. The general numerical minimization has been described in Section III, which consists of two steps: First, the momentum density distribution is partially optimized under the constraint of nℓn_{\ell}, Δℓ\Delta_{\ell}, 𝒜<ℓ\mathcal{A}_{<\ell}, and 𝒜>ℓ\mathcal{A}_{>\ell}, or through four Lagrange multiplier a<ℓa_{<\ell}, a>ℓ,a_{>\ell}, b<ℓb_{<\ell}, and b>ℓb_{>\ell}. Second, one needs to minimize over the remaining 22​No​r​b+3×2​No​r​b−12^{2N_{orb}}+3\times 2N_{orb}-1 independent variational parameters subjected to the inequality constraint given by Eq. (70). For the half-filled, particle-hole symmetric case, there are several simplifications. First, the optimized momentum density distribution now only depends on Δℓ\Delta_{\ell} and Aℓ=𝒜<ℓ+𝒜>ℓA_{\ell}=\mathcal{A}_{<\ell}+\mathcal{A}_{>\ell}, or just two Lagrange multipliers a=a<σ=−a>σa=a_{<\sigma}=-a_{>\sigma} and b=b>σ=b<σb=b_{>\sigma}=b_{<\sigma}, and the partially optimized momentum density distribution is given as

n⁡(ϵ,a,b)={12​(1−a+ϵ(a+ϵ)2+b2)ϵ>012​(1+a−ϵ(a−ϵ)2+b2)ϵ<0,n\left(\epsilon,a,b\right)=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{a+\epsilon}{\sqrt{(a+\epsilon)^{2}+b^{2}}}\right)&\epsilon>0\\ \frac{1}{2}\left(1+\frac{a-\epsilon}{\sqrt{(a-\epsilon)^{2}+b^{2}}}\right)&\epsilon<0\end{cases}, (414)

where the Lagrange multipliers aa and bb are determined by Δ\Delta and AA via inverting the following relation

A⁡(a,b)=∫−∞∞d​ϵ​D​(ϵ)​n⁡(ϵ,a,b)​(1−n⁡(ϵ,a,b)),\displaystyle A(a,b)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\epsilon D(\epsilon)\sqrt{n(\epsilon,a,b)\left(1-n(\epsilon,a,b)\right)}, (415)
Δ⁡(a,b)=∫0∞d​ϵ​D​(ϵ)​n​(ϵ,a,b),\displaystyle\Delta(a,b)=\int_{0}^{\infty}d\epsilon D(\epsilon)n(\epsilon,a,b), (416)

which yields a⁡(Δ,A)a\left(\Delta,A\right) and b⁡(Δ,A)b\left(\Delta,A\right). In order to better appreciate the flexibility of n⁡(ϵ,a,b)n\left(\epsilon,a,b\right), it is useful to examine the behavior for various choices of aa and bb (see Figure 1). For a>0a>0 and b>0b>0, the distribution corresponds to a Fermi liquid, given that the discontinuity of n⁡(ϵ,a,b)n\left(\epsilon,a,b\right) at ϵ=0\epsilon=0 yields a quasi-particle weight ZZ of

Z=aa2+b2,Z=\frac{a}{\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}}, (417)

which will be between zero and one. For the special case where a→∞a\rightarrow\infty and b→∞b\rightarrow\infty with a/ba/b remaining finite, the distribution recovers a flat distribution, which is obtained for an optimized ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2}. Finally, when a=0a=0 and b>0b>0, the system is in the Mott phase where Z=0Z=0.

The second simplification for half-filling and particle-hole symmetry is that the number of independent parameters is 22​No​r​b+2​No​r​b−12^{2N_{orb}}+2N_{orb}-1, given that nℓ=1/2n_{\ell}=1/2 and 𝒜<ℓ=𝒜>ℓ\mathcal{A}_{<\ell}=\mathcal{A}_{>\ell}. If we have further symmetry between different spin orbitals, the number of independent parameters can further be reduced. For example, for the single-orbital case with spin symmetry, we have Aℓ=AA_{\ell}=A and Δℓ=Δ\Delta_{\ell}=\Delta, and therefore the number of independent parameters is 22+2−1−2=32^{2}+2-1-2=3. As discussed in Section III, there are two possible strategies. The first strategy starts from a,ba,b, which determines n⁡(ϵ)n\left(\epsilon\right), and 𝝆\bm{\rho} is specified via 𝒟\mathcal{D}, which will have a range given by Eq. (408). Mathematically, this qubit trial energy is given by

E⁡(a,b,𝒟)=\displaystyle E(a,b,\mathcal{D})= 2​∫−∞∞d​ϵ​D​(ϵ)​ϵ​n​(ϵ,a,b)\displaystyle 2\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\epsilon D\left(\epsilon\right)\epsilon n\left(\epsilon,a,b\right)
+U​d​(Δ⁡(a,b),A⁡(a,b),𝒟).\displaystyle+Ud(\Delta(a,b),A(a,b),\mathcal{D}). (418)

This strategy allows the energy to be explicitly written in terms of the variational parameters, and thus it is straightforward to compute the derivatives via automatic differentiation. For the multiorbital case, the constraint between 𝝆\bm{\rho} and {Δℓ}\{\Delta_{\ell}\} is given by Eq. (413), which is not straightforward to implement for a given {Δℓ}\{\Delta_{\ell}\}. Therefore, it is useful to pursue a second strategy.

We begin by illustrating the second strategy in the single-orbital case. This strategy begins by specifying 𝝆\bm{\rho} via 𝒟\mathcal{D}, then the range of Δ\Delta can be determined from the constraint given by Eq. (402), and then Δ\Delta and bb can be specified, which determines aa via inverting Eq. (416), denoted as a⁡(Δ,b)a\left(\Delta,b\right). Mathematically, the resulting qubit trial energy is given by

E⁡(Δ,b,𝒟)=\displaystyle E(\Delta,b,\mathcal{D})= 2​∫−∞∞d​ϵ​D​(ϵ)​ϵ​n​(ϵ,a⁡(Δ,b),b)\displaystyle 2\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\epsilon D\left(\epsilon\right)\epsilon n\left(\epsilon,a(\Delta,b),b\right)
+U​d​(Δ,A⁡(a⁡(Δ,b),b),𝒟).\displaystyle+Ud(\Delta,A(a(\Delta,b),b),\mathcal{D}). (419)

For the multiorbital case, the qubit trial energy is given as

E⁡({Δℓ},{bℓ},𝝆)\displaystyle E(\{\Delta_{\ell}\},\{b_{\ell}\},\bm{\rho})
=∑ℓ∫−∞∞d​ϵ​Dℓ​(ϵ)​ϵ​n​(ϵ,aℓ​(Δℓ,bℓ),bℓ)\displaystyle=\sum_{\ell}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\epsilon D_{\ell}\left(\epsilon\right)\epsilon n\left(\epsilon,a_{\ell}(\Delta_{\ell},b_{\ell}),b_{\ell}\right)
+∑ℓ<ℓ′ℱℓℱℓ′Uℓ​ℓ′⟨δn^ℓδn^ℓ′⟩𝝆,\displaystyle+\sum_{\ell<\ell^{\prime}}\mathcal{F}_{\ell}\mathcal{F}_{\ell^{\prime}}U_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}\langle\delta\hat{n}_{\ell}\delta\hat{n}_{\ell^{\prime}}\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}, (420)
ℱℓ=ℱ⁡(Δℓ,Aℓ​(aℓ​(Δℓ,bℓ),bℓ),12​⟨σ^ℓx⟩𝝆),\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{\ell}=\mathcal{F}(\Delta_{\ell},A_{\ell}(a_{\ell}(\Delta_{\ell},b_{\ell}),b_{\ell}),\frac{1}{2}\langle\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{x}\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}), (421)

where aℓ​(Δℓ,bℓ)a_{\ell}(\Delta_{\ell},b_{\ell}) and Aℓ​(aℓ,bℓ)A_{\ell}(a_{\ell},b_{\ell}) are the multiorbital versions of a⁡(Δ,b)a(\Delta,b) and A⁡(a,b)A(a,b). The second strategy allows one to automatically implement all of the constraints in the multiorbital case, and the only downside is that aℓ​(Δℓ,bℓ)a_{\ell}(\Delta_{\ell},b_{\ell}) must be numerically evaluated, though this is a trivial task.

VII.2 Understanding the Mott transition in the single orbital model

In the preceding section, the resulting qubit trial energy for the single orbital model at half-filling is either parametrized by aa, bb, and 𝒟\mathcal{D} (i.e. Eq. (418)), or Δ\Delta, bb and 𝒟\mathcal{D} (i.e. Eq. (419)), which both allow for straightforward numerical minimization for a given UU and D⁡(ϵ)D(\epsilon). In this section, we explore a different perspective based on the one body reduced density matrix viewpoint (see Ref. [1]), which provides a clearer understanding of the Mott transition. The first step begins with the parametrization of the qubit trial energy using Δ\Delta, AA, and 𝒟\mathcal{D}, where the local interaction energy is U​d​(Δ,A,𝒟)Ud(\Delta,A,\mathcal{D}), where d⁡(Δ,A,𝒟)d(\Delta,A,\mathcal{D}) is defined in Eq. (406). It should be noted that d⁡(Δ,A,𝒟)d(\Delta,A,\mathcal{D}) has the form 1/4+A4​f​(Δ,𝒟)1/4+A^{4}f(\Delta,\mathcal{D}), and therefore we can optimize d⁡(Δ,A,𝒟)d(\Delta,A,\mathcal{D}) with respect to 𝒟\mathcal{D} for fixed Δ\Delta and AA, yielding an optimized 𝒟\mathcal{D} as a function of Δ\Delta, denoted as 𝒟⁡(Δ)\mathcal{D}\left(\Delta\right). Therefore, the interaction energy is purely a function of Δ\Delta and AA, which can be viewed as a one body reduced density matrix functional, yielding a simple picture of the Mott transition. Two key points should be appreciated. First, 𝒟⁡(Δ)\mathcal{D}\left(\Delta\right) has a critical value of Δ\Delta, denoted Δc\Delta_{c}, and 𝒟⁡(Δ)=0\mathcal{D}\left(\Delta\right)=0 for Δ≥Δc\Delta\geq\Delta_{c}, which corresponds to the Mott insulator. The second point is that Δc\Delta_{c} is independent of D⁡(ϵ)D(\epsilon). While the total energy can be obtained by numerically minimizing over Δ\Delta and AA, further insight can be obtained by expressing UU and the total energy as functions of Δ\Delta.

VII.2.1 Qubit trial energy in terms of Δ\Delta and AA

As outlined in Section VII.1.2, the qubit trial energy can be parametrized as

E⁡(Δ,A,𝒟)=K⁡(Δ,A)+U​d​(Δ,A,𝒟),\displaystyle E(\Delta,A,\mathcal{D})=K(\Delta,A)+Ud(\Delta,A,\mathcal{D}), (422)
K⁡(Δ,A)=2​∫−∞∞d​ϵ​D​(ϵ)​ϵ​n​(ϵ,a⁡(Δ,A),b⁡(Δ,A)).\displaystyle K(\Delta,A)=2\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\epsilon D\left(\epsilon\right)\epsilon n\left(\epsilon,a(\Delta,A),b(\Delta,A)\right). (423)

For simplicity, we study the case where U≥0U\geq 0. We now consider how to minimize the total energy over 𝒟\mathcal{D}, which amounts to minimizing d⁡(Δ,A,𝒟)d(\Delta,A,\mathcal{D}) over 𝒟\mathcal{D}. In order to visualize the minimization, we plot dd as a function of 𝒟\mathcal{D} for a given Δ\Delta and AA. Given that AA will not influence the minimization over 𝒟\mathcal{D}, we choose A=(2−4​Δ)​ΔA=\sqrt{\left(2-4\Delta\right)\Delta} from a flat momentum density distribution (see Figure 2). For a given Δ\Delta curve, there are four distinct sets of points denoted as ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2}, ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}, ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3}, and m​a​xmax, where the ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3} points provide the optimized values for 𝒟\mathcal{D}, the ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} and ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2} points provide the 𝒟\mathcal{D} values for ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} and ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}, respectively, and a m​a​xmax point provides the maximum value for 𝒟\mathcal{D} given by 𝒟−\mathcal{D}_{-} in Eq. (409). For small values of Δ\Delta, the optimized value of 𝒟\mathcal{D} is nonzero, and 𝒟\mathcal{D} monotonically decreases with increasing Δ\Delta. For Δ\Delta larger than some critical value, the optimized value for 𝒟\mathcal{D} is zero. Having obtained a graphical understanding of this function, we proceed to mathematically minimize the dd over 𝒟\mathcal{D} for a given Δ\Delta and AA, which is a constrained minimization given that 𝒟∈[0,𝒟−]\mathcal{D}\in[0,\mathcal{D}_{-}]. Solving ∂d/∂𝒟=0\partial d/\partial\mathcal{D}=0 yields

𝒟⋆​(Δ)=14−14​6​(Δ−1)​Δ+(3​Δ−32)​h1+92,\displaystyle\mathcal{D}^{\star}(\Delta)=\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{6(\Delta-1)\Delta+\left(3\Delta-\frac{3}{2}\right)h_{1}+\frac{9}{2}}, (424)
h1=4​(Δ−1)​Δ+9.\displaystyle h_{1}=\sqrt{4(\Delta-1)\Delta+9}. (425)

When 𝒟⋆​(Δ)∈[0,𝒟−]\mathcal{D}^{\star}(\Delta)\in[0,\mathcal{D}_{-}], then 𝒟⋆​(Δ)\mathcal{D}^{\star}(\Delta) yields the optimized value for 𝒟\mathcal{D}, and otherwise the optimized value is given by the minimum value for the boundary points. It is useful to solve 𝒟⋆​(Δ)=0\mathcal{D}^{\star}(\Delta)=0, yielding

Δc=16​(3−3)≈0.211325.\Delta_{c}=\frac{1}{6}\left(3-\sqrt{3}\right)\approx 0.211325. (426)

Therefore, the optimized value for 𝒟\mathcal{D} is

𝒟⁡(Δ)={𝒟⋆​(Δ),Δ<Δc,0,Δ≥Δc,\mathcal{D}(\Delta)=\begin{cases}\mathcal{D}^{\star}(\Delta),&\Delta<\Delta_{c},\\ 0,&\Delta\geq\Delta_{c},\end{cases} (427)

having two distinct regimes as a function of Δ\Delta (see inset of Figure 2). Finally, the physical double occupancy can be written as a function of Δ\Delta and AA as

d⁡(Δ,A)={d⁡(Δ,A,𝒟⋆​(Δ)),Δ<Δc,14−4​A4,Δ≥Δc.d(\Delta,A)=\begin{cases}d(\Delta,A,\mathcal{D}^{\star}(\Delta)),&\Delta<\Delta_{c},\\ \frac{1}{4}-4A^{4},&\Delta\geq\Delta_{c}.\end{cases} (428)

Therefore, the total trial energy can be written purely in terms of Δ\Delta and AA, given as

E⁡(Δ,A)=K⁡(Δ,A)+U​d​(Δ,A).E(\Delta,A)=K(\Delta,A)+Ud(\Delta,A). (429)

In order to find the ground state for a given D⁡(ϵ)D(\epsilon) and UU, it is necessary to minimize over Δ\Delta and AA, which cannot be performed analytically in general. However, it is important to appreciate that the optimized value of Δ\Delta is sufficient to determine if the system is in the Mott phase. For Δ=0\Delta=0, the ansatz corresponds to the Hartree-Fock wave function, while the maximum value of Δ=1/4\Delta=1/4 corresponds to a collection of isolated atoms, and the Mott transition occurs when Δ=Δc\Delta=\Delta_{c}, before the system becomes a collection of atoms. We now verify that the system is indeed a Mott insulator for Δ>Δc\Delta>\Delta_{c}. First, the local interaction energy is independent of Δ\Delta for Δ>Δc\Delta>\Delta_{c} (see Eq. (427)), dictating that a=0a=0 for the optimized Δ\Delta. Second, Eq. (417) dictates that the quasiparticle weight is zero when a=0a=0, implying a Mott insulating state. Alternatively, when Δ<Δc\Delta<\Delta_{c}, the ansatz describes a metallic phase.

Following the results of Sections VI.4.2 and VI.4.3, we illustrate how the qubit energy form for ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} and ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2} can be recovered from ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3} when properly restricting the variational parameters. We begin with ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}, which can be viewed as a continuation of the Mott phase for ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3}, where 𝒟=0\mathcal{D}=0 and dd is given by 14−4​A4\frac{1}{4}-4A^{4} (see Figure 2). Alternatively, the ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} is characterized by a flat momentum density distribution determined by Δ\Delta where dd and 𝒟\mathcal{D} are identical, given as

dG​2=𝒟G​2=14​(1−2​Δ).d_{G2}=\mathcal{D}_{G2}=\frac{1}{4}\left(1-2\sqrt{\Delta}\right). (430)

It is well known that for ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} the Mott transition occurs when the system becomes a collection of isolated atoms, meaning that the transition happens for Δ=1/4\Delta=1/4.

VII.2.2 Solution for the two-peak density of states

In Section VII.2.1, we demonstrated that the interaction energy can be written analytically in terms of Δ\Delta and AA, but the kinetic energy must be numerically determined in terms of Δ\Delta and AA. While the latter is a trivial numerical problem, it still precludes a completely analytic solution for the energy in terms of UU. Therefore, we introduce the two-peak density of states, where the kinetic energy can be analytically evaluated in terms of Δ\Delta and AA, allowing for an analytical relation between the total energy and the Hubbard U/|K0|U/|K_{0}| in all three ansatz, where K0<0K_{0}<0 is the non-interacting kinetic energy for the lattice. Specifically, the two-peak density of states is given by

D⁡(ϵ)=12​(δ⁡(ϵ−K0)+δ⁡(ϵ+K0)).D\left(\epsilon\right)=\frac{1}{2}\left(\delta\left(\epsilon-K_{0}\right)+\delta\left(\epsilon+K_{0}\right)\right). (431)

While this density of states is somewhat unphysical, the results retain all of the qualitative features of the Bethe lattice, in addition to being quantitatively very similar assuming the same K0K_{0} (see Figure 3). As expected, the ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} solution is identical for both density of states, given that ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} only depends on K0K_{0}, independent of the details of D⁡(ϵ)D(\epsilon). Interestingly, ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3} has a very similar critical value of U/|K0|U/|K_{0}| for both density of states, with small differences differences in the double occupancy for a given U/|K0|U/|K_{0}|.

We now proceed to analytically evaluate the total trial energy as a function of Δ\Delta for the two-peak model. Using Eqns. (431), (400), and (399), the kinetic energy and AA are determined as K=(1−4​Δ)​K0K=\left(1-4\Delta\right)K_{0} and A=(2−4​Δ)​ΔA=\sqrt{\left(2-4\Delta\right)\Delta}, yielding the total trial energy in terms of the single variational parameter Δ\Delta, given as

E⁡(Δ)=(1−4​Δ)​K0+U​d​(Δ),E\left(\Delta\right)=\left(1-4\Delta\right)K_{0}+Ud\left(\Delta\right), (432)

where

d⁡(Δ)={d1​(Δ),Δ≤Δc14−16​(1−2​Δ)2​Δ2,Δ>Δc\displaystyle d(\Delta)=\begin{cases}d_{1}(\Delta),&\Delta\leq\Delta_{c}\\ \frac{1}{4}-16(1-2\Delta)^{2}\Delta^{2},&\Delta>\Delta_{c}\end{cases} (433)

and d1​(Δ)d_{1}(\Delta) is defined in Eq. (97). The d⁡(Δ)d(\Delta) is plotted in Figure 4aa. While for a given UU the energy cannot be analytically minimized over Δ\Delta, it is straightforward to find UU for a given value of Δ\Delta that satisfies d​E​(Δ)/d​Δ=0dE(\Delta)/d\Delta=0, given as

U⁡(Δ)=−4​|K0|​(dd​Δ​d​(Δ))−1,U(\Delta)=-4\left|K_{0}\right|\left(\frac{d}{d\Delta}d(\Delta)\right)^{-1}, (434)

and U/|K0|U/|K_{0}| is plotted as a function of Δ\Delta in Figure 4bb. The critical value of UU and double occupancy at the Mott transition, where Δ=Δc\Delta=\Delta_{c}, are given as

Uc/|K0|=38​(9+5​3)≈6.6226,\displaystyle U_{c}/|K_{0}|=\frac{3}{8}\left(9+5\sqrt{3}\right)\approx 6.6226, (435)
dc=136​(32​3−55)≈0.0118229.\displaystyle d_{c}=\frac{1}{36}\left(32\sqrt{3}-55\right)\approx 0.0118229. (436)

These values are the same from both the metallic and insulating sides of the Mott transition, which can be seen in Figure 4, confirming that the transition is continuous.

Corresponding equations for dd and U/|K0|U/|K_{0}| as functions of Δ\Delta can be obtained for ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} and ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2} by substituting the corresponding d⁡(Δ)d(\Delta) relations into Eq. (434) (see Figure 4 for plots). For ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2}, we have

dG​2​(Δ)=14​(1−2​Δ),\displaystyle d_{G2}(\Delta)=\frac{1}{4}\left(1-2\sqrt{\Delta}\right), (437)
UG​2​(Δ)=16​|K0|​Δ,\displaystyle U_{G2}(\Delta)=16\left|K_{0}\right|\sqrt{\Delta}, (438)

which recovers the Gutzwiller approximation, and the Mott transition occurs at Δ=1/4\Delta=1/4, where Uc,G​2/|K0|=8U_{c,G2}/\left|K_{0}\right|=8 and dc,G​2=0d_{c,G2}=0. For ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}, there are some subtleties to consider. For a given UU, there are several candidate values of Δ\Delta: the value given by the saddle point Eq. (434), which yields

dB​2​(Δ)=14−16​(1−2​Δ)2​Δ2,\displaystyle d_{B2}(\Delta)=\frac{1}{4}-16(1-2\Delta)^{2}\Delta^{2}, (439)
UB​2​(Δ)=|K0|64​Δ3−48​Δ2+8​Δ,\displaystyle U_{B2}(\Delta)=\frac{\left|K_{0}\right|}{64\Delta^{3}-48\Delta^{2}+8\Delta}, (440)

and the boundary values of Δ=0\Delta=0 and Δ=1/2\Delta=1/2. The total energy must be used to evaluate these candidate values of Δ\Delta and select the global minimum. It should be noted that Δ=0\Delta=0 recovers the Hartree-Fock solution. There are two critical points to consider: the local stability of ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2} and a transition from a saddle point solution to the Hartree-Fock solution. The local stability of the ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2} is determined by the minimal value of UU in Eq. 440, which is given by

Uc,B​2/|K0|=3​32≈2.59808,\displaystyle U_{c,B2}/\left|K_{0}\right|=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\approx 2.59808, (441)
dc,B​2=536≈0.138889,\displaystyle d_{c,B2}=\frac{5}{36}\approx 0.138889, (442)
Δc,B​2=112​(3−3)≈0.105662.\displaystyle\Delta_{c,B2}=\frac{1}{12}\left(3-\sqrt{3}\right)\approx 0.105662. (443)

For any U>Uc,B​2U>U_{c,B2}, there exists a locally stable ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2} solution. However, one should compare the energy of the saddle-point solution to the Hartree-Fock solution, which yields another critical value of Uc,B​2′/|K0|=3.375U_{c,B2}^{\prime}/|K_{0}|=3.375. For U>Uc,B​2′U>U_{c,B2}^{\prime}, the saddle point solution is the global minimum, while for U<Uc,B​2′U<U_{c,B2}^{\prime} the Hartree-Fock solution is the global minimum. We summarize all the critical points for ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3}, ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2}, and ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2} in Table 1.

VII.2.3 Solution for a general density of states

In Section VII.2.2, we demonstrated that the qubit trial energy can be written solely in terms of Δ\Delta for the case of a two-peak density of states. Here we extend this strategy for a general density of states, allowing for the optimized value of AA to be evaluated as a function of Δ\Delta, which is completely independent of UU. Therefore, this approach is particularly useful for analyzing the Mott transition. We begin by rewriting the qubit trial energy from Eq. (429) using the result of Eq. (433), yielding

E⁡(Δ,A)=K⁡(Δ,A)+14​U+U​A4​O~​(Δ),E(\Delta,A)=K\left(\Delta,A\right)+\frac{1}{4}U+UA^{4}\tilde{O}\left(\Delta\right), (444)

where O~​(Δ)\tilde{O}\left(\Delta\right) is given in Eq. (96). We proceed by constructing the saddle point equations of Δ\Delta and AA for a given UU, yielding the following two equations

∂K∂Δ=−4​a=−U​A4​∂O~​(Δ)∂Δ,\displaystyle\frac{\partial K}{\partial\Delta}=-4a=-UA^{4}\frac{\partial\tilde{O}\left(\Delta\right)}{\partial\Delta}, (445)
∂K∂A=2​b=−4​U​A3​O~​(Δ),\displaystyle\frac{\partial K}{\partial A}=2b=-4UA^{3}\tilde{O}\left(\Delta\right), (446)

where aa and bb are the Lagrange multipliers from Eq. (414). A practical approach for solving the two preceding equations for a given UU is to express AA and Δ\Delta in terms of aa and bb, denoted as A⁡(a,b)A(a,b) and Δ⁡(a,b)\Delta(a,b), and then solve for aa and bb. However, we take an alternative approach, as our goal is to determine the optimized value of AA for a given Δ\Delta. Therefore, we proceed by dividing Eq. (445) by Eq. (446), which yields

−8​aA⁡(a,b)​b=d​ln⁡|O~​(Δ)|d​Δ.-\frac{8a}{A\left(a,b\right)b}=\frac{d\ln\left|\tilde{O}\left(\Delta\right)\right|}{d\Delta}. (447)

Moreover, aa and bb are required to yield the given value of Δ\Delta, such that

Δ⁡(a,b)=Δ.\Delta\left(a,b\right)=\Delta. (448)

Simultaneously solving Eqns. (447) and (448) yields aa and bb as functions of Δ\Delta, and therefore all quantities that depend on n⁡(ϵ)n(\epsilon), including AA and KK, are now functions purely of Δ\Delta. Subsequently, the double occupancy and UU can be determined as a function of Δ\Delta as

d⁡(Δ)=14+U​A4​(Δ)​O~​(Δ),\displaystyle d(\Delta)=\frac{1}{4}+UA^{4}\left(\Delta\right)\tilde{O}\left(\Delta\right), (449)
U⁡(Δ)=−b⁡(Δ)2​A3​(Δ)​O~​(Δ).\displaystyle U(\Delta)=-\frac{b(\Delta)}{2A^{3}(\Delta)\tilde{O}\left(\Delta\right)}. (450)

Alternatively, the UU can also be expressed as

U⁡(Δ)=−d​Kd​Δ​(dd​Δ​d​(Δ))−1,U(\Delta)=-\frac{dK}{d\Delta}\left(\frac{d}{d\Delta}d(\Delta)\right)^{-1}, (451)

which will recover Eq. (434) when evaluating the two peak model. For the case of the Bethe lattice, we plot AA, aa, and bb as functions of Δ\Delta in Figure 5, and the critical values of all quantities are listed in Table 2.

VII.3 Understanding the effect of Hund’s coupling in the multiorbital Hubbard model

Here we generalize the treatment from Section VII.2 to the multiorbital case including the Hund coupling JJ. The key difference is that in the multiorbital case, one cannot analytically minimize over the local variational parameters, though these parameters can easily be numerically minimized as a function of Δ\Delta for a given J/UJ/U. The remaining procedure closely follows the single orbital case.

Consider the multiorbital Hubbard model defined in Eq. (94). The qubit trial energy can be written as

E⁡(Δ,A,𝝆)=K⁡(Δ,A)+El​o​c​(Δ,A,𝝆),\displaystyle E\left(\Delta,A,\bm{\rho}\right)=K\left(\Delta,A\right)+E_{loc}\left(\Delta,A,\bm{\rho}\right), (452)
K⁡(Δ,A)=2​No​r​b​∫−∞∞d​ϵ​D​(ϵ)​ϵ​n​(ϵ,a⁡(Δ,A),b⁡(Δ,A)),\displaystyle K(\Delta,A)=2N_{orb}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\epsilon D\left(\epsilon\right)\epsilon n\left(\epsilon,a(\Delta,A),b(\Delta,A)\right), (453)
El​o​c​(Δ,A,𝝆)=U​ℱ2​(Δ,A,ξ⁡(𝝆))​⟨O^⟩𝝆,\displaystyle E_{loc}\left(\Delta,A,\bm{\rho}\right)=U\mathcal{F}^{2}\left(\Delta,A,\xi(\bm{\rho})\right)\langle\hat{O}\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}, (454)

where ℱ⁡(Δ,A,ξ)\mathcal{F}\left(\Delta,A,\xi\right) is defined in Eq. (398), ξ⁡(𝝆)=12​⟨σ^ℓx⟩𝝆\xi(\bm{\rho})=\frac{1}{2}\langle\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{x}\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}, and

O^=O^1+(1−2​JU)​O^2+(1−3​JU)​O^3,\hat{O}=\hat{O}_{1}+\left(1-2\frac{J}{U}\right)\hat{O}_{2}+\left(1-3\frac{J}{U}\right)\hat{O}_{3}, (455)

where O^i\hat{O}_{i} are defined in Eq. (94). Having defined the qubit trial energy, we proceed to obtain the solutions for the two-peak density of states and the Bethe lattice using the Δ\Delta parametrization. We first rewrite the local interaction energy as

El​o​c​(Δ,A,𝝆)=U​A4​ℱ~2​(Δ,ξ⁡(𝝆))​⟨O^⟩𝝆,E_{loc}\left(\Delta,A,\bm{\rho}\right)=UA^{4}\tilde{\mathcal{F}}^{2}\left(\Delta,\xi\left(\bm{\rho}\right)\right)\langle\hat{O}\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}, (456)

where

ℱ~​(Δ,ξ)=21−4​ξ2​(1−4​ξ2(1−2Δ)2+1),\tilde{\mathcal{F}}\left(\Delta,\xi\right)=\frac{2}{1-4\xi^{2}}\left(\sqrt{1-\frac{4\xi^{2}}{\left(1-2\Delta\right){}^{2}}}+1\right), (457)

which is obtained from ℱ⁡(Δ,A,ξ)/A2\mathcal{F}\left(\Delta,A,\xi\right)/A^{2}. Given the form of Eq. (456), the optimized 𝝆\bm{\rho} will only depend on Δ\Delta, motivating the definition of the following function

O~​(Δ)=min𝝆⁡ℱ~2​(Δ,ξ⁡(𝝆))​⟨O^⟩𝝆.\tilde{O}\left(\Delta\right)=\min_{\bm{\rho}}\tilde{\mathcal{F}}^{2}\left(\Delta,\xi\left(\bm{\rho}\right)\right)\langle\hat{O}\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}. (458)

A convenient way to generate this function is to perform a two stage minimization. First, we perform a constrained minimization with the restriction ξ⁡(𝝆)=ξ\xi\left(\bm{\rho}\right)=\xi on 𝝆\bm{\rho}. Second, we minimize the expression over ξ\xi. In the first stage, given that ℱ~2​(Δ,ξ​(𝝆))\tilde{\mathcal{F}}^{2}\left(\Delta,\xi\left(\bm{\rho}\right)\right) is fixed, we only need to minimize ⟨O^⟩𝝆\langle\hat{O}\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}, which can be mathematically expressed as

𝒪(ξ)=min𝝆{⟨O^⟩𝝆|12⟨σ^ℓx⟩𝝆=ξ,⟨σ^ℓz⟩𝝆=0}.\displaystyle\mathcal{O}(\xi)=\min_{\bm{\rho}}\{\langle\hat{O}\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}|\frac{1}{2}\langle\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{x}\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}=\xi,\hskip 1.99997pt\langle\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{z}\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}=0\}. (459)

To efficiently generate 𝒪⁡(ξ)\mathcal{O}\left(\xi\right) , we can introduce a Lagrange multiplier λ\lambda and determine the ground state for ℋ^=O^−λ​∑α​σξ^α​σ\hat{\mathcal{H}}=\hat{O}-\lambda\sum_{\alpha\sigma}\hat{\xi}_{\alpha\sigma}, yielding the optimal 𝝆\bm{\rho} and corresponding ξ\xi and ⟨O^⟩𝝆\langle\hat{O}\rangle_{\bm{\rho}} for a given λ\lambda. One can then perform such calculations over a grid of λ\lambda, and then spline the relationship between ⟨O^⟩𝝆\langle\hat{O}\rangle_{\bm{\rho}} and ξ\xi. A plot of 𝒪⁡(ξ)\mathcal{O}(\xi) is provided in Figure 2 of Ref. [1]. Finally, the partially optimized local energy can be written as

El​o​c​(Δ,A)=U​A4​O~​(Δ).\displaystyle E_{loc}\left(\Delta,A\right)=UA^{4}\tilde{O}\left(\Delta\right). (460)
O~​(Δ)=minξ∈[0,12−Δ]⁡ℱ~2​(Δ,ξ)​𝒪​(ξ).\displaystyle\tilde{O}\left(\Delta\right)=\min_{\xi\in\left[0,\frac{1}{2}-\Delta\right]}\tilde{\mathcal{F}}^{2}\left(\Delta,\xi\right)\mathcal{O}(\xi). (461)

In order to visualize O~​(Δ)\tilde{O}\left(\Delta\right) and ξ\xi as a function of Δ\Delta, we plot these quantities for J/U=0,0.05,0.25J/U=0,0.05,0.25 and No​r​b=2,3,5,7N_{orb}=2,3,5,7 (see Figure 6). For J/U=0J/U=0, one can clearly observe that ξ\xi continuously goes to zero, while there is a discontinuity for J/U=0.05J/U=0.05. For J/U=0.25J/U=0.25, ξ\xi discontinuously goes to zero for No​r​b=2,3N_{orb}=2,3 and continuously goes to zero for No​r​b=5,7N_{orb}=5,7. It should be noted that O~​(Δ)\tilde{O}\left(\Delta\right) can be applied to solve an arbitrary particle-hole symmetric D⁡(ϵ)D(\epsilon), and therefore captures the essence of the Mott transition for a given J/UJ/U.

VII.3.1 Understanding the non-analytic behavior of O~​(Δ)\tilde{O}\left(\Delta\right) via a Taylor series

In Section VII.2, we demonstrated that there is non-analyticity in O~​(Δ)\tilde{O}\left(\Delta\right) at Δ=Δc\Delta=\Delta_{c}. Here we provide a Taylor series analysis to explain how the non-analyticity emerges. Equation (461) indicates that O~​(Δ)\tilde{O}\left(\Delta\right) is the minimum of ℱ~2​(Δ,ξ)​𝒪​(ξ)\tilde{\mathcal{F}}^{2}\left(\Delta,\xi\right)\mathcal{O}(\xi) within the range ξ∈[0,12−Δ]\xi\in\left[0,\frac{1}{2}-\Delta\right], and it is convenient to study the quantity

ℒ⁡(Δ,ξ)=−ℱ~2​(Δ,ξ)ℱ~2​(Δ,0)​𝒪⁡(ξ)𝒪⁡(0).\mathcal{L}\left(\Delta,\xi\right)=-\frac{\tilde{\mathcal{F}}^{2}\left(\Delta,\xi\right)}{\mathcal{\tilde{F}}^{2}\left(\Delta,0\right)}\frac{\mathcal{O}\left(\xi\right)}{\mathcal{O}\left(0\right)}. (462)

Finding the minimum of ℒ⁡(Δ,ξ)\mathcal{L}\left(\Delta,\xi\right) will yield the minimum of ℱ~2​(Δ,ξ)​𝒪​(ξ)\tilde{\mathcal{F}}^{2}\left(\Delta,\xi\right)\mathcal{O}(\xi) given that ℱ~​(Δ,0)=4\tilde{\mathcal{F}}\left(\Delta,0\right)=4 and 𝒪⁡(0)=−14​No​r​b​(1+(No​r​b−1)​J/U)\mathcal{O}\left(0\right)=-\frac{1}{4}N_{orb}\left(1+\left(N_{orb}-1\right)J/U\right).

We begin by Taylor series expanding ℒ⁡(Δ,ξ)\mathcal{L}\left(\Delta,\xi\right) to sixth order in ξ\xi about ξ=0\xi=0, and the second order coefficient in ξ\xi is expanded in Δ\Delta about Δc,I\Delta_{c,I} such that it is zero for Δ=Δc,I\Delta=\Delta_{c,I}, yielding

ℒ⁡(Δ,ξ)≈−1+c2​(Δ−Δc,I)​ξ2+c4​ξ4+c6​ξ6,\mathcal{L}\left(\Delta,\xi\right)\approx-1+c_{2}\left(\Delta-\Delta_{c,I}\right)\xi^{2}+c_{4}\xi^{4}+c_{6}\xi^{6}, (463)

where c2c_{2}, c4c_{4}, c6c_{6}, and Δc,I\Delta_{c,I} are constants for a given No​r​bN_{orb} and J/UJ/U. Given that the optimized ξ\xi goes to zero with increasing Δ\Delta (see Figure 6), this requires c2>0c_{2}>0. Furthermore, we take c6>0c_{6}>0, though there will be cases where c6c_{6} is negative and a higher order expansion is necessary. Therefore, we only need to understand how the sign of c4c_{4} influences the non-analyticity in O~​(Δ)\tilde{O}\left(\Delta\right). For c4>0c_{4}>0, when Δ>Δc;I\Delta>\Delta_{c;I}, the minimum of ℒ\mathcal{L} is given by ℒ=−1\mathcal{L}=-1 with ξ=0\xi=0, while for Δ<Δc;I\Delta<\Delta_{c;I}, the minimum of ℒ\mathcal{L} is obtained with

ξ2=3​c2​c6​(Δc,I−Δ)+c42−c43​c6.\xi^{2}=\frac{\sqrt{3c_{2}c_{6}\left(\Delta_{c,I}-\Delta\right)+c_{4}^{2}}-c_{4}}{3c_{6}}. (464)

Notice that ξ2\xi^{2} continuously increases from 00 when Δ\Delta decreases from Δc;I\Delta_{c;I}. Therefore the critical value of Δ\Delta is given by Δc=Δc;I\Delta_{c}=\Delta_{c;I}. Moreover, using

d​O~​(Δ)d​Δ=(∂∂ξ​ℱ~2​(Δ,ξ))​𝒪​(ξ),\frac{d\tilde{O}\left(\Delta\right)}{d\Delta}=\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial\xi}\tilde{\mathcal{F}}^{2}\left(\Delta,\xi\right)\right)\mathcal{O}\left(\xi\right), (465)

we find that d​O~​(Δ)d​Δ\frac{d\tilde{O}\left(\Delta\right)}{d\Delta} is continuous and only has a kink at Δ=Δc\Delta=\Delta_{c}. For c4<0c_{4}<0, when Δ>Δc;I\Delta>\Delta_{c;I} there is a local minimum at ξ=0\xi=0, while for Δ<Δc,I+c423​c2​c6\Delta<\Delta_{c,I}+\frac{c_{4}^{2}}{3c_{2}c_{6}} there is a local minimum given by Eq. (464). The two saddle points need to be compared to obtain the global minimum, which yields Δc=Δc,I+c424​c2​c6.\Delta_{c}=\Delta_{c,I}+\frac{c_{4}^{2}}{4c_{2}c_{6}}. Therefore, ξ\xi jumps from zero to a finite value when Δ\Delta decreases from Δc\Delta_{c}, implying that d​O~​(Δ)d​Δ\frac{d\tilde{O}\left(\Delta\right)}{d\Delta} is discontinuous at Δ=Δc\Delta=\Delta_{c}. It should be noted that for c4>0c_{4}>0, Δc=Δc;I\Delta_{c}=\Delta_{c;I} is exact, while for c4<0c_{4}<0, the expression Δc=Δc,I+c424​c2​c6\Delta_{c}=\Delta_{c,I}+\frac{c_{4}^{2}}{4c_{2}c_{6}} is an approximation, and in this case one should use the exact form of ℒ⁡(Δ,ξ)\mathcal{L}\left(\Delta,\xi\right) to determine Δc\Delta_{c} if precision is needed.

We now proceed to analytically compute the expansion for two cases: J/U=0J/U=0 with No​r​b≥1N_{orb}\geq 1 , and J/U>0J/U>0 with No​r​b=2N_{orb}=2 . We begin by expanding

ℱ~2​(Δ,ξ)ℱ~2​(Δ,0)=1+a2​ξ2+a4​ξ4+a6​ξ6+…,\frac{\mathcal{\tilde{F}}^{2}\left(\Delta,\xi\right)}{\mathcal{\tilde{F}}^{2}\left(\Delta,0\right)}=1+a_{2}\xi^{2}+a_{4}\xi^{4}+a_{6}\xi^{6}+\dots, (466)

where

a2=8−2(1−2​Δ)2,\displaystyle a_{2}=8-\frac{2}{(1-2\Delta)^{2}}, (467)
a4=−16(1−2​Δ)2−1(1−2​Δ)4+48,\displaystyle a_{4}=-\frac{16}{(1-2\Delta)^{2}}-\frac{1}{(1-2\Delta)^{4}}+48, (468)

[σ^ℓx]i,i+1=[σ^ℓx]i+1,i=(No​r​b−i)​(i+No​r​b+1)2​No​r​b​2−δ0,i.\left[\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{x}\right]_{i,i+1}=\left[\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{x}\right]_{i+1,i}=\frac{\sqrt{\left(N_{orb}-i\right)\left(i+N_{orb}+1\right)}}{\sqrt{2}N_{orb}\sqrt{2-\delta_{0,i}}}. (473)

where

h=209​No​r​b​(No​r​b+1)+146.\displaystyle h=209N_{orb}\left(N_{orb}+1\right)+146. (477)

VII.3.2 Solution for the two-peak density of states

We now consider the two peak density of states

D⁡(ϵ)=12​(δ⁡(ϵ−1No​r​b​K0)+δ⁡(ϵ+1No​r​b​K0)),D\left(\epsilon\right)=\frac{1}{2}\left(\delta\left(\epsilon-\frac{1}{N_{orb}}K_{0}\right)+\delta\left(\epsilon+\frac{1}{N_{orb}}K_{0}\right)\right), (490)

where K0K_{0} is the total non-interacting kinetic energy per site. For the two-peak density of states, A=Δ⁡(2−4​Δ)A=\sqrt{\Delta(2-4\Delta)}, and the qubit trial energy can be written purely in terms of Δ\Delta as

E⁡(Δ)=(1−4​Δ)​K0+U​Ot​p​(Δ),\displaystyle E\left(\Delta\right)=\left(1-4\Delta\right)K_{0}+UO_{tp}(\Delta), (491)
Ot​p​(Δ)=(2−4​Δ)2​Δ2​O~​(Δ).\displaystyle O_{tp}(\Delta)=\left(2-4\Delta\right)^{2}\Delta^{2}\widetilde{O}\left(\Delta\right). (492)

Following the single orbital case, Δ\Delta can be used to determine UU from d​E​(Δ)/d​Δ=0,dE\left(\Delta\right)/d\Delta=0, which yields

U⁡(Δ)=−4​|K0|​(d​Ot​p​(Δ)d​Δ)−1,U(\Delta)=-4\left|K_{0}\right|\left(\frac{dO_{tp}(\Delta)}{d\Delta}\right)^{-1}, (493)

thus providing a succinct solution parametrized by Δ\Delta. The relation U⁡(Δ)U(\Delta) can be used to determine the nature of the Mott transition from O~​(Δ)\widetilde{O}\left(\Delta\right), given that this quantity will allow any observable to be expressed in terms of UU. We plot d​Ot​pd​Δ\frac{dO_{tp}}{d\Delta} versus Δ\Delta for various No​r​bN_{orb} and J/UJ/U, which demonstrates three types of non-analytical scenarios for Ot​p​(Δ)O_{tp}\left(\Delta\right) (see Fig. 7, panel aa). First, for all J/U=0J/U=0, the d​Ot​pd​Δ\frac{dO_{tp}}{d\Delta} is continuous with a positive slope and has a kink at Δ=Δc\Delta=\Delta_{c}. Second, for J/U>0J/U>0 and small No​r​bN_{orb}, the d​Ot​pd​Δ\frac{dO_{tp}}{d\Delta} is discontinuous at Δ=Δc\Delta=\Delta_{c} with a negative slope for Δc−\Delta_{c}^{-}. Third, for J/U=0.25J/U=0.25 and No​r​b=7N_{orb}=7, the d​Ot​pd​Δ\frac{dO_{tp}}{d\Delta} is continuous and has a kink at Δ=Δc\Delta=\Delta_{c}, and the slope is negative for Δc−\Delta_{c}^{-}. The d​Ot​pd​Δ\frac{dO_{tp}}{d\Delta} can now be used to determine U⁡(Δ)U(\Delta), which yields the order of the Mott transition (see Fig. 7, panel bb). First, for all J/U=0J/U=0, UU increases monotonically and continuously with Δ\Delta, with a kink at Δ=Δc\Delta=\Delta_{c}, and therefore there are no metastable regions and the Mott transition is continuous. Second, for J/U>0J/U>0, there is an unstable region in the metal phase where d​Ud​Δ<0\frac{dU}{d\Delta}<0, and the total energy can be used to determine the transition between the metal and insulating phase, corresponding to a horizontal line, and the transition is first-order.

In summary, we have demonstrated that the nature of the Mott transition for the two peak density of states is determined purely by O~​(Δ)\widetilde{O}\left(\Delta\right), and below we demonstrate that the Bethe lattice has the same behavior. Therefore, it appears that O~​(Δ)\widetilde{O}\left(\Delta\right) is the essence of what determines the nature of the Mott transition in d=∞d=\infty.

We now execute a similar strategy for a general density of states. Using Eq. (460), the qubit trial energy can be written as

E⁡(Δ,A)=K⁡(Δ,A)+U​A4​O~​(Δ).E\left(\Delta,A\right)=K\left(\Delta,A\right)+UA^{4}\widetilde{O}\left(\Delta\right). (494)

∂K∂Δ=−4​No​r​b​a=−U​A4​d​O~​(Δ)d​Δ,\displaystyle\frac{\partial K}{\partial\Delta}=-4N_{orb}a=-UA^{4}\frac{d\widetilde{O}\left(\Delta\right)}{d\Delta}, (495)

For a given Δ\Delta, aa and bb can be determined from Eqns. (497) and (498), AA can be determined from A⁡(a,b)A\left(a,b\right), and UU can be determined using Eq. (496) as

allowing for the evaluation of the total energy.

For the case of a continuous transition, the UcU_{c} will be determined by Δc\Delta_{c}, while for a first-order transition, one must explicitly determine the UcU_{c} where the insulating and metallic states cross in energy. VIII Summary and Conclusions

We begin by providing a high level overview of the variational discrete action theory (VDAT), such that the developments of the present work can be properly understood. VDAT is a variational approach to the many-body body problem that consists of two main components: a variational ansatz for the many-body wave function or density-matrix, known as the sequential product density matrix (SPD), and a formalism for evaluating expectation values under the SPD, known as the discrete action theory [13, 14]. The SPD has a natural mechanism to trade off between efficiency and accuracy, where the integer 𝒩\mathcal{N} monotonically increases the variational power of the SPD and guarantees the ability to recover the ground state solution for 𝒩→∞\mathcal{N}\rightarrow\infty. Moreover, there are two distinct types of SPD which satisfy the properties of a many-body density matrix, denoted as G-type and B-type. The G-type 𝒩=1\mathcal{N}=1, 𝒩=2\mathcal{N}=2, and 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3 SPD encapsulate the Hartree-Fock wave function, the Gutzwiller wave function, and the Gutzwiller-Baeriswyl wave function, respectively. The key breakthrough using VDAT was the demonstration that the SPD can be exactly evaluated for multiorbital Hubbard models in d=∞d=\infty. We demonstrated that the G-type 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3 SPD accurately solves the Anderson impurity model on a ring [14], the single band Hubbard model over all parameter space [14], the two orbital Hubbard model including a crystal field and the full rotationally invariant Hund’s coupling [12], and the S​U​(2​No​r​b)SU(2N_{orb}) Hubbard model for No​r​b≤8N_{orb}\leq 8 [15]. Moreover, we demonstrated that the computational cost of solving a G-type 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3 SPD is comparable to a G-type 𝒩=2\mathcal{N}=2 SPD, meaning that VDAT can provide a sufficiently accurate solution at a cost not far beyond the Gutzwiller approximation. The success of VDAT at 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3 motivated a search for the best possible algorithm for executing calculations using a G-type 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3 SPD [15], which is essential for detailed exploration of the multiorbital Hubbard model and merging VDAT with realistic electronic structure methods.

The VDAT algorithm in d=∞d=\infty consists of two steps: the exact evaluation of the SPD via the self-consistent canonical discrete action theory (SCDA) and the optimization of the energy with respect to the variational parameters. The SCDA requires the numerical solution of a set of self-consistency conditions, and therefore can be inconvenient when minimizing over the variational parameters. For the case of a G-type 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3 SPD with certain restrictions (see Sections I, VI.1, and VI.2 for further details), the SCDA self-consistency condition can be automatically satisfied, which we refer to as the gauge constrained SCDA algorithm [15]. In the present work, we introduce the so-called qubit parametrization of the gauge constrained SCDA algorithm, which is mathematically equivalent to the original gauge constrained SCDA algorithm. The qubit parametrization offers several key improvements. The qubit parametrization analytically resolves some constraints over the variational parameters, thus reducing the number of variational parameters by one per spin orbital. Additionally, the variational parameters are physically intuitive and facilitate a deeper understanding of how the SPD captures Mott and Hund physics. Therefore, the qubit parametrization achieves the long sought goal of resolving the shortcomings of the Gutzwiller approximation while maintaining the computational simplicity and physical appeal.

The variational parameters of the qubit parametrization consist of the momentum density distribution, the non-interacting reference momentum density distribution, and the pure state of a qubit system with a dimension of the local Hilbert space. The qubit system naturally arises from reparametrizing the variational parameters of the interacting projector, and the renormalized correlations within the qubit space yield the physical local correlations. The variational parameters are restricted by two constraints per spin orbital, requiring that the local density computed from the momentum density distribution is the same as that computed from the non-interacting reference momentum density distribution, and the same as the density computed from the qubit system. The qubit trial energy has a very intuitive form: the kinetic energy is determined by the momentum density distributions, while the local interaction energy is the expectation value of an effective Hamiltonian within the qubit system. Interestingly, the effective Hamiltonian has the same form as the local interacting Hamiltonian where the local density operator is substituted by an effective density operator of the qubit system. The effective density operator for a given spin-orbital ℓ\ell depends on five parameters: the density nℓn_{\ell}, the magnetization in the xx direction for the ℓ\ell-th qubit, denoted ξℓ\xi_{\ell}, and three quantities determined from the momentum density distribution, denoted as Δℓ\Delta_{\ell}, 𝒜<ℓ\mathcal{A}_{<\ell}, and 𝒜>ℓ\mathcal{A}_{>\ell}. The quantity Δℓ\Delta_{\ell} characterizes the number of electrons promoted across the reference Fermi surface, while 𝒜<ℓ\mathcal{A}_{<\ell} and 𝒜>ℓ\mathcal{A}_{>\ell} characterize the momentum density distribution below and above the reference Fermi surface, respectively. The quantity ξℓ\xi_{\ell} is an important variable which differentiates between a zero and non-zero quasiparticle weight when all variables are fully optimized, where ξℓ=0\xi_{\ell}=0 indicates zero quasiparticle weight for spin-orbital ℓ\ell. The main computational cost for evaluating the ansatz is dictated by computing expectation values within the qubit system.

While evaluating the trial qubit energy ansatz is a straightforward task, optimizing over all the variational parameters remains nontrivial. In general, the qubit trial energy can be partially optimized over the momentum density distribution by introducing four Lagrange multipliers per spin-orbital, replacing the continuous momentum density distribution with four variables. For a system with 2​No​r​b2N_{orb} spin-orbitals per site, there remain 22​No​r​b+3×2​No​r​b−12^{2N_{orb}}+3\times 2N_{orb}-1 variational parameters which must be optimized in general. However, this number may be greatly reduced by symmetry, and it is likely possible to compress these variables into a smaller number of parameters without a serious loss of fidelity. For the special case of half-filled orbitals with particle hole symmetry, we demonstrate that one can efficiently minimize over all variational parameters, with a computational cost proportional to computing the ground state of a Hamiltonian defined within the qubit system.

In order to demonstrate the power of the qubit parametrization, we studied the ground state properties of the multiorbital Hubbard model at half-filling with particle-hole symmetry for various J/UJ/U and No​r​b=2−7N_{orb}=2-7. For a given J/UJ/U, the majority of the energy minimization can be encapsulated into the computation of a single variable function O~​(Δ)\tilde{O}(\Delta), which can then be used to obtain the solution at a negligible cost for an arbitrary UU and density-of-states. The entire function O~​(Δ)\tilde{O}(\Delta) is evaluated by solving a collection of qubit systems, which has a relatively small computational cost. For example, for No​r​b=7N_{orb}=7, the ground state for a given qubit system can be solved in several seconds on a typical single desktop computer core, and taking on the order of 100 samples, the entire function O~​(Δ)\tilde{O}(\Delta) can be accurately obtained on the order of hundreds of seconds. The extreme computational efficiency of the qubit parametrization in this case allows one to easily map out all of parameter space, which is not possible with DMFT given the lack of efficient impurity solvers for the zero temperature multiorbital problem. We find that for J/U=0J/U=0, the Mott transition is continuous, while it is first-order for J/U>0J/U>0, consistent with previous Gutzwiller [7], slave boson [32], and DMFT [71] studies.

While the key result of this paper is formulating the qubit parametrization of the gauge constrained SCDA algorithm for a G-type 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3 SPD, we also demonstrate that the qubit parametrization can be applied to the G-type and B-type 𝒩=2\mathcal{N}=2 SPD. Moreover, we demonstrate that properly restricting the variational parameters of the qubit trial energy for the G-type 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3 SPD can recover the corresponding qubit trial energy for the G-type and B-type 𝒩=2\mathcal{N}=2 SPD. Interestingly, the qubit trial energy for the G-type 𝒩=2\mathcal{N}=2 SPD has an identical form to the slave spin mean-field theory (see Appendix B), and thus the 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3 qubit trial energy may provide insights for proceeding beyond mean-field theory in the slave spin formalism.

The qubit parametrization of the gauge constrained SCDA algorithm at 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3 is likely the optimal form when evaluating an SPD with a kinetic projector that is diagonal in both the momentum and spin-orbital indices and an interacting projector that consists of diagonal Hubbard operators. For the Hamiltonians treated in the present study, which have density-density interactions and hopping parameters that are diagonal in the spin-orbital index, the aforementioned restrictions on the SPD do not limit the variational power. When solving a general Hamiltonian which includes the full rotationally invariant form of the Hund exchange or non-diagonal hopping terms, the qubit parametrization can still be applied and it will still yield an upper bound on the energy in d=∞d=\infty, but it will not contain the full variational power of 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3. Ongoing research is addressing how to generalize the qubit parametrization to handle an arbitrary 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3 G-type SPD, with aspirations of completely superseding our general decoupled minimization algorithm for 𝒩=3\mathcal{N}=3 [12].
