Appendix A One-body reduced density matrix functional for the Hubbard model

An important application of the qubit energy form for ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3} is the construction of a one body reduced density matrix functional (1RDMF) for the multi-orbital Hubbard model, which is the focus of our companion manuscript [1]. Here we derive the corresponding results for ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} and ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}. Additionally, we evaluate existing 1RDMF’s from the literature for the single band Hubbard model at half-filling in d=∞d=\infty.

A.1 The 1RDMF’s for the multi-orbital Hubbard model from ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} and ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}

We begin by presenting the 1RDMF from ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2} using the qubit parametrization. The interaction energy is given as

Ei​n​t​({nk​ℓ})=min𝝆⁡⟨Hl​o​c​({n^e​f​f,ℓ})⟩𝝆\displaystyle E_{int}\left(\left\{n_{k\ell}\right\}\right)=\min_{\bm{\rho}}\left\langle H_{loc}\left(\left\{\hat{n}_{eff,\ell}\right\}\right)\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}} (502)
subject to ​⟨n^ℓ⟩𝝆=nℓ,\displaystyle\textrm{subject to\ }\left\langle\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}=n_{\ell}, (503)

where nℓ=∫d​k​nk​ℓn_{\ell}=\int dkn_{k\ell}, the effective density operator is n^e​f​f,ℓ=nℓ+Aℓ2ξℓ,02​(n^ℓ−nℓ)\hat{n}_{eff,\ell}=n_{\ell}+\frac{A_{\ell}^{2}}{\xi_{\ell,0}^{2}}\left(\hat{n}_{\ell}-n_{\ell}\right) with Aℓ=∫d​k​nk​ℓ​(1−nk​ℓ)A_{\ell}=\int dk\sqrt{n_{k\ell}\left(1-n_{k\ell}\right)} and ξℓ,0=nℓ​(1−nℓ)\xi_{\ell,0}=\sqrt{n_{\ell}(1-n_{\ell})}, and both 𝝆\bm{\rho} and Hl​o​c​({n^e​f​f,ℓ})H_{loc}\left(\left\{\hat{n}_{eff,\ell}\right\}\right) are diagonal in the Pauli-Z basis of the qubit system. For the case of half-filling, the minimization yields

Ei​n​t​({nk​ℓ})=16​U​A4​𝒪​(0),E_{int}\left(\left\{n_{k\ell}\right\}\right)=16UA^{4}\mathcal{O}\left(0\right), (504)

where 𝒪⁡(0)=−14​No​r​b​(1+(No​r​b−1)​J/U)\mathcal{O}\left(0\right)=-\frac{1}{4}N_{orb}\left(1+\left(N_{orb}-1\right)J/U\right).

We now present the 1RDMF for ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2}. Unlike ρ^G​3\hat{\rho}_{G3} or ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}, the variational parameters do not explicitly contain nk​ℓ,n_{k\ell}, but instead nk​ℓ−nℓ=ξℓ2/ξℓ,02​(nk​ℓ,0−nℓ)n_{k\ell}-n_{\ell}=\xi_{\ell}^{2}/\xi_{\ell,0}^{2}\left(n_{k\ell,0}-n_{\ell}\right), where nk​ℓ,0∈[0,1]n_{k\ell,0}\in\left[0,1\right]. Therefore, for a given {nk​ℓ}\left\{n_{k\ell}\right\}, we have |ξℓ/ξℓ,0|≥Zℓ,m​i​n\left|\xi_{\ell}/\xi_{\ell,0}\right|\geq\sqrt{Z_{\ell,min}}, where Zℓ,m​i​n=max⁡(nℓ,m​a​x−nℓ1−nℓ,nℓ−nℓ,m​i​nnℓ)Z_{\ell,min}=\max\left(\frac{n_{\ell,max}-n_{\ell}}{1-n_{\ell}},\frac{n_{\ell}-n_{\ell,min}}{n_{\ell}}\right), where nℓ,m​a​xn_{\ell,max} and nℓ,m​i​nn_{\ell,min} are the maximum and minimum values of {nk​ℓ}\left\{n_{k\ell}\right\} for a given ℓ\ell. It should be noted that the gauge symmetry can be used to restrict ξℓ≥0\xi_{\ell}\geq 0. The interaction energy can then be written as

Ei​n​t​({nk​ℓ})=minρ⁡⟨Hl​o​c​({n^ℓ})⟩𝝆\displaystyle E_{int}\left(\left\{n_{k\ell}\right\}\right)=\min_{\rho}\left\langle H_{loc}\left(\left\{\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\}\right)\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}} (505)
subject to12​⟨σ^ℓx⟩𝝆≥ξℓ;m​i​n,⟨n^ℓ⟩𝝆=nℓ,\displaystyle\textrm{subject to}\hskip 10.00002pt\frac{1}{2}\langle\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{x}\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}\geq\xi_{\ell;min},\hskip 10.00002pt\left\langle\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}=n_{\ell}, (506)

where ξℓ;m​i​n=ξℓ;0​Zm​i​n\xi_{\ell;min}=\xi_{\ell;0}\sqrt{Z_{min}}. Notice that the interaction energy will decrease with decreasing ξℓ\xi_{\ell}, and therefore the restriction in Eq. (506) can be replaced with 12​⟨σ^ℓx⟩𝝆=ξℓ;m​i​n\frac{1}{2}\langle\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{x}\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}=\xi_{\ell;min} . For the case of half-filling, we have

Ei​n​t​({nk​ℓ})=U​𝒪​(12​1−2​nℓ;m​i​n),E_{int}\left(\left\{n_{k\ell}\right\}\right)=U\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{1-2n_{\ell;min}}\right), (507)

where 𝒪⁡(ξ)\mathcal{O}(\xi) is defined in Eq. (459).

Using the above interaction energy functionals will yield results identical to the corresponding VDAT results, such as the ones provided in Fig. 3.

A.2 Results using published 1RDMF’s for the single-orbital Hubbard model in d=∞d=\infty

We are not aware of any applications of existing 1RDMF’s to the Hubbard model in d=∞d=\infty, though there are various studies of Hubbard clusters [38, 65] and d=1d=1 [58, 66] and d=2d=2 Hubbard models [79, 64]. It is important to emphasize that d=∞d=\infty is the most relevant test of local electronic correlations, and is emblematic of typical three dimensional strongly correlated materials in that d=∞d=\infty hosts a standard Fermi liquid in the metal phase and exhibits a Mott transition at a finite value of UU. While d=1d=1 is exactly solvable via the Bethe ansatz, the Mott transition occurs at an infinitesimal UU [54]. Alternatively, d=2d=2 is a testbed for the most advanced and expensive computational approaches, and the properties at half-filling and low temperatures are still actively studied [87, 82, 10, 25]. While it is still very interesting to compare total energies from 1RDMF’s in d=1d=1 and d=2d=2, if the goal is to determine whether or not a 1RDMF can describe the Mott transition, then it is most critical to first benchmark in d=∞d=\infty.

In this section, we discuss how to use various 1RDMF’s to solve the one band Hubbard model at half-filling, including the MBB [67], CA [18], CGA [19], power [84], PNOF5 [76], PNOF7 [75], and dimer [79] functionals. The interaction energy is given by U​dUd, where dd is the double occupancy and is a functional of {nk​σ}\left\{n_{k\sigma}\right\}. If the interaction Hamiltonian is rewritten as U2​∑i​σ​σ′a^i​σ†​a^i​σ′†​a^i​σ′​a^i​σ\frac{U}{2}\sum_{i\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}\hat{a}_{i\sigma}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{i\sigma^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{i\sigma^{\prime}}\hat{a}_{i\sigma}, the interaction energy for the MBB, CA, CGA, and power functionals can be viewed as a modification of the Hartree-Fock (HF) energy where the Fock term is altered [65]. We begin by writing the local interaction as Ei​n​t=U2​∑σ​σ′⟨a^i​σ†​a^i​σ′†​a^i​σ′​a^i​σ⟩E_{int}=\frac{U}{2}\sum_{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}\left\langle\hat{a}_{i\sigma}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{i\sigma^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{i\sigma^{\prime}}\hat{a}_{i\sigma}\right\rangle, which can be written in momentum space as

Ei​n​t=U2​L2​∑k1​k2​k1′​k2′​σ​σ′δk1+k2,k1′+k2′​⟨a^k1​σ†​a^k2​σ′†​a^k2′​σ′​a^k1′​σ⟩,E_{int}=\frac{U}{2L^{2}}\sum_{k_{1}k_{2}k^{\prime}_{1}k^{\prime}_{2}\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}\hskip-10.00002pt\delta_{k_{1}+k_{2},k^{\prime}_{1}+k^{\prime}_{2}}\left\langle\hat{a}_{k_{1}\sigma}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{k_{2}\sigma^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{k^{\prime}_{2}\sigma^{\prime}}\hat{a}_{k^{\prime}_{1}\sigma}\right\rangle, (508)

where LL is the number of kk-points. The MBB, CA, CGA, and power functionals are all defined using the following approximation

⟨a^k1​σ†​a^k2​σ′†​a^k2′​σ′​a^k1′​σ⟩≈nk1​nk2​δk1​k1′​δk2​k2′\displaystyle\left\langle\hat{a}_{k_{1}\sigma}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{k_{2}\sigma^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{k^{\prime}_{2}\sigma^{\prime}}\hat{a}_{k^{\prime}_{1}\sigma}\right\rangle\approx n_{k_{1}}n_{k_{2}}\delta_{k_{1}k^{\prime}_{1}}\delta_{k_{2}k^{\prime}_{2}}
−ℱ⁡(nk1,nk2)​δk1​k2′​δk2​k1′​δσ​σ′,\displaystyle-\mathcal{F}\left(n_{k_{1}},n_{k_{2}}\right)\delta_{k_{1}k^{\prime}_{2}}\delta_{k_{2}k^{\prime}_{1}}\delta_{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}, (509)

where nkn_{k} is defined through ⟨a^k​σ†​a^k′​σ′⟩=nk​δk​k′​δσ​σ′\left\langle\hat{a}_{k\sigma}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{k^{\prime}\sigma^{\prime}}\right\rangle=n_{k}\delta_{kk^{\prime}}\delta_{\sigma\sigma^{\prime}}. The ℱ⁡(ni,nj)\mathcal{F}\left(n_{i},n_{j}\right) and Ei​n​tE_{int} are given for each functional in Table 4, and our values of ℱ⁡(ni,nj)\mathcal{F}\left(n_{i},n_{j}\right) are identical to those provided in Ref. [65]. It is worth noting that the MBB, CA, and CGA recover the atomic limit where Ei​n​t=0E_{int}=0 when nk=1/2n_{k}=1/2, while the power functional does not if α≠1/2\alpha\neq 1/2.

Now we discuss how to minimize the total energy over {nk}\{n_{k}\}. Given that MBB is a special case of the power functional, we first consider the power functional. Given that the interaction energy for the power functional is fixed for a given ∫d​k​nkα\int dkn_{k}^{\alpha} and ∫d​k​nk\int dkn_{k}, the kinetic energy can be minimized by introducing two Lagrange multipliers aa and bb, yielding a target functional K=∫d​k​(ϵk−a)​nk−b​∫d​k​nkαK=\int dk\left(\epsilon_{k}-a\right)n_{k}-b\int dkn_{k}^{\alpha} to be minimized, and the partially optimized nkn_{k} are obtained as

nk={1ϵk≤a+α​b(ϵk−aα​b)1α−1ϵk>a+α​b.n_{k}=\begin{cases}1&\epsilon_{k}\leq a+\alpha b\\ \left(\frac{\epsilon_{k}-a}{\alpha b}\right)^{\frac{1}{\alpha-1}}&\epsilon_{k}>a+\alpha b\end{cases}. (510)

The ground state energy for a given UU is then obtained by optimizing the total energy over aa and bb.

We now consider the CA and CGA, which can be viewed in a unified way by writing the interaction energy functional as

Ei​n​t=U⁡((12−14​θ)−1θ​(∫d​k​nk​(θ−nk))2),E_{int}=U\left(\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{4\theta}\right)-\frac{1}{\theta}\left(\int dk\sqrt{n_{k}\left(\theta-n_{k}\right)}\right)^{2}\right), (511)

where θ=1\theta=1 corresponds to CA and θ=2\theta=2 corresponds to CGA. We can similarly introduce two Lagrange multipliers, yielding a target functional

K=∫d​k​(ϵk−a)​nk−b​∫d​k​nk​(θ−nk),K=\int dk\left(\epsilon_{k}-a\right)n_{k}-b\int dk\sqrt{n_{k}\left(\theta-n_{k}\right)}, (512)

where θ≥1\theta\geq 1 and the partially optimized value of nkn_{k} is given as

nk={1ϵ≤a+b⁡(θ−2)2​θ−1θ2​(1−(ϵk−a)(ϵk−a)2+b2)ϵ>a+b⁡(θ−2)2​θ−1.n_{k}=\begin{cases}1&\epsilon\leq a+\frac{b(\theta-2)}{2\sqrt{\theta-1}}\\ \frac{\theta}{2}\left(1-\frac{(\epsilon_{k}-a)}{\sqrt{(\epsilon_{k}-a)^{2}+b^{2}}}\right)&\epsilon>a+\frac{b(\theta-2)}{2\sqrt{\theta-1}}\end{cases}. (513)

For a given UU, one can then optimize the Lagrange multipliers to obtain the ground-state energy and other observables. Plots of the double occupancy as a function of U/tU/t are provided in Ref. [1].

An important drawback of the MBB, power, CA, and CGA functionals is that the anti-symmetry of the two-body reduced density matrix (2RDM) is violated when ℱ⁡(ni,nj)\mathcal{F}\left(n_{i},n_{j}\right) deviates from the HF value [65]. The Piris natural orbital functionals (PNOF) [74] resolve this issue by approximating the form of the 2RDM Di​j,k​lα​β=12​⟨a^i​α†​a^j​β†​a^l​β​a^k​α⟩D_{ij,kl}^{\alpha\beta}=\frac{1}{2}\langle\hat{a}_{i\alpha}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{j\beta}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{l\beta}\hat{a}_{k\alpha}\rangle as [65]

Di​j,k​lσ​σ=ni​nj−Δi​j2​(δi​k​δj​l−δi​l​δj​k),\displaystyle D_{ij,kl}^{\sigma\sigma}=\frac{n_{i}n_{j}-\Delta_{ij}}{2}\left(\delta_{ik}\delta_{jl}-\delta_{il}\delta_{jk}\right), (514)
Di​j,k​lσ​σ¯=ni​nj−Δi​j2​δi​k​δj​l+Πi​k2​δi​j​δk​l,\displaystyle D_{ij,kl}^{\sigma\bar{\sigma}}=\frac{n_{i}n_{j}-\Delta_{ij}}{2}\delta_{ik}\delta_{jl}+\frac{\Pi_{ik}}{2}\delta_{ij}\delta_{kl}, (515)

where Δi​j\Delta_{ij} and Πi​k\Pi_{ik} are explicitly defined in PNOF5 and PNOF7. In the previous calculations [65, 77], it was found that the optimized natural orbital often breaks symmetry in order to further minimize the energy, and translational symmetry breaking in the Hubbard model allows PNOF5 and PNOF7 to recover the correct atomic limit [65]. In our context, we require translational symmetry to be respected, so we will examine PNOF5 and PNOF7 in this case. PNOF5 only includes intra-pair correlation (i.e. Πi​k=0\Pi_{ik}=0 when i,ki,k belong to different pairs), and therefore the deviation of the summation in Eq. (508) from the corresponding Hartree-Fock value scales like LL in the thermodynamic limit while there is a prefactor of 1/L21/L^{2}, and thus PNOF5 will yield the same energy form as HF in the thermodynamic limit. PNOF7 accounts for interpair correlation, which will provide a thermodynamic contribution, and for half-filling we find Ei​n​t=14−12​A2E_{int}=\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{2}A^{2}, which is similar to the CA but with different prefactor for A2A^{2}.

Finally, we discuss the interaction energy of the dimer functional at half-filling, given as

Ei​n​t=U4​(1−1−(K/K0)2),E_{int}=\frac{U}{4}\left(1-\sqrt{1-\left(K/K_{0}\right)^{2}}\right), (516)

where K=2​∫d​k​ϵk​nkK=2\int dk\epsilon_{k}n_{k} and K0K_{0} is the non-interacting kinetic energy. Minimizing the total energy over {nk}\{n_{k}\} yields the double occupancy as a function of UU as

d=14​(1−1−11+(U/(4​K0))2).d=\frac{1}{4}\left(1-\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{1+\left(U/\left(4K_{0}\right)\right)^{2}}}\right). (517)

Appendix B Equivalence between the Qubit energy form for ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} and the Slave Spin Mean Field Theory

Here we prove that the slave spin mean-field theory (SSMF) is identical to the qubit energy form for ρG​2\rho_{G2}. We begin by describing the SSMF using the conventions in our work, as there are trivial differences. We associate the spin state |↑⟩|\uparrow\rangle with the fermionic state |0⟩|0\rangle, while the standard SSMF associates |↓⟩|\downarrow\rangle with |0⟩|0\rangle. To restore the enlarged Hilbert space of the SSMF back to the physical space, we require that n^i​ℓ=1−σ^i​ℓz2\hat{n}_{i\ell}=\frac{1-\hat{\sigma}_{i\ell}^{z}}{2} holds for every local site ii and spin-orbital index ℓ\ell. Then, the local Hamiltonian at site ii can be written as Hl​o​c​({n^i​ℓ})=Hl​o​c​({1−σ^i​ℓz2})H_{loc}\left(\left\{\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\}\right)=H_{loc}\left(\left\{\frac{1-\hat{\sigma}_{i\ell}^{z}}{2}\right\}\right), while the hopping term can be written as a^i​ℓ†​a^j​ℓ=f^i​ℓ†​O^i​ℓ†​O^j​ℓ​f^j​ℓ\hat{a}_{i\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{j\ell}=\hat{f}_{i\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{O}_{i\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{O}_{j\ell}\hat{f}_{j\ell}, where O^i​ℓ=S^i​ℓ++ci​ℓ​S^i​ℓ−\hat{O}_{i\ell}=\hat{S}_{i\ell}^{+}+c_{i\ell}\hat{S}_{i\ell}^{-} , S^i​ℓ±=σ^i​ℓx±σ^i​ℓy2\hat{S}_{i\ell}^{\pm}=\frac{\hat{\sigma}_{i\ell}^{x}\pm\hat{\sigma}_{i\ell}^{y}}{2}, ci​ℓc_{i\ell} is an arbitrary complex number, and f^j​ℓ\hat{f}_{j\ell} is a fermionic annihilation operator. While the preceding transformations are exact for any ci​ℓc_{i\ell}, an appropriate choice of ci​ℓc_{i\ell} is indeed critical when making mean-field approximations. In Ref. [21], which only addressed half-filling, the ci​ℓ=1c_{i\ell}=1 and O^i​ℓ=σ^i​ℓx\hat{O}_{i\ell}=\hat{\sigma}_{i\ell}^{x}, while later work generalized this result [33], choosing ci​ℓc_{i\ell} such that the non-interacting limit can always be correctly recovered within the mean field approximation. We follow the latter choice. Finally, the Hamiltonian in the slave spin representation is given as

H^=∑i​j​ℓti​ℓ,j​ℓ​f^i​ℓ†​O^i​ℓ†​O^j​ℓ​f^j​ℓ+∑iHl​o​c​({1−σ^i​ℓz2}),\hat{H}=\sum_{ij\ell}t_{i\ell,j\ell}\hat{f}_{i\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{O}_{i\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{O}_{j\ell}\hat{f}_{j\ell}+\sum_{i}H_{loc}\left(\left\{\frac{1-\hat{\sigma}_{i\ell}^{z}}{2}\right\}\right), (518)

with the operator constraint f^i​ℓ†​f^i​ℓ=1−σ^i​ℓz2\hat{f}_{i\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{f}_{i\ell}=\frac{1-\hat{\sigma}_{i\ell}^{z}}{2} for every site and spin-orbital. There are two ways to derive the SSMF. The first approach introduces a mean-field decoupling for the hopping term and treats the operator constraint in the mean field level, yielding decoupled Hamiltonians for electrons and spins that must be solved self-consistently. The second approach [28, 61, 62, 17] uses the variational principle, assuming a trial wave-function |Ψ⟩=|Ψf⟩⊗|Ψs⟩|\Psi\rangle=|\Psi_{f}\rangle\otimes|\Psi_{s}\rangle which is a direct product of a fermionic part |Ψf⟩|\Psi_{f}\rangle and a spin part |Ψs⟩|\Psi_{s}\rangle. Furthermore, the |Ψf⟩|\Psi_{f}\rangle is assumed to be Slater determinant and the |Ψs⟩|\Psi_{s}\rangle is assumed to be a direct product in real space, such that |Ψs⟩=⊗i|Ψs;i⟩|\Psi_{s}\rangle=\otimes_{i}|\Psi_{s;i}\rangle. Therefore, the trial energy of Eq. (518) is given as

E=\displaystyle E= ∑i​j​ℓti​ℓ,j​ℓ​⟨Ψf|f^i​ℓ†​f^j​ℓ​|Ψf⟩​⟨Ψs;i|O^i​ℓ†|Ψs;i⟩​⟨Ψs;j|​O^j​ℓ|Ψs;j⟩\displaystyle\sum_{ij\ell}t_{i\ell,j\ell}\langle\Psi_{f}|\hat{f}_{i\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{f}_{j\ell}|\Psi_{f}\rangle\langle\Psi_{s;i}|\hat{O}_{i\ell}^{\dagger}|\Psi_{s;i}\rangle\langle\Psi_{s;j}|\hat{O}_{j\ell}|\Psi_{s;j}\rangle
+∑i⟨Ψs;i|Hl​o​c({1−σ^i​ℓz2})|Ψs;i⟩,\displaystyle+\sum_{i}\langle\Psi_{s;i}|H_{loc}\left(\left\{\frac{1-\hat{\sigma}_{i\ell}^{z}}{2}\right\}\right)|\Psi_{s;i}\rangle, (519)

subject to the constraint

⟨Ψf|f^i​ℓ†​f^i​ℓ|Ψf⟩=⟨Ψs;i|1−σ^i​ℓz2|Ψs;i⟩=nℓ.\left\langle\Psi_{f}|\hat{f}_{i\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{f}_{i\ell}|\Psi_{f}\right\rangle=\langle\Psi_{s;i}|\frac{1-\hat{\sigma}_{i\ell}^{z}}{2}|\Psi_{s;i}\rangle=n_{\ell}. (520)

Given translational symmetry and the correspondence 𝝆↔|Ψs;j⟩​⟨Ψs;j|\bm{\rho}\leftrightarrow|\Psi_{s;j}\rangle\langle\Psi_{s;j}| and nk​ℓ;0↔⟨Ψf|fk​ℓ†​fk​ℓ|Ψf⟩n_{k\ell;0}\leftrightarrow\langle\Psi_{f}|f_{k\ell}^{\dagger}f_{k\ell}|\Psi_{f}\rangle, we can prove that trial energy in Eq. (519) is identical to the qubit trial energy for ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} given in Eq. (50) and the constraint in Eq. (520) is identical to Eq. (54). The key step is to evaluate

⟨Ψs;j|O^j​ℓ|Ψs;j⟩=(1+cℓ)​⟨12​σ^ℓx⟩𝝆,\langle\Psi_{s;j}|\hat{O}_{j\ell}|\Psi_{s;j}\rangle=\left(1+c_{\ell}\right)\langle\frac{1}{2}\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{x}\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}, (521)

where gauge symmetry allows ⟨σ^ℓy⟩𝝆=0\langle\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{y}\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}=0. To ensure ⟨Ψs;j|O^j​ℓ|Ψs;j⟩=1\langle\Psi_{s;j}|\hat{O}_{j\ell}|\Psi_{s;j}\rangle=1 in the non-interacting limit, we must choose cℓc_{\ell} such that (1+cℓ)​ξℓ;0=1\left(1+c_{\ell}\right)\xi_{\ell;0}=1, where ξℓ;0=nℓ​(1−nℓ)\xi_{\ell;0}=\sqrt{n_{\ell}\left(1-n_{\ell}\right)} is the value for ξℓ=⟨12​σ^ℓx⟩𝝆\xi_{\ell}=\langle\frac{1}{2}\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{x}\rangle_{\bm{\rho}} in the non-interacting limit. Plugging cℓc_{\ell} into Eq. (521), we have ⟨Ψs;j|O^j​ℓ|Ψs;j⟩=ξℓ/ξℓ;0\langle\Psi_{s;j}|\hat{O}_{j\ell}|\Psi_{s;j}\rangle=\xi_{\ell}/\xi_{\ell;0}, completing the proof.

The preceding proof demonstrates the equivalence of the qubit energy form for ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} and the trial energy for the SSMF. Now we demonstrate how to obtain a Hamiltonian form for the SSMF using the saddle point equations for the trial energy. The total energy under a fixed {nℓ}\{n_{\ell}\} can be minimized by introducing Lagrange multipliers for the electron and spin systems, yielding

E\displaystyle E =1L​∑k​ℓϵk​ℓ​(nℓ+ξℓ2​(nk​ℓ,0−nℓ)nℓ​(1−nℓ))+⟨Hl​o​c​({n^ℓ})⟩𝝆\displaystyle=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{k\ell}\epsilon_{k\ell}\left(n_{\ell}+\frac{\xi_{\ell}^{2}\left(n_{k\ell,0}-n_{\ell}\right)}{n_{\ell}\left(1-n_{\ell}\right)}\right)+\left\langle H_{loc}\left(\left\{\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\}\right)\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}
−∑ℓ(λℓ(1L∑knk​ℓ;0−nℓ)+λℓ′(⟨n^ℓ⟩𝝆−nℓ)).\displaystyle-\sum_{\ell}\left(\lambda_{\ell}\left(\frac{1}{L}\sum_{k}n_{k\ell;0}-n_{\ell}\right)+\lambda^{\prime}_{\ell}\left(\left\langle\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\rangle_{\bm{\rho}}-n_{\ell}\right)\right). (522)

Taking the derivative with respect to 𝝆\bm{\rho} yields the mean-field Hamiltonian for the spin system as

H^e​f​fs=∂E∂𝝆=Hl​o​c​({n^ℓ})+2​∑ℓhℓ​ξ^ℓ−λℓ′​n^ℓ+C,\hat{H}_{eff}^{s}=\frac{\partial E}{\partial\bm{\rho}}=H_{loc}\left(\left\{\hat{n}_{\ell}\right\}\right)+2\sum_{\ell}h_{\ell}\hat{\xi}_{\ell}-\lambda^{\prime}_{\ell}\hat{n}_{\ell}+C, (523)

where n^ℓ=12​(1−σ^ℓz)\hat{n}_{\ell}=\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{z}\right) , ξ^ℓ=12​σ^ℓx\hat{\xi}_{\ell}=\frac{1}{2}\hat{\sigma}_{\ell}^{x}, hℓ=1L​ξℓnℓ​(1−nℓ)​∑kϵk​ℓ​nk​ℓ,0h_{\ell}=\frac{1}{L}\frac{\xi_{\ell}}{n_{\ell}\left(1-n_{\ell}\right)}\sum_{k}\epsilon_{k\ell}n_{k\ell,0}, CC is a constant that does not influence the results, and we assume ∑kϵk​ℓ=0\sum_{k}\epsilon_{k\ell}=0. Now consider the derivative of the electron components as

∂E∂nk​ℓ;0=Zℓ​ϵk​ℓ−λℓ,\frac{\partial E}{\partial n_{k\ell;0}}=Z_{\ell}\epsilon_{k\ell}-\lambda_{\ell}, (524)

where Zℓ=ξℓ2nℓ​(1−nℓ)Z_{\ell}=\frac{\xi_{\ell}^{2}}{n_{\ell}\left(1-n_{\ell}\right)}, which can be connected to a non-interacting fermionic Hamiltonian as

H^e​f​ff=∑k​ℓ(Zℓ​ϵk​ℓ−λℓ)​n^k​ℓ.\hat{H}_{eff}^{f}=\sum_{k\ell}\left(Z_{\ell}\epsilon_{k\ell}-\lambda_{\ell}\right)\hat{n}_{k\ell}. (525)

The ground states for Eqns. (523) and (525) will yield an updated 𝝆\bm{\rho} and nk​ℓn_{k\ell}, yielding new Hamiltonians for Eqns. (523) and (525), and this procedure is iterated until self-consistency is achieved.

Appendix C The Central Point Expansion (CPE)

The central point expansion (CPE) can be viewed as an approach to evaluate both a G-type and B-type SPD at 𝒩=2\mathcal{N}=2 by expanding about a reference SPD referred to as the central point. The CPE can be applied in arbitrary dimensions, and it is formally exact if all orders are summed, though it has only ever been applied at first-order. Interestingly, for the G-type 𝒩=2\mathcal{N}=2 SPD, the first-order CPE yields the same result as the Gutzwiller approximation (GA) and the SCDA in any dimension, and the derivation offers an alternative perspective from the GA and the SCDA. For the B-type 𝒩=2\mathcal{N}=2 SPD, the first-order CPE yields the same result as the SCDA in d=∞d=\infty, while providing a different approximation in finite dimensions. The CPE was originally developed in the context of the off-shell effective energy theory (OET) [16], where the CPE was renormalized using both weak coupling and strong coupling perturbation theory to ensure the correct limiting behavior, yielding excellent results for the Hubbard model in d=1,2,∞d=1,2,\infty.

C.1 The CPE for ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2}

In this section, we use the first-order CPE to evaluate ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2}, which will be shown to be equivalent to the GA and the SCDA. The first-order CPE can be motivated by the fact that the GA relation between nk​ℓ−nℓn_{k\ell}-n_{\ell} and nk​ℓ;0−nℓn_{k\ell;0}-n_{\ell} is a linear form (see Eq. (111)) given by

nk​ℓ−nℓ=𝒵ℓ​(nk​ℓ;0−nℓ),n_{k\ell}-n_{\ell}=\mathcal{Z}_{\ell}\left(n_{k\ell;0}-n_{\ell}\right), (526)

which is valid for an arbitrary nk​ℓ;0∈[0,1]n_{k\ell;0}\in\left[0,1\right] with a constraint (1/L)​∑knk​ℓ;0=nℓ\left(1/L\right)\sum_{k}n_{k\ell;0}=n_{\ell}, where LL is the number of sites in the lattice. This remarkably simple relation motivates the use of nk​ℓ;0−nℓn_{k\ell;0}-n_{\ell} as the expansion parameters, where 𝒵ℓ\mathcal{Z}_{\ell} can be determined using a ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} with nk​ℓ;0n_{k\ell;0} slightly deviating from the uniform distribution nℓn_{\ell} at first order. Alternatively, the relation between nk​ℓ;0n_{k\ell;0} and γk​ℓ\gamma_{k\ell} is highly nonlinear, suggesting that a first-order approximation in γk​ℓ\gamma_{k\ell} cannot be applied to the Gutzwiller wavefunction.

The CPE begins by choosing an expansion point for ρ^G​2=P^1​K^2​P^1\hat{\rho}_{G2}=\hat{P}_{1}\hat{K}_{2}\hat{P}_{1} as ρ^G​2⋆=P^1​K^2⋆​P^1\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}=\hat{P}_{1}\hat{K}_{2}^{\star}\hat{P}_{1}, where K^2⋆=exp⁡(∑k​ℓγℓ⋆​n^k​ℓ)\hat{K}_{2}^{\star}=\exp\left(\sum_{k\ell}\gamma_{\ell}^{\star}\hat{n}_{k\ell}\right) and γℓ⋆\gamma_{\ell}^{\star} is chosen to reproduce the non-interacting local density nℓ;0≡⟨n^i​ℓ⟩K^2=⟨n^i​ℓ⟩K^2⋆n_{\ell;0}\equiv\left\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{K}_{2}}=\left\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{K}_{2}^{\star}} through nℓ;0=1/(1+exp⁡(−γℓ⋆))n_{\ell;0}=1/\left(1+\exp\left(-\gamma_{\ell}^{\star}\right)\right). Considering a kinetic projector that deviates slightly from K^2⋆\hat{K}_{2}^{\star} as K^2=exp⁡(∑k​ℓγk​ℓ​n^k​ℓ)\hat{K}_{2}=\exp\left(\sum_{k\ell}\gamma_{k\ell}\hat{n}_{k\ell}\right), where γk​ℓ=γℓ⋆+δ​γk​ℓ\gamma_{k\ell}=\gamma_{\ell}^{\star}+\delta\gamma_{k\ell} , we compute the response of the expectation value ⟨O^⟩ρ^G​2\langle\hat{O}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}} to γk​ℓ\gamma_{k\ell} to the first order about the central point, given as

∂⟨O^⟩ρ^G​2∂γk​ℓ|ρ^G​2=ρ^G​2∗=∂∂γk​ℓ​Tr​(P^1​K^2​P1^​O^)Tr​(P^1​K^2​P1^)|ρ^G​2=ρ^G​2∗\displaystyle\frac{\partial\langle\hat{O}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}}}{\partial\gamma_{k\ell}}\bigg|_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}=\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{*}}=\frac{\partial}{\partial\gamma_{k\ell}}\frac{\text{Tr}\left(\hat{P}_{1}\hat{K}_{2}\hat{P_{1}}\hat{O}\right)}{\text{Tr}\left(\hat{P}_{1}\hat{K}_{2}\hat{P_{1}}\right)}\bigg|_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}=\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{*}} (527)
=Tr​(P^1​K^2⋆​n^k​ℓ​K^2⋆​P1^​O^)Tr​(ρ^G​2⋆)\displaystyle=\frac{\text{Tr}\left(\hat{P}_{1}\sqrt{\hat{K}_{2}^{\star}}\hat{n}_{k\ell}\sqrt{\hat{K}_{2}^{\star}}\hat{P_{1}}\hat{O}\right)}{\text{Tr}\left(\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}\right)}
−Tr​(P^1​K^2⋆​n^k​ℓ​K^2⋆​P1^)​Tr​(ρ^G​2⋆​O^)Tr​(ρ^G​2⋆)2\displaystyle-\frac{\text{Tr}\left(\hat{P}_{1}\sqrt{\hat{K}_{2}^{\star}}\hat{n}_{k\ell}\sqrt{\hat{K}_{2}^{\star}}\hat{P_{1}}\right)\text{Tr}\left(\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}\hat{O}\right)}{\text{Tr}\left(\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}\right)^{2}} (528)
=⟨n^k​ℓ;O^⟩ρ^G​2⋆−⟨n^k​ℓ⟩ρ^G​2⋆​⟨O^⟩ρ^G​2⋆,\displaystyle=\langle\hat{n}_{k\ell};\hat{O}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}}-\left\langle\hat{n}_{k\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}}\langle\hat{O}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}}, (529)

where we have utilized that fact that K^2⋆\hat{K}_{2}^{\star} commutes with P^1\hat{P}_{1} [16], ρ^G​2⋆=P^1​K^2⋆=K^2⋆​P1^\sqrt{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}}=\hat{P}_{1}\sqrt{\hat{K}_{2}^{\star}}=\sqrt{\hat{K}_{2}^{\star}}\hat{P_{1}}, and the notation ⟨A^;B^⟩ρ^\langle\hat{A};\hat{B}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}} is defined as

⟨A^;B^⟩ρ^=⟨B^;A^⟩ρ^=Tr​(ρ^​A^​ρ^​B^)/Tr​(ρ^).\langle\hat{A};\hat{B}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}}=\langle\hat{B};\hat{A}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}}=\text{Tr}\left(\sqrt{\hat{\rho}}\hat{A}\sqrt{\hat{\rho}}\hat{B}\right)/\text{Tr}\left(\hat{\rho}\right). (530)

The response coefficient of ⟨O^⟩ρ^G​2\langle\hat{O}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}} to γk​ℓ\gamma_{k\ell} at a general ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} can be conveniently expressed via the integer time correlation function in the compound space as

∂⟨O^⟩ρ^G​2∂γk​ℓ=⟨$̱\hat{n}$k​ℓ(1)​$̱\hat{O}$(2)⟩$̱\hat{\rho}$G​2−⟨$̱\hat{n}$k​ℓ(1)⟩$̱\hat{\rho}$G​2​⟨$̱\hat{O}$(2)⟩$̱\hat{\rho}$G​2.\frac{\partial\langle\hat{O}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}}}{\partial\gamma_{k\ell}}=\left\langle\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{n}$}}_{k\ell}^{\left(1\right)}\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{O}$}}^{\left(2\right)}\right\rangle_{\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{G2}}-\left\langle\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{n}$}}_{k\ell}^{\left(1\right)}\right\rangle_{\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{G2}}\left\langle\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{O}$}}^{\left(2\right)}\right\rangle_{\textrm{\@text@baccent{$\hat{\rho}$}}_{G2}}. (531)

While Eq. (531) is difficult to evaluate in general, the CPE circumvents this problem by observing that Eq. (531) becomes trivial to evaluate at the central point given that ρ^G​2⋆\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star} and ρ^G​2⋆\sqrt{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}} are direct product states in real space. Though it is not yet clear, it will prove critical to exploit the gauge symmetry of the SPD to restrict P^1\hat{P}_{1} such that ⟨n^i​ℓ⟩ρ^G​2⋆=⟨n^i​ℓ⟩K^2⋆=nℓ;0\left\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}}=\left\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{K}_{2}^{\star}}=n_{\ell;0}. The response for the momentum density distribution nk​ℓn_{k\ell} to γk′​ℓ′\gamma_{k^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}} can be obtained as

∂⟨n^k​ℓ⟩ρ^G​2∂γk′​ℓ′|ρ^G​2=ρ^G​2∗=⟨n^k​ℓ;n^k′​ℓ′⟩ρ^G​2⋆−nℓ;0​nℓ′;0,\frac{\partial\left\langle\hat{n}_{k\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}}}{\partial\gamma_{k^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}}}\bigg|_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}=\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{*}}=\langle\hat{n}_{k\ell};\hat{n}_{k^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}}-n_{\ell;0}n_{\ell^{\prime};0}, (532)

where the correlation function ⟨n^k​ℓ;n^k′​ℓ′⟩ρ^G​2⋆\langle\hat{n}_{k\ell};\hat{n}_{k^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}} can be computed by transforming to real space as

⟨n^k​ℓ;n^k′​ℓ′⟩ρ^G​2⋆=1L2​∑j1​j2​j3​j4ei​k​(j1−j2)+i​k′​(j3−j4)\displaystyle\langle\hat{n}_{k\ell};\hat{n}_{k^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}}=\frac{1}{L^{2}}\sum_{j_{1}j_{2}j_{3}j_{4}}e^{ik\left(j_{1}-j_{2}\right)+ik^{\prime}\left(j_{3}-j_{4}\right)}
×⟨a^j1​ℓ†​a^j2​ℓ;a^j3​ℓ′†​a^j4​ℓ′⟩ρ^G​2⋆.\displaystyle\times\left\langle\hat{a}_{j_{1}\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{j_{2}\ell};\hat{a}_{j_{3}\ell^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{j_{4}\ell^{\prime}}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}}. (533)

Utilizing the fact that ρ^G​2⋆=⊗iρ^G​2;i⋆\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}=\otimes_{i}\hat{\rho}_{G2;i}^{\star}, where ρ^G​2;i⋆\hat{\rho}_{G2;i}^{\star} is the local reduced density matrix for ρ^G​2⋆\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}, then ⟨a^j1​ℓ†​a^j2​ℓ;a^j3​ℓ′†​a^j4​ℓ′⟩ρ^G​2⋆\langle\hat{a}_{j_{1}\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{j_{2}\ell};\hat{a}_{j_{3}\ell^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{j_{4}\ell^{\prime}}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}} is only non-zero in the following cases: (1) when j1=j2j_{1}=j_{2}, j3=j4,j_{3}=j_{4}, and j1≠j4j_{1}\neq j_{4}, the value is nℓ;0​nℓ′;0n_{\ell;0}n_{\ell^{\prime};0}; (2) when j1=j4j_{1}=j_{4}, j2=j3j_{2}=j_{3}, j1≠j2j_{1}\neq j_{2}, and ℓ=ℓ′\ell=\ell^{\prime}, the value is Aℓ2A_{\ell}^{2}, where Aℓ≡⟨a^j​ℓ†;a^j​ℓ′⟩ρ^G​2⋆=⟨a^j​ℓ;a^j​ℓ′†⟩ρ^G​2⋆A_{\ell}\equiv\langle\hat{a}_{j\ell}^{\dagger};\hat{a}_{j\ell^{\prime}}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}}=\langle\hat{a}_{j\ell};\hat{a}_{j\ell^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}}; (3) when j1=j2=j3=j4,j_{1}=j_{2}=j_{3}=j_{4}, and ℓ=ℓ′\ell=\ell^{\prime}, the value is nℓ;0=Aℓ;02−nℓ;02n_{\ell;0}=A_{\ell;0}^{2}-n_{\ell;0}^{2}, where Aℓ;0≡⟨a^j​ℓ†;a^j​ℓ′⟩K^2⋆=(1−nℓ;0)​nℓ;0A_{\ell;0}\equiv\langle\hat{a}_{j\ell}^{\dagger};\hat{a}_{j\ell^{\prime}}\rangle_{\hat{K}_{2}^{\star}}=\sqrt{\left(1-n_{\ell;0}\right)n_{\ell;0}}; (4) when j1=j2=j3=j4j_{1}=j_{2}=j_{3}=j_{4}, and ℓ≠ℓ′\ell\neq\ell^{\prime}, the value is ⟨n^i​ℓ​n^i​ℓ′⟩ρ^G​2⋆\left\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell}\hat{n}_{i\ell^{\prime}}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}}. Combining these four cases, we have

⟨a^j1​ℓ†​a^j2​ℓ;a^j3​ℓ′†​a^j4​ℓ′⟩ρ^G​2⋆=δj1​j2​δj3​j4​nℓ;0​nℓ′;0\displaystyle\langle\hat{a}_{j_{1}\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{j_{2}\ell};\hat{a}_{j_{3}\ell^{\prime}}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{j_{4}\ell^{\prime}}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}}=\delta_{j_{1}j_{2}}\delta_{j_{3}j_{4}}n_{\ell;0}n_{\ell^{\prime};0}
+δj1​j4​δj2​j3​δℓ​ℓ′​Aℓ2+δj1​j4​δj2​j3​δj1​j3​Cℓ​ℓ′,\displaystyle+\delta_{j_{1}j_{4}}\delta_{j_{2}j_{3}}\delta_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}A_{\ell}^{2}+\delta_{j_{1}j_{4}}\delta_{j_{2}j_{3}}\delta_{j_{1}j_{3}}C_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}, (534)

where Cℓ​ℓ′C_{\ell\ell^{\prime}} is defined as

Cℓ​ℓ′={Aℓ;02−Aℓ2ℓ=ℓ′⟨n^i​ℓ​n^i​ℓ′⟩ρ^G​2⋆−nℓ;0​nℓ′;0ℓ≠ℓ′.C_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}=\begin{cases}A_{\ell;0}^{2}-A_{\ell}^{2}&\ell=\ell^{\prime}\\ \left\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell}\hat{n}_{i\ell^{\prime}}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}}-n_{\ell;0}n_{\ell^{\prime};0}&\ell\neq\ell^{\prime}\end{cases}. (535)

Therefore, the response coefficient of nk​ℓn_{k\ell} to γk′​ℓ′\gamma_{k^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}} is given as

∂⟨n^k​ℓ⟩ρ^G​2∂γk′​ℓ′|ρ^G​2=ρ^G​2∗=δℓ​ℓ′​δk​k′​Aℓ2+Cℓ​ℓ′/L,\displaystyle\frac{\partial\left\langle\hat{n}_{k\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}}}{\partial\gamma_{k^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}}}\bigg|_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}=\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{*}}=\delta_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}\delta_{kk^{\prime}}A_{\ell}^{2}+C_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}/L, (536)

which consists of two contributions: (1) the coherent contribution δℓ​ℓ′​δk​k′​Aℓ2\delta_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}\delta_{kk^{\prime}}A_{\ell}^{2}, which reflects the hopping renormalization captured in the GA, and (2) the incoherent contribution Cℓ​ℓ′/LC_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}/L, which has no contribution to the momentum density distribution given that the constraint ⟨n^i​ℓ⟩K^2=⟨n^i​ℓ⟩K^2⋆\left\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{K}_{2}}=\left\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{K}_{2}^{\star}} requires

∑kδ​γk​ℓ=0.\sum_{k}\delta\gamma_{k\ell}=0. (537)

When applying Eq. (536) with P^1→1\hat{P}_{1}\rightarrow 1 such that ρ^G​2⋆→K^2⋆\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}\rightarrow\hat{K}_{2}^{\star}, the response for the bare momentum density distribution nk​ℓ;0n_{k\ell;0} to γk′​ℓ′\gamma_{k^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}} is given by

∂⟨n^k​ℓ⟩K^2∂γk′​ℓ′|K^2=K^2∗=δℓ​ℓ′​δk​k′​Aℓ;02.\frac{\partial\left\langle\hat{n}_{k\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{K}_{2}}}{\partial\gamma_{k^{\prime}\ell^{\prime}}}\bigg|_{\hat{K}_{2}=\hat{K}_{2}^{*}}=\delta_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}\delta_{kk^{\prime}}A_{\ell;0}^{2}. (538)

The next stage is to find the relation between δ​nk​ℓ=⟨n^k​ℓ⟩ρ^G​2−⟨n^k​ℓ⟩ρ^G​2⋆\delta n_{k\ell}=\left\langle\hat{n}_{k\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}}-\left\langle\hat{n}_{k\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}} and δ​nk​ℓ;0=⟨n^k​ℓ⟩K^2−⟨n^k​ℓ⟩K^2⋆\delta n_{k\ell;0}=\left\langle\hat{n}_{k\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{K}_{2}}-\left\langle\hat{n}_{k\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{K}_{2}^{\star}}. We first compute the response of δ​nk​ℓ\delta n_{k\ell} and δ​nk​ℓ;0\delta n_{k\ell;0} for a given δ​γk​ℓ\delta\gamma_{k\ell} with the constraint given by Eq. (537), and then solve δ​γk​ℓ\delta\gamma_{k\ell} from δ​nk​ℓ;0\delta n_{k\ell;0} and express δ​nk​ℓ\delta n_{k\ell} in terms of δ​nk​ℓ;0\delta n_{k\ell;0}, given as

nk​ℓ−nℓ;0=Aℓ2Aℓ;02​(nk​ℓ;0−nℓ;0).n_{k\ell}-n_{\ell;0}=\frac{A_{\ell}^{2}}{A_{\ell;0}^{2}}\left(n_{k\ell;0}-n_{\ell;0}\right). (539)

The constraint given by Eq. (537) for δ​γk​ℓ\delta\gamma_{k\ell} naturally yields the following relation

nℓ≡1L​∑knk​ℓ=nℓ;0=1L​∑knk​ℓ;0,n_{\ell}\equiv\frac{1}{L}\sum_{k}n_{k\ell}=n_{\ell;0}=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{k}n_{k\ell;0}, (540)

which is the constraint imposed in the GA.

Finally, to connect Eq. (539) with Eq. (107), we need to show ℛℓ=Aℓ/Aℓ;0\mathcal{R}_{\ell}=A_{\ell}/A_{\ell;0}, which can be accomplished by proving that ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} and ρ^G​2⋆\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star} have the same local reduced density matrix. To prove this, we need to consider the expectation of a given Hubbard operator under ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2}, which can be accomplished by considering the linear response of a general diagonal Hubbard operator X^i​Γ\hat{X}_{i\Gamma} at site ii to γk​ℓ\gamma_{k\ell} as

∂⟨X^i​Γ⟩ρ^G​2∂γk​ℓ|ρ^G​2=ρ^G​2∗=⟨X^i​Γ;n^k​ℓ⟩ρ^G​2⋆−⟨X^i​Γ⟩ρ^G​2⋆​nℓ,\displaystyle\frac{\partial\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}}}{\partial\gamma_{k\ell}}\bigg|_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}=\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{*}}=\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma};\hat{n}_{k\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}}-\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}}n_{\ell}, (541)
⟨X^i​Γ;n^k​ℓ⟩ρ^G​2⋆=1L​∑j​j′ei​k​(j−j′)​⟨X^i​Γ;a^j​ℓ†​a^j′​ℓ⟩ρ^G​2⋆,\displaystyle\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma};\hat{n}_{k\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}}=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{jj^{\prime}}e^{ik\left(j-j^{\prime}\right)}\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma};\hat{a}_{j\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{j^{\prime}\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}}, (542)
⟨X^i​Γ;a^j​ℓ†​a^j′​ℓ⟩ρ^G​2⋆=δj​j′​⟨X^i​Γ⟩ρ^G​2⋆​nℓ+δj​j′​δi​j​CΓ​ℓ,\displaystyle\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma};\hat{a}_{j\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{j^{\prime}\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}}=\delta_{jj^{\prime}}\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}}n_{\ell}+\delta_{jj^{\prime}}\delta_{ij}C_{\Gamma\ell}, (543)
CΓ​ℓ=⟨X^i​Γ​n^i​ℓ⟩ρ^G​2⋆−⟨X^i​Γ⟩ρ^G​2⋆​nℓ,\displaystyle C_{\Gamma\ell}=\left\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}}-\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}}n_{\ell}, (544)
∂⟨X^i​Γ⟩ρ^G​2∂γk​ℓ|ρ^G​2=ρ^G​2∗=1L​CΓ​ℓ.\displaystyle\frac{\partial\left\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}}}{\partial\gamma_{k\ell}}\bigg|_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}=\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{*}}=\frac{1}{L}C_{\Gamma\ell}. (545)

Given the constraint on γk​ℓ\gamma_{k\ell} (see Eq. 537), the first order change in ⟨X^i​Γ⟩ρ^G​2\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}} is zero and therefore we have

⟨X^i​Γ⟩ρ^G​2=⟨X^i​Γ⟩ρ^G​2⋆.\left\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}}=\left\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\right\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}}. (546)

Similarly, with P^1→1\hat{P}_{1}\rightarrow 1 and ρ^G​2→K2^,\hat{\rho}_{G2}\rightarrow\hat{K_{2}},we have

⟨X^i​Γ⟩K^2=⟨X^i​Γ⟩K^2⋆.\left\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\right\rangle_{\hat{K}_{2}}=\left\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\right\rangle_{\hat{K}_{2}^{\star}}. (547)

Therefore, we have recovered Eq. (102). Moreover, we have

AℓAℓ;0=Tr​(ρ^G​2⋆​a^i​ℓ†​ρ^G​2⋆​a^i​ℓ)/Tr​(ρ^G​2⋆)Tr​(K^2⋆​a^i​ℓ†​K^2⋆​a^i​ℓ)/Tr​(K^2⋆)=ℛℓ,\frac{A_{\ell}}{A_{\ell;0}}=\frac{\text{Tr}\left(\sqrt{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}}\hat{a}_{i\ell}^{\dagger}\sqrt{\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}}\hat{a}_{i\ell}\right)/\text{Tr}\left(\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}\right)}{\text{Tr}\left(\sqrt{\hat{K}_{2}^{\star}}\hat{a}_{i\ell}^{\dagger}\sqrt{\hat{K}_{2}^{\star}}\hat{a}_{i\ell}\right)/\text{Tr}\left(\hat{K}_{2}^{\star}\right)}=\mathcal{R}_{\ell}, (548)

where we have used the fact that the local reduced density matrix of ρ^G​2⋆\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star} is same as the local reduced density matrix of ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2}, as indicated in Eq. (546), and represented as ρl​o​c\rho_{loc} in Eq. (105). Similarly, the local reduced density matrix of K^2⋆\hat{K}_{2}^{\star} is the same as the local reduced density matrix of K^2\hat{K}_{2}, as indicated in Eq. (547), and represented as ρl​o​c;0\rho_{loc;0} in Eq. (106).

In summary, we have demonstrated that the first order CPE is equivalent to the GA and the SCDA. The key steps in the proof include: (1) the local reduced density matrix for ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2} is the same as for ρ^G​2⋆\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}, with no dependency on the details of nk​ℓ;0n_{k\ell;0} except its average value and (2) the momentum density distribution nk​ℓn_{k\ell} is uniformly shrunk towards nℓn_{\ell} through 𝒵ℓ\mathcal{Z}_{\ell}, which is uniquely determined by ρ^G​2⋆\hat{\rho}_{G2}^{\star}. Finally, it would be interesting to explore the behavior of the CPE beyond first order in finite dimensions, which provides insight beyond the GA for evaluating ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2}.

C.2 The CPE for ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}

In this section, we use the first-order CPE to evaluate ρ^B​2=K^1​P^1​K^1\hat{\rho}_{B2}=\hat{K}_{1}\hat{P}_{1}\hat{K}_{1}, where P^1=exp⁡(∑i​ΓυΓ​X^i​Γ)\hat{P}_{1}=\exp\left(\sum_{i\Gamma}\upsilon_{\Gamma}\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\right) and K^1=exp⁡(∑k​ℓγk​ℓ​n^k​ℓ)\hat{K}_{1}=\exp\left(\sum_{k\ell}\gamma_{k\ell}\hat{n}_{k\ell}\right), demonstrating the equivalence to the SCDA in d=∞d=\infty. The CPE for ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2} can be viewed as a dual version of the CPE for the ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2}, which has various correspondences [16]. First, in the CPE for the ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2}, the central projector K^2\hat{K}_{2} determines the local density, and is invariant after applying the interacting projector P^1\hat{P}_{1}. Correspondingly, in the CPE for ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}, the central projector P^1\hat{P}_{1} determines the local density, and is invariant after applying K^1\hat{K}_{1}. Second, in the CPE for the ρ^G​2\hat{\rho}_{G2}, the physical momentum density distribution is linearly related to the bare momentum density distribution, and the local reduced density matrix is independent of the details of the momentum density distribution. Correspondingly, in the CPE for the ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2}, the local reduced density matrix is linearly related to the reference local reduced density matrix, and the momentum density distribution is independent of the details of the local reduced density matrix.

We proceed in evaluating ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2} via the CPE by choosing the central point for ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2} as ρ^B​2⋆=K^1​P^1⋆​K^1\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}=\hat{K}_{1}\hat{P}_{1}^{\star}\hat{K}_{1}, where P^1⋆=exp⁡(∑i​ℓγℓ⋆​n^i​ℓ)\hat{P}_{1}^{\star}=\exp\left(\sum_{i\ell}\gamma_{\ell}^{\star}\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right) and γℓ⋆\gamma_{\ell}^{\star} is chosen such that nℓ⋆≡⟨n^i​ℓ⟩P^1=⟨n^i​ℓ⟩P^1⋆n_{\ell}^{\star}\equiv\left\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{P}_{1}}=\left\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell}\right\rangle_{\hat{P}_{1}^{\star}}. We can also rewrite P^1⋆=exp⁡(∑i​ΓυΓ⋆​X^i​Γ)\hat{P}_{1}^{\star}=\exp\left(\sum_{i\Gamma}\upsilon_{\Gamma}^{\star}\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\right) by expressing n^i​ℓ\hat{n}_{i\ell} as a linear combination of Hubbard operators, where υΓ⋆=∑ℓγℓ⋆​Γ​(ℓ)\upsilon_{\Gamma}^{\star}=\sum_{\ell}\gamma_{\ell}^{\star}\Gamma(\ell). Considering the linear response of υΓ\upsilon_{\Gamma} about υΓ⋆\upsilon_{\Gamma}^{\star}, similar to Eqns. (527)-(529), we have

∂⟨O^⟩ρ^B​2∂υi​Γ|ρ^B​2=ρ^B​2∗=∂∂υi​Γ​Tr​(K^1​P^1​K1^​O^)Tr​(K^1​P^1​K1^)\displaystyle\frac{\partial\langle\hat{O}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}}}{\partial\upsilon_{i\Gamma}}\bigg|_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}=\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{*}}=\frac{\partial}{\partial\upsilon_{i\Gamma}}\frac{\text{Tr}\left(\hat{K}_{1}\hat{P}_{1}\hat{K_{1}}\hat{O}\right)}{\text{Tr}\left(\hat{K}_{1}\hat{P}_{1}\hat{K_{1}}\right)} (549)
=Tr​(K^1​P^1⋆​X^i​Γ​P^1⋆​K^1​O^)Tr​(ρ^B​2⋆)\displaystyle=\frac{\text{Tr}\left(\hat{K}_{1}\sqrt{\hat{P}_{1}^{\star}}\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\sqrt{\hat{P}_{1}^{\star}}\hat{K}_{1}\hat{O}\right)}{\text{Tr}\left(\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}\right)}
−Tr​(K^1​P^1⋆​X^i​Γ​P^1⋆​K^1)​Tr​(ρ^B​2⋆​O^)Tr​(ρ^B​2⋆)2\displaystyle-\frac{\text{Tr}\left(\hat{K}_{1}\sqrt{\hat{P}_{1}^{\star}}\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\sqrt{\hat{P}_{1}^{\star}}\hat{K}_{1}\right)\text{Tr}\left(\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}\hat{O}\right)}{\text{Tr}\left(\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}\right)^{2}} (550)
=⟨X^i​Γ;O^⟩ρ^B​2⋆−⟨X^i​Γ⟩ρ^B​2⋆​⟨O^⟩ρ^B​2⋆,\displaystyle=\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma};\hat{O}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}-\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}\langle\hat{O}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}, (551)

where we similarly utilize the fact that P^1⋆\hat{P}_{1}^{\star} commutes with K^1\hat{K}_{1} and ρ^B​2⋆=K^1​P^1⋆=P^1⋆​K^1\sqrt{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}=\hat{K}_{1}\sqrt{\hat{P}_{1}^{\star}}=\sqrt{\hat{P}_{1}^{\star}}\hat{K}_{1}. We proceed by computing the response

∂⟨X^i′​Γ′⟩ρ^B​2∂υi​Γ|ρ^B​2=ρ^B​2∗\displaystyle\frac{\partial\langle\hat{X}_{i^{\prime}\Gamma^{\prime}}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}}}{\partial\upsilon_{i\Gamma}}\bigg|_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}=\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{*}} =⟨X^i​Γ;X^i′​Γ′⟩ρ^B​2⋆\displaystyle=\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma};\hat{X}_{i^{\prime}\Gamma^{\prime}}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}
−⟨X^i​Γ⟩ρ^B​2⋆​⟨X^i′​Γ′⟩ρ^B​2⋆.\displaystyle-\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}\langle\hat{X}_{i^{\prime}\Gamma^{\prime}}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}. (552)

Directly computing Eq. (552) is cumbersome, and this can be avoided by decomposing X^i​Γ\hat{X}_{i\Gamma} into an alternate form using Eq. (3), resulting in

X^i​Γ=∏ℓX^i​Γ;ℓ=∏ℓ(Xi​Γ;ℓ⋆+δ​X^i​Γ;ℓ),\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}=\prod_{\ell}\hat{X}_{i\Gamma;\ell}=\prod_{\ell}\left(X_{i\Gamma;\ell}^{\star}+\delta\hat{X}_{i\Gamma;\ell}\right), (553)

where

Xi​Γ;ℓ⋆≡⟨X^i​Γ;ℓ⟩ρ^B​2⋆=(1−nℓ⋆)​δ0,Γ⁡(ℓ)+nℓ⋆​δ1,Γ⁡(ℓ),\displaystyle X_{i\Gamma;\ell}^{\star}\equiv\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma;\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}=\left(1-n_{\ell}^{\star}\right)\delta_{0,\Gamma\left(\ell\right)}+n_{\ell}^{\star}\delta_{1,\Gamma\left(\ell\right)}, (554)
δ​X^i​Γ;ℓ≡X^i​Γ;ℓ−Xi​Γ;ℓ⋆=(n^i​ℓ−nℓ⋆)​(δ1,Γ⁡(ℓ)−δ0,Γ⁡(ℓ)).\displaystyle\delta\hat{X}_{i\Gamma;\ell}\equiv\hat{X}_{i\Gamma;\ell}-X_{i\Gamma;\ell}^{\star}=\left(\hat{n}_{i\ell}-n_{\ell}^{\star}\right)\left(\delta_{1,\Gamma\left(\ell\right)}-\delta_{0,\Gamma\left(\ell\right)}\right). (555)

We introduce the density fluctuation operator δ​D^i​I=∏ℓ∈Iδ​n^i​ℓ\delta\hat{D}_{iI}=\prod_{\ell\in I}\delta\hat{n}_{i\ell}, where δ​n^i​ℓ=n^i​ℓ−nℓ⋆\delta\hat{n}_{i\ell}=\hat{n}_{i\ell}-n_{\ell}^{\star}, and δ​D^I=1^\delta\hat{D}_{I}=\hat{1} when I={}I=\left\{\right\}, and we use δ​D^i​I\delta\hat{D}_{iI} as a new basis for the CPE expansion. The diagonal Hubbard operator X^i​Γ\hat{X}_{i\Gamma} can be written as

X^i​Γ=∑I(∏ℓ∈I¯Xi​Γ;ℓ⋆)​(∏ℓ∈I(δ1,Γ⁡(ℓ)−δ0,Γ⁡(ℓ)))​δ​D^i​I,\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}=\sum_{I}\left(\prod_{\ell\in\bar{I}}X_{i\Gamma;\ell}^{\star}\right)\left(\prod_{\ell\in I}\left(\delta_{1,\Gamma\left(\ell\right)}-\delta_{0,\Gamma\left(\ell\right)}\right)\right)\delta\hat{D}_{iI}, (556)

where II enumerates over all subsets of {1,2,…,2​No​r​b}\left\{1,2,\dots,2N_{orb}\right\} and I¯={1,2,…,No​r​b}−I\bar{I}=\left\{1,2,\dots,N_{orb}\right\}-I . The interacting projector can be written as P^1=exp⁡(∑i​Iηi​I​δ​D^i​I)\hat{P}_{1}=\exp\left(\sum_{iI}\eta_{iI}\delta\hat{D}_{iI}\right), and at the central point ηi​{ℓ}⋆=γℓ⋆\eta_{i\left\{\ell\right\}}^{\star}=\gamma_{\ell}^{\star}, with ηi​{}⋆\eta_{i\left\{\right\}}^{\star} absorbing the constant contribution, while ηi​I⋆=0\eta_{iI}^{\star}=0 if |I|>1\left|I\right|>1. Similar to Eq. (551), for |I|>0\left|I\right|>0 we have

∂⟨O^⟩ρ^B​2∂ηi​I|ρ^B​2=ρ^B​2∗=⟨δ​D^i​I;O^⟩ρ^B​2⋆,\frac{\partial\langle\hat{O}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}}}{\partial\eta_{iI}}\bigg|_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}=\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{*}}=\langle\delta\hat{D}_{iI};\hat{O}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}, (557)

given that ⟨δ​D^i​I⟩ρ^B​2⋆=0\langle\delta\hat{D}_{iI}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}=0 in this case. It should be noted that ηi​{}\eta_{i\{\}} has no effect on the expectation values so we implicitly only consider cases with |I|>0\left|I\right|>0. The response of ⟨δ​D^i′​I′⟩ρ^B​2\langle\delta\hat{D}_{i^{\prime}I^{\prime}}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}} to ηi​I\eta_{iI} is given as

∂⟨δ​D^i′​I′⟩ρ^B​2∂ηi​I|ρ^B​2=ρ^B​2⋆=⟨δ​D^i​I;δ​D^i′​I′⟩ρ^B​2⋆.\frac{\partial\langle\delta\hat{D}_{i^{\prime}I^{\prime}}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}}}{\partial\eta_{iI}}\bigg|_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}=\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}=\langle\delta\hat{D}_{iI};\delta\hat{D}_{i^{\prime}I^{\prime}}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}. (558)

Since ρ^B​2⋆\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star} is diagonal in ℓ\ell, the correlation function on the right side of Eq. (558) is only non-zero when I=I′I=I^{\prime}, and it can be written as the product of contributions from each relevant spin-orbital as

⟨δ​D^i​I;δ​D^i′​I′⟩ρ^B​2⋆=δI​I′​∏ℓ∈I⟨δ​n^i​ℓ;δ​n^i′​ℓ⟩ρ^B​2⋆,\langle\delta\hat{D}_{iI};\delta\hat{D}_{i^{\prime}I^{\prime}}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}=\delta_{II^{\prime}}\prod_{\ell\in I}\langle\delta\hat{n}_{i\ell};\delta\hat{n}_{i^{\prime}\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}, (559)

requiring the evaluation of

⟨δ​n^i​ℓ;δ​n^i′​ℓ⟩ρ^B​2⋆=⟨n^i​ℓ;n^i′​ℓ⟩ρ^B​2⋆−(nℓ⋆)2,\langle\delta\hat{n}_{i\ell};\delta\hat{n}_{i^{\prime}\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}=\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell};\hat{n}_{i^{\prime}\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}-(n_{\ell}^{\star})^{2}, (560)

and ⟨n^i​ℓ;n^i′​ℓ⟩ρ^B​2⋆\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell};\hat{n}_{i^{\prime}\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}} can be evaluated similarly to Eq. (533) as

⟨n^j​ℓ;n^j′​ℓ⟩ρ^B​2⋆=1L2​∑k1​k2​k3​k4ei⁡(k2−k1)​j+i⁡(k4−k3)​j′\displaystyle\langle\hat{n}_{j\ell};\hat{n}_{j^{\prime}\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}=\frac{1}{L^{2}}\sum_{k_{1}k_{2}k_{3}k_{4}}e^{i\left(k_{2}-k_{1}\right)j+i\left(k_{4}-k_{3}\right)j^{\prime}}
×⟨a^k1​ℓ†​a^k2​ℓ;a^k3​ℓ†​a^k4​ℓ⟩ρ^B​2⋆.\displaystyle\times\langle\hat{a}_{k_{1}\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{k_{2}\ell};\hat{a}_{k_{3}\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{k_{4}\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}. (561)

Given that ρ^B​2⋆=⊗k​ℓρ^B​2;k​ℓ⋆\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}=\otimes_{k\ell}\hat{\rho}_{B2;k\ell}^{\star} is a direct product state in momentum space, ⟨a^k1​ℓ†​a^k2​ℓ;a^k3​ℓ†​a^k4​ℓ⟩ρ^B​2⋆\langle\hat{a}_{k_{1}\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{k_{2}\ell};\hat{a}_{k_{3}\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{k_{4}\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}} is only non-zero in the following cases. (1) k1=k2k_{1}=k_{2}, k3=k4k_{3}=k_{4}, and k1≠k4k_{1}\neq k_{4} results in nk1​ℓ⋆​nk3​ℓ⋆n_{k_{1}\ell}^{\star}n_{k_{3}\ell}^{\star}, where nk​ℓ⋆=⟨n^k​ℓ⟩ρ^B​2⋆n_{k\ell}^{\star}=\langle\hat{n}_{k\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}, (2) k1=k4k_{1}=k_{4}, k2=k3k_{2}=k_{3}, and k1≠k2k_{1}\neq k_{2} results in Ak1​ℓ​Ak2​ℓA_{k_{1}\ell}A_{k_{2}\ell}, where Ak​ℓ≡⟨a^k​ℓ†;a^k​ℓ⟩ρ^B​2⋆=⟨a^k​ℓ;a^k​ℓ†⟩ρ^B​2⋆A_{k\ell}\equiv\langle\hat{a}_{k\ell}^{\dagger};\hat{a}_{k\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}=\langle\hat{a}_{k\ell};\hat{a}_{k\ell}^{\dagger}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}} and Ak​ℓ=nk​ℓ⋆​(1−nk​ℓ⋆)A_{k\ell}=\sqrt{n_{k\ell}^{\star}\left(1-n_{k\ell}^{\star}\right)}, (3) k1=k2=k3=k4k_{1}=k_{2}=k_{3}=k_{4} results in nk​ℓ⋆=(nk​ℓ⋆)2+Ak​ℓ2n_{k\ell}^{\star}=\left(n_{k\ell}^{\star}\right)^{2}+A_{k\ell}^{2}. In summary, we have

⟨a^k1​ℓ†​a^k2​ℓ;a^k3​ℓ†​a^k4​ℓ⟩ρ^B​2⋆=δk1​k2​δk3​k4​nk1​ℓ⋆​nk3​ℓ⋆\displaystyle\langle\hat{a}_{k_{1}\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{k_{2}\ell};\hat{a}_{k_{3}\ell}^{\dagger}\hat{a}_{k_{4}\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}=\delta_{k_{1}k_{2}}\delta_{k_{3}k_{4}}n_{k_{1}\ell}^{\star}n_{k_{3}\ell}^{\star}
+δk1​k4​δk2​k3​Ak1​ℓ​Ak2​ℓ,\displaystyle+\delta_{k_{1}k_{4}}\delta_{k_{2}k_{3}}A_{k_{1}\ell}A_{k_{2}\ell}, (562)

which can be used to obtain

⟨n^j​ℓ;n^j′​ℓ⟩ρ^B​2⋆=(1L​∑knk​ℓ⋆)2+|1L​∑kei​k​(j−j′)​Ak​ℓ|2,\langle\hat{n}_{j\ell};\hat{n}_{j^{\prime}\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}=\left(\frac{1}{L}\sum_{k}n_{k\ell}^{\star}\right)^{2}+\left|\frac{1}{L}\sum_{k}e^{ik\left(j-j^{\prime}\right)}A_{k\ell}\right|^{2},

where LL is the number of sites in the lattice. A constraint is imposed on K^1\hat{K}_{1} such that

⟨n^i​ℓ⟩ρ^B​2⋆=nℓ⋆,\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}=n_{\ell}^{\star}, (563)

resulting in (1/L)​∑knk​ℓ⋆=nℓ⋆\left(1/L\right)\sum_{k}n_{k\ell}^{\star}=n_{\ell}^{\star} and

⟨δ​n^j​ℓ;δ​n^j′​ℓ⟩ρ^B​2⋆=|1L​∑kei​k​(j−j′)​Ak​ℓ|2.\langle\delta\hat{n}_{j\ell};\delta\hat{n}_{j^{\prime}\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}=\left|\frac{1}{L}\sum_{k}e^{ik\left(j-j^{\prime}\right)}A_{k\ell}\right|^{2}. (564)

In infinite dimensions, only local contributions need to be accounted for, which is used in the following steps. Considering the response δ​Di​I=⟨δ​D^i​I⟩ρ^B​2\delta D_{iI}=\langle\delta\hat{D}_{iI}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}} and δ​Di​I;0=⟨δ​D^i​I⟩P^1\delta D_{iI;0}=\langle\delta\hat{D}_{iI}\rangle_{\hat{P}_{1}} to first order in ηi​I\eta_{iI} and solving for ηi​I\eta_{iI} as a function of δ​Di​I;0\delta D_{iI;0}, the response in infinite dimensions is

δ​Di​I=(∏ℓ∈Iℱℓ)​δ​Di​I;0,\delta D_{iI}=\left(\prod_{\ell\in I}\mathcal{F}_{\ell}\right)\delta D_{iI;0}, (565)

where the renormalization factor is given by

ℱℓ≡(∑kAk​ℓ)2/(∑kAk​ℓ;0)2,\mathcal{F}_{\ell}\equiv\left(\sum_{k}A_{k\ell}\right)^{2}\bigg/\left(\sum_{k}A_{k\ell;0}\right)^{2}, (566)

where Ak​ℓ=nk​ℓ⋆​(1−nk​ℓ⋆)A_{k\ell}=\sqrt{n_{k\ell}^{\star}\left(1-n_{k\ell}^{\star}\right)} and Ak​ℓ;0=nℓ⋆​(1−nℓ⋆)A_{k\ell;0}=\sqrt{n_{\ell}^{\star}\left(1-n_{\ell}^{\star}\right)}.

Finally, we need to consider how the momentum density distribution is influenced by ηi​I\eta_{iI} using the response

∂⟨n^k​ℓ⟩ρ^B​2∂ηi​I|ρ^B​2=ρ^B​2∗=⟨δ​D^i​I;n^k​ℓ⟩ρ^B​2⋆\displaystyle\frac{\partial\langle\hat{n}_{k\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}}}{\partial\eta_{iI}}\bigg|_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}=\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{*}}=\langle\delta\hat{D}_{iI};\hat{n}_{k\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}} (567)
=∏ℓ′∈I⟨δ​n^i​ℓ′;n^k​ℓ⟩ρ^B​2⋆,\displaystyle=\prod_{\ell^{\prime}\in I}\langle\delta\hat{n}_{i\ell^{\prime}};\hat{n}_{k\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}, (568)

which is only non-zero when I={ℓ}I=\left\{\ell\right\}. To first order, ηi​{ℓ}=ηi​{ℓ}⋆\eta_{i\{\ell\}}=\eta_{i\{\ell\}}^{\star} and the contribution from ηi​I\eta_{iI} where |I|>0\left|I\right|>0 yields

nk​ℓ≡⟨n^k​ℓ⟩ρ^B​2=⟨n^k​ℓ⟩ρ^B​2⋆≡nk​ℓ⋆,n_{k\ell}\equiv\langle\hat{n}_{k\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}}=\langle\hat{n}_{k\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}\equiv n_{k\ell}^{\star}, (569)

and

nℓ≡⟨n^i​ℓ⟩ρ^B​2=⟨n^i​ℓ⟩ρ^B​2⋆=nℓ⋆.n_{\ell}\equiv\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}}=\langle\hat{n}_{i\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}^{\star}}=n_{\ell}^{\star}. (570)

In conclusion, if we write the local Hamiltonian as H^l​o​c=∑i​IEl​o​c;I​δ​D^i​I\hat{H}_{loc}=\sum_{iI}E_{loc;I}\delta\hat{D}_{iI}, the total energy per site for ρ^B​2\hat{\rho}_{B2} is given as

E=∑ℓ∫d​k​ϵk​ℓ​nk​ℓ+∑IEl​o​c;I​(∏ℓ∈Iℱℓ)​δ​Di​I;0,E=\sum_{\ell}\int dk\epsilon_{k\ell}n_{k\ell}+\sum_{I}E_{loc;I}\left(\prod_{\ell\in I}\mathcal{F}_{\ell}\right)\delta D_{iI;0},

where δ​Di​I;0=⟨δ​D^i​I⟩P^1\delta D_{iI;0}=\langle\delta\hat{D}_{iI}\rangle_{\hat{P}_{1}} with δ​Di​I;0=0\delta D_{iI;0}=0 for |I|=1\left|I\right|=1, and nk​ℓ≡⟨n^k​ℓ⟩ρ^B​2∈[0,1]n_{k\ell}\equiv\langle\hat{n}_{k\ell}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}}\in\left[0,1\right] is the physical momentum density distribution and is constrained by (1/L)​∑knk​ℓ=nℓ\left(1/L\right)\sum_{k}n_{k\ell}=n_{\ell}. The nk​ℓn_{k\ell} can be viewed as variational parameters determined from the γk​ℓ\gamma_{k\ell} within K^1\hat{K}_{1}. Combining Eq. (566) and Eq. (569), we can explicitly express ℱℓ\mathcal{F}_{\ell} as

ℱℓ=|∫d​k​nk​ℓ​(1−nk​ℓ)nℓ​(1−nℓ)|2.\mathcal{F}_{\ell}=\left|\frac{\int dk\sqrt{n_{k\ell}\left(1-n_{k\ell}\right)}}{\sqrt{n_{\ell}\left(1-n_{\ell}\right)}}\right|^{2}. (571)

To evaluate the Hamiltonian in the usual Hubbard operator representation for a given Xi​Γ;0=⟨X^i​Γ⟩P^1X_{i\Gamma;0}=\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\rangle_{\hat{P}_{1}} while respecting the density constraint, we can compute δ​Di​I;0\delta D_{iI;0} from Xi​Γ;0X_{i\Gamma;0}, and then use Eq. (565) to evaluate δ​Di​I\delta D_{iI} and then use Eq. (556) to compute Xi​Γ=⟨X^i​Γ⟩ρ^B​2.X_{i\Gamma}=\langle\hat{X}_{i\Gamma}\rangle_{\hat{\rho}_{B2}}. Finally, we remark that Eq. (565) is derived by ignoring non-local contributions, which is equivalent to taking the limit of infinite dimensions. One could straightforwardly account for non-local contributions using Eq. (564), which will be explored in the future work.
